hubs.title: Measure the real floor and locate obstacles
Give spectators a deliberate viewing plan
Build tactics around ordered captures and safe squares
Ask platform and feelings before detailed design
Design for the cleared floor, not the room size
Let audience and desired feelings set family-game pacing
Build MR horror without startle reflexes
Size a busy booth for queue flow, not maximum play
Dark, spooky or neon themes in bright daylight

nodes.title: Shooting is not in any engine: offer the sword or the dodge instead
nodes.text: Creators often ask for guns, bows or blasters. No genre can shoot: battle has a melee sword (in MR the right controller is the sword), tactics captures by moving, runner only walks. Say so kindly and offer the closest buildable thing: a battle option where enemies walk in and are struck up close, or a runner where red hazard rings are the 'shots' to dodge.

nodes.title: No inventory or collecting items: use ordered checkpoints as the 'collection'
nodes.text: Wishes like 'pick up keys', 'collect 10 gems' or 'open your bag' need an inventory that no engine has. In a runner, each checkpoint label can be the thing collected ('Find the jade key'), touched in a fixed order, and the score already rewards each one with +100. In tactics, the targets captured in order play the same role.

nodes.title: No NPC conversations: put the story on the intro card and checkpoint labels
nodes.text: Players cannot talk to characters and characters cannot answer. A 'talk to the village elder' idea becomes a still elder model beside the route plus a checkpoint label like 'Bring the lantern to the elder'. The story itself lives on the intro card (2-4 sentences) and in the order of the checkpoint labels.

nodes.title: No voice chat or in-game talking: let real voices do it
nodes.text: There is no voice chat in any mode. In MR this rarely matters: players in a shared floor session stand in the same real room and can simply talk, and spectators can call out hints. For remote friends, offer an online race with the live leaderboard instead of conversation.

nodes.title: No crafting, building or base upgrades during play
nodes.text: Crafting, building a base or combining items is not something any engine runs. Creative players can still get expression: in tactics they plan their own path to capture targets, and in a runner the route order and the race time show their skill. The creator, not the player, is the builder of the Land.

nodes.title: No joystick, teleport or flying movement in MR
nodes.text: In MR the player walks with their own legs on the real floor; there is no stick movement, teleport, jump or flight. Ideas like 'fly over the city' or 'run a 200 m track' must shrink to the real floor size. Use the void floor or tall scenery below to give the feeling of height while the player still walks a real route.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Do not design for running in MR battle or runner
nodes.text: Players in passthrough must walk, not sprint: real walls, furniture and people are near, and the battle engine is built so the player steps out of red rings rather than runs. Time limits that can only be beaten by running push players to unsafe speeds. Set time limits so a calm walk finishes with about 20-30 percent spare time.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Three options that are reskins of one idea
nodes.text: A pirate course, a jungle course and a space course with the same loop are one game in three skins, and the checks reject them. The 3 options must use 3 different genres (battle, tactics, runner) and any two must differ on at least 2 of the axes aesthetic, loop, social and route. Change the core activity first, then the look.
nodes.source: design practice; Luminate and design fixation studies, CHI 2024

nodes.title: Under 3 m on a side, battle and tactics do not fit in MR
nodes.text: When the MR space is under 3 m on its shortest side, only runner fits; battle needs room to step out of rings and tactics needs a board with walkable squares. All 3 options are then runners, so they must differ through loop, social mode, route shape and aesthetic instead of genre.

nodes.title: All options scored the same
nodes.text: Giving every option 4/4/4/4 hides the real trade-offs and gives the creator nothing to choose on. Use the whole 1-5 scale and tie each score to a brief or venue fact in scores_why, for example mr_fit 2 because a tactics board squeezed into a 3 x 3 m room makes squares only about 0.3 m wide.

nodes.title: Too many checkpoints in a small room
nodes.text: A 3 x 3 m living room has only about 1.8 m of usable side after the 0.6 m edge margin, which allows 3-4 checkpoints spaced roughly 0.8-1.2 m apart. Eight checkpoints there would sit on top of each other and players would bump the walls. Count checkpoints from the usable floor: small rooms 3-6, halls 4-8, courts 4-10.

nodes.title: Hazards on or right next to the spawn or a checkpoint
nodes.text: A red hazard circle at the start sends a player back before they have learned anything, and one touching a checkpoint makes it unfair to reach. Keep the spawn clear (about 0.8 m in small rooms, 1.2 m in halls, 1.5 m on courts) and keep a gap between each hazard edge and every stop (0.4, 0.7 or 1 m by size).

nodes.title: Dark, spooky or neon themes in bright daylight
nodes.text: Outdoor noon sun washes out glow, emissive colour and dark scenes in passthrough, so a haunted night theme in a sunny garden looks flat and grey. Outdoors by day choose bright, high-contrast themes with noon or morning lighting; keep spooky, neon and night for indoor spaces or after dark.

nodes.title: Scary content for young children
nodes.text: Children under about 8 in a headset cannot look away from a fright as easily as on a screen, and a scare can make them run into real walls. For young kids avoid ghosts that loom, sudden appearances and spooky lighting; use friendly creatures, toys, candy or farm themes with morning or default light. Keep any 'danger' cartoonish, such as puddles or sleeping dragons.
nodes.source: design practice; Yamada-Rice et al. 2017 on children and VR

nodes.title: Text-heavy HUD
nodes.text: A HUD with paragraphs, many counters or a quest log cannot be read while walking, and in MR text floating in view hides real obstacles. Keep 2-4 HUD items, short and numeric, such as timer, score and next checkpoint label; put the story on the intro card before play.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Boss fight at the start of a battle
nodes.text: The battle engine runs chapters first and the boss at the end, and players need the early chapters to learn the sword and the step-out rings. A boss in chapter 1 skips the learning and ends the arc too early. Chapter 1 is a few grunts only, the middle chapters add shields and rain, and the boss closes the game.

nodes.title: Beast enemy in the first chapter
nodes.text: The beast is big and charges, and the check rejects it in chapter 1. Early chapters should teach one thing at a time: grunts to learn striking, then shields to learn hitting from the side, then a beast once players can step aside. In MR keep each chapter at 6 enemies or fewer; on PC up to 9.

nodes.title: Tactics guards moving too fast in MR
nodes.text: In MR the player has to walk onto a real square, which takes much longer than a mouse click, so guards must move every 3 s or slower. A 1.5 s beat is fine on PC but impossible to read while walking. The first board should also have at most 2 guards.

nodes.title: Do not design an exact or impossible tactics board
nodes.text: The tactics engine builds each board from counts (piece, targets, guards, cracks, tables, beat) and proves it can be solved. The AI cannot place squares by hand, and intents like 'a trick board no one can solve' or 'trap the player' are not possible. Express difficulty with counts and piece choice instead.

nodes.title: Storyboard without a climax
nodes.text: A storyboard of 'start, walk, walk, end' shows no peak and is rejected. Panels go in play order, the first is the start, each beat is used once, and one panel is the climax: the boss, the last board with the most guards, or the final hazard run before the portal. Put the climax where spectators can see it.
nodes.source: design practice; Fullerton, Game Design Workshop

nodes.title: Key art prompt with text, logos or UI
nodes.text: The picture maker draws the key art from an English prompt, and asking for a title, score, health bar or logo produces garbled letters and a fake-looking image. Describe one moment of real play: camera, player view, what is on screen, setting, light. For MR say it is seen through a headset with the real room visible and only the floor changed. End with 'no text, logos or interface'.

nodes.title: Route crowded into one corner
nodes.text: Routes the model writes often bunch the checkpoints in one corner and leave most of the floor empty, which wastes the space and makes players collide. Spread stops across the whole area using the full width and depth, keep each pair inside the spacing range for the room size, and keep 0.6 m from every edge.

nodes.title: Giving spectators tasks inside the play area
nodes.text: Spectators cannot see the virtual floor and anyone stepping onto the play area is a collision risk for players in headsets. Never ask spectators to hold props, stand as gates or walk the route. Give them roles from outside the boundary: cheer, call out hints, watch the leaderboard on a screen, or take the next turn.
nodes.source: Reeves et al. 2005, Designing the spectator experience (CHI)

nodes.title: Sacred places and religious objects as game props
nodes.text: Thai temples, Buddha images, monks and stupas carry deep respect; using a Buddha image as a hazard, a target to capture, a boss or something to step on or strike is offensive. Temple scenery can appear as respectful background far from the action, but never as something hit, captured or trampled. Prefer folklore spirits, nature, markets or fantasy kingdoms for game action.

nodes.title: Royal symbols and real national figures in a game
nodes.text: Royal emblems, portraits of the royal family, the royal crown and similar symbols are protected by law and custom in Thailand, so they must not appear as props, prizes, enemies or jokes. A 'kingdom' theme should use an invented fantasy court with its own made-up crest and characters.

nodes.title: Recreating a named existing game, its characters or its look
nodes.text: Briefs often say 'make it like' a famous game, cartoon or film. Never recreate a named existing game, its characters, logos, levels or signature look. Take the abstract feeling the creator loves (fast dodging, cosy exploring, block-like style) and build an original world with invented names on our engine.

nodes.title: Long sessions at events with queues
nodes.text: At a booth or mall activation a 15-minute game means a queue of 40 minutes for the fifth family and headsets sitting idle during setup. Aim for 3-5 minutes of play per turn, a one-screen intro and a clear finish. Races of 2-6 players at once raise throughput if the floor is large enough.

nodes.title: Ignoring real obstacles in the space
nodes.text: A pillar, sofa, tree or table inside the floor is real and invisible to the route unless named. Ask about obstacles in the interview, write them in the brief, and route around them with at least 1.2 m clear walking width and nothing placed on them. Better still, use them: a pillar becomes the 'tree' the route circles.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Tasks that need looking up while walking
nodes.text: Players in passthrough need to see the floor and the people near them. Putting the next goal high in the sky, or asking them to read signs above head height while walking fast, causes trips and collisions. Keep labels and goals at chest height or on the floor, and put sky-high scenery only where players stand still.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Sudden scares that make players run
nodes.text: A jump scare in passthrough can send a player backwards into a wall or another person. Even in a horror event, build dread with lighting, slow-moving scenery and story, and keep the route clear so a startled step is safe. Never place a scare near the area edge.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Void floor for beginners, kids or seniors
nodes.text: The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop with scenery below. It is dramatic but can cause vertigo, freezing or anxiety, especially for first-time VR players, young kids and seniors. Use it only for adults or teens who ask for thrill, in short sessions, and offer a normal floor version.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Races and many players in small rooms
nodes.text: Under about 4 x 4 m there is room for 1-2 players only; four people walking the same small floor at once will collide. A 'race' there should be turn-based: each player walks alone and the online race leaderboard compares times. Save simultaneous races of up to 6 for floors over 10 x 10 m.

nodes.title: Asking about room size for a PC game
nodes.text: On PC there is no real room. Asking for floor size, obstacles or indoor light wastes interview turns and can leak into wrong fields. Once the creator says computer, skip the environment question and do not set venue, width_m, depth_m or indoor; spend the turns on players, feelings and session instead.

nodes.title: Asking questions whose answer changes nothing
nodes.text: Every extra question delays the creator; the interview should take 4-7 questions and never more than 9. Skip anything with a sensible default (session 5 minutes, solo play for one player, default lighting) and write the default into the brief. Ask only what would change the 3 options, like floor size or the youngest player's age. Never ask for personal data such as names, schools, phone numbers or photos; age range and group size are enough.
nodes.source: design practice; Kuhn et al. 2023 CLAM on clarifying questions

nodes.title: Time limits outside 30-3600 seconds or written in minutes
nodes.text: game.timeLimit is seconds between 30 and 3600, or null. Writing 5 (meaning minutes) gives a 5-second game and is rejected. For a calm walk set it from route length; for submission or relaxing games use null so no one is rushed.

nodes.title: Family living room 3 x 3 m: a gentle loop runner
nodes.text: Brief: 'Something for my kids (6 and 9) in our living room, about 3 x 3 m, sofa on one side.' Decisions: MR; at exactly 3 m a side all three genres are allowed, but battle and tactics are cramped (tactics squares only about 0.3 m), so runner leads and the other two score low on mr_fit with honest reasons; 1 player at a time, turn-based with the online leaderboard for sibling rivalry; feelings discovery and submission; friendly toy or candy theme with default lighting; 3-4 checkpoints on a small loop, 1-2 tiny hazards after checkpoint 2; sofa listed as obstacle and kept outside the route. If the room were under 3 m, all 3 options would be runners. Key spectator moment: the portal faces the sofa where parents sit.

nodes.title: School class in an 8 x 8 m hall: three genres for 30 students
nodes.text: Brief: 'Grade 5 class of 30, school hall about 8 x 8, one hour.' Decisions: MR, medium space, 2-4 players at once while others watch from one side; feelings challenge and fellowship. Options: a runner race of 2 lanes with 5-7 checkpoints themed as a science journey; a tactics board on the floor (squares about 0.85 m) where classmates call out hints; a battle with grunts only in early chapters. Turns of 3-4 minutes so every student plays. Key moment: the finish portal on the audience side.

nodes.title: Songkran outdoor booth at noon: bright water festival runner
nodes.text: Brief: 'งานสงกรานต์ บูธกลางแจ้ง อยากได้เกมสนุก ๆ คนต่อคิวเยอะ' (Songkran outdoor booth, lots of people queueing). Decisions: MR outdoors at noon so noon lighting and bright water, flower and festival scenery, no dark or glow themes; 5 x 5 m floor, 1-2 players; 3-minute turns, timeLimit 150 s; 5 checkpoints like 'Pour water for luck', hazards themed as slippery puddles. Avoid temple or Buddha images as props; keep it a festive street. Key moment: the last hazard dodge right in front of the queue.

nodes.title: Haunted night event for teens: slow-dread story walk
nodes.text: Brief: 'Halloween night event for high schoolers, indoor hall 10 x 12 m, they want it scary.' Decisions: MR indoors at night, spooky lighting; original folklore spirits as scenery standing beside the route; runner with 6-8 checkpoints telling a ghost story, hazards as cursed ground; dread from lighting and slow reveals, no jump scares, nothing near the walls. Battle option: enemies walk in slowly from the edges, chapter 1 grunts only. Key moment: the final portal reveal facing the audience.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Kindergarten 5 x 5 m playroom: one tiny adventure
nodes.text: Brief: 'Kids aged 4-5, a playroom, teachers help.' Decisions: MR, short 2-minute turns with headsets fitted by teachers; feelings discovery and submission; farm or friendly animal theme, morning or default lighting; runner with 4 big, clearly spaced checkpoints ('Say hi to the cow'), no hazards or only one soft one, timeLimit null. One child at a time, others sit on a mat outside the area. Key moment: each child reaches the portal near the mat and classmates clap.
nodes.source: design practice; Yamada-Rice et al. 2017 on children and VR

nodes.title: Seniors' centre: a calm garden walk with stops
nodes.text: Brief: 'Elderly group, community room 6 x 8 m, many never used VR.' Decisions: MR indoors with studio or morning light; runner with 5 checkpoints spaced 2-3 m apart on a gentle loop, no hazards or very few, timeLimit null; theme a flower garden or old market; no void floor; seated rest chairs outside the area; labels at chest height. Tactics option with a rook (straight walks) and a 3.5 s beat for those who like puzzles. Key moment: arriving at the portal beside their friends.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Gamers at a PC: battle, tactics and a speedrun runner
nodes.text: Brief: 'For gamer friends on a computer, they like hard stuff.' Decisions: PC, no venue fields; feelings challenge and expression. Options: battle with the lava theme, chapter 1 grunts, later shields, beast and rain, up to 9 enemies per chapter, then a boss; tactics with a knight first board at 2 guards and later boards at 1.5-2 s beats; a WASD runner speedrun with tight timeLimit and hazards. Scores differ: battle highest fun, tactics highest expression. Spectators are friends watching the screen and the leaderboard.

nodes.title: Museum education about dinosaurs: a timeline walk
nodes.text: Brief: 'พิพิธภัณฑ์อยากให้เด็กเรียนรู้เรื่องไดโนเสาร์' (a museum wants kids to learn about dinosaurs). Decisions: MR in a 7 x 9 m gallery space, indoor default lighting; runner with 6 checkpoints in time order ('Meet the long-neck', 'Find the egg nest'), dinosaur models beside each stop as vignettes, hazards as tar pits; 4-minute turns; story told by labels. Tactics option: the player is a bishop crossing a fossil dig. Key moment: a giant dinosaur model at the end, visible to parents behind the rope line.

nodes.title: Brand activation in a mall: original mascot world, 3-minute race
nodes.text: Brief: 'A snack brand wants a booth in the mall atrium, 8 x 10 m, lots of shoppers.' Decisions: MR indoors, neon or studio lighting; original candy-world scenery and invented characters, no copying of famous games or mascots not owned by the brand; runner race of 2-4 players, 5-6 checkpoints, timeLimit 180 s; leaderboard on a screen facing the walkway. Battle option: 3 short chapters with grunts as snack crumbs. Key moment: the finish portal facing the shoppers.

nodes.title: Fortal court 14 x 22 m: 6-player two-lane race
nodes.text: Brief: 'Race for 6 friends at the Fortal court.' Decisions: venue fortal-court, indoor steady light so neon or spooky works; runner race with 8-10 checkpoints spaced 2.5-9 m, two lanes or a long zigzag using the full 22 m, hazards between stops; live leaderboard on the wall screen; spectators along the long side. Battle option for 2-3 players in their own space; tactics board squares at 1 m. Key moment: last hazard and portal near the spectator side.

nodes.title: Rooftop at sunset: city skyline as backdrop
nodes.text: Brief: 'A rooftop bar event at sunset, open floor 6 x 6 m, adults.' Decisions: MR outdoors at evening, evening lighting; the real skyline becomes the 'edge of the world', so low scenery in front keeps the view; runner loop with 5 checkpoints and a slow pace; battle option with enemies coming in from the parapet side but stopping well inside; no void floor near real edges. Key moment: the final checkpoint faces the sunset where guests sit.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Tiny 2 x 2 m room: three different runners
nodes.text: Brief: 'I only have a 2 x 2 m space in my bedroom.' Decisions: MR, under 3 m so all 3 options are runners; usable side is tiny, so 3-4 checkpoints spaced about 0.5-1 m, hazards radius about 0.35 m or none; options differ on loop and route: a story out-and-back, a tour loop played twice, a dodge zigzag with one hazard. Solo, 2 minutes. Suggest PC for battle or tactics if the creator wants them.

nodes.title: Chess club: walk-on boards with rising pieces
nodes.text: Brief: 'Our chess club wants to be the pieces.' Decisions: MR in a 6 x 8 m room so the 6 x 8 board fits with squares about 0.8 m; tactics as the lead option: boards from rook to bishop to knight to queen, targets 2 then up to 5, first board 1-2 guards, beat 3-3.5 s; time race with leaderboard. Contrast options: a runner of 'opening moves' as checkpoints and a battle where pieces walk in. Key moment: capturing the last target while members shout move hints from the side.

nodes.title: Birthday party in a garden: treasure walk race by turns
nodes.text: Brief: 'วันเกิดลูก 8 ขวบ จัดที่สนามหญ้าบ้าน ช่วงบ่าย เพื่อน 10 คน' (8-year-old's birthday, home lawn, afternoon, 10 friends). Decisions: MR outdoors daytime, noon lighting, bright candy or pirate theme; lawn 6 x 6 m with a tree listed as an obstacle and circled by the route; runner with 5 checkpoints as 'treasure' labels, 2 hazards as sticky jam; 2 kids at a time, 3-minute turns, leaderboard. Key moment: blowing-out-candles style finish portal near the cake table.

nodes.title: Office team-building: shared floor together mode
nodes.text: Brief: 'Team-building for 12 office staff, meeting room cleared to 9 x 9 m.' Decisions: MR indoors, studio lighting; 'together' runner on a shared floor where 3-4 colleagues see each other's avatars and must all reach checkpoints, 6-7 stops; tactics option as a team relay where each person plays one board and the team's total time counts; battle option with players back to back. Real talking replaces voice chat. Key moment: the team finish with everyone watching.

nodes.title: Tourist night market in Chiang Mai: lantern walk
nodes.text: Brief: 'Booth at a Chiang Mai night market for tourists, 5 x 6 m, evening.' Decisions: MR outdoors after dark so night lighting and glowing lanterns work; original Lanna-inspired market and lantern scenery, no temple objects as props; runner of 5 checkpoints ('Light the lantern'), hazards as puddles; 3-minute turns, multilingual-friendly short labels; intro card short. Key moment: the final lantern release checkpoint facing the walkway.

nodes.title: Rainy season move indoors: a classroom swap
nodes.text: Brief: 'It was going to be outside but it rains every afternoon, now a classroom 6 x 7 m with desks pushed aside.' Decisions: MR indoors, stacked desks listed as obstacles and kept outside the area; indoor light means spooky or neon themes now become possible; runner 5-6 checkpoints with a storm or jungle theme, battle with rain rings fitting the season, tactics squares about 0.75 m. Key moment: battle rain chapter in front of the doorway where classmates watch.

nodes.title: Solo relaxation after work: slow zen walk
nodes.text: Brief: 'I just want to relax alone at home, 4 x 5 m spare room.' Decisions: MR, solo, submission and sensation; runner loop with 4-5 checkpoints like 'Breathe by the pond', no hazards, timeLimit null; ice, garden or morning lighting; tactics option with a rook and slow 3.5 s beat as a quiet puzzle; battle option clearly marked as the energetic one. 5-10 minutes. Spectators none.

nodes.title: 'Make a fun game' with no details: what to resolve first
nodes.text: Brief: 'ทำเกมสนุก ๆ ให้หน่อย' (make a fun game). Resolve in order: platform (headset or computer), who plays and how many, the top 1-3 feelings, then for MR the floor size, indoor or outdoor and spectators. With those five facts the engine choices follow: floor size sets genres and checkpoint counts, light sets lighting presets, age sets theme and hazards. Use defaults for session (5 minutes) and play mode (solo).
nodes.source: design practice; Kuhn et al. 2023 CLAM on clarifying questions

nodes.title: 'A space adventure' in a 10 x 10 m hall
nodes.text: Brief: 'Space adventure for teens, hall 10 x 10.' Decisions: MR indoor, neon or night lighting; options: runner story through 7 planet checkpoints with meteor hazards; battle on the neon theme where alien grunts walk in and the right controller is the energy sword (no blasters); tactics where the player is a queen crossing a space station board. Axes differ on loop, social and route. Key moment: the battle boss or the portal near the audience side.

nodes.title: Computer lab lesson: PC tactics as a logic lesson
nodes.text: Brief: 'Grade 8 computer lab, 40 minutes, teach logical thinking.' Decisions: PC, no venue; tactics leads: 4 boards rising from rook to knight, first board 1 guard, later beats 2-2.5 s, board stories about a logic quest; runner WASD option as a warm-up; battle option for the last 10 minutes as a reward. Class leaderboard on the projector. Students in pairs: one plays, one advises.

nodes.title: PC story fan: a short fantasy saga across three genres
nodes.text: Brief: 'I want a fantasy story game on my computer, not too hard.' Decisions: PC, narrative and fantasy; runner option as a story walk with 8 labelled checkpoints in a forest theme; battle option in forest theme with 3 short chapters (grunts, then shields, then boss) and a named original boss; tactics option with a knight crossing a castle board story by story. Easy settings: few enemies per chapter, slow beats. Storyboard climax = boss or last board.

nodes.title: Tech expo with first-time VR visitors: a 2-minute taster
nodes.text: Brief: 'At a tech expo, most visitors have never worn a headset, booth 6 x 6 m.' Decisions: MR indoors, studio lighting; runner with 4-5 checkpoints and one hazard, timeLimit null or 150 s, intro of 2 lines; battle option with only 2-3 grunts per chapter and 3 chapters; staff spotter outside the edge. Session 2-3 minutes. Key moment: the first sword strike or the finish, seen from the aisle.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Hall with two pillars: make the pillars part of the world
nodes.text: Brief: 'Community hall 12 x 12 m but there are two big pillars in the middle.' Decisions: MR; obstacles recorded in the brief; runner route as a figure-eight looping around both pillars with 1.2 m clear width, pillars themed as ancient tree trunks with scenery kept off them; battle arena on the free half; tactics board fitted to the clear side only. Key moment: the hazard dodge between the pillars where the audience looks in.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Two players at home: shared floor date night
nodes.text: Brief: 'Me and my partner, living room cleared 4 x 4 m.' Decisions: MR, 2 players together on a shared floor (they see each other's avatars and the real room), 4-5 checkpoints on a loop, gentle hazards; evening lighting indoors; battle option where they take turns and compare chapters; tactics option as a team where one walks and one advises from the sofa. 5 minutes per round.

nodes.title: Fitness-minded adults: an active battle with rain rings
nodes.text: Brief: 'Gym members want something active, studio 7 x 7 m.' Decisions: MR indoors; battle as the lead with 5 chapters building from grunts to shields to beast, rain from chapter 3, max 6 enemies each, then a boss; stepping out of rings and swinging gives real exercise without running; runner option as an interval walk with timeLimit; tactics as a cool-down puzzle. Spectators watch movements through the glass wall.

nodes.title: Thai folklore for adults: original spirits, respectful setting
nodes.text: Brief: 'ผีไทยแต่ไม่อยากให้ลบหลู่' (Thai ghosts but not disrespectful). Decisions: MR indoors at night, spooky lighting; use the catalogue's Thai ghost models as standing scenery beside a village route, with invented spirit names; temples only as distant background, never touched or stepped on; runner with 6 story checkpoints, battle where spirits walk in and are sent away with the sword. No Buddha images, monks or sacred rituals as game parts. Key moment: dawn finish at the portal.

nodes.title: Car park evening event 20 x 25 m: big race
nodes.text: Brief: 'Evening event in an empty car park, 20 x 25 m, lots of teens.' Decisions: MR outdoors after dark, night or neon lighting; large space rules: runner race for up to 6 players with 8-10 checkpoints 2.5-9 m apart in two lanes; painted lines and lamp posts noted as obstacles; leaderboard on a portable screen. Battle and tactics run in a separate fenced section. Key moment: finish portal under the main lights where the crowd stands.

nodes.title: Garden in the morning: dinosaur egg hunt walk
nodes.text: Brief: 'Saturday morning in the garden, 7 x 8 m, kids 7-10, two trees.' Decisions: MR outdoors, morning lighting, bright dinosaur and jungle scenery; trees as obstacles circled by a loop route; runner with 6 checkpoints ('Find the blue egg'), 2 hazards as mud pits; tactics option with a rook on a 'nest board'; battle option with grunts as playful raptors in 3 short chapters. 2 kids at a time.

nodes.title: Creator asks to combine two options
nodes.text: Brief follow-up: 'I like the dinosaur look of option 1 and the race of option 2.' Decisions: keep the named parts (dinosaur theme and race social mode), keep it buildable, and still return 3 different options, for example a dinosaur runner race, a dinosaur battle with a leaderboard time, and a dinosaur tactics board race. Each still uses a different genre and differs on at least 2 axes.

nodes.title: Thai ghosts / ผีไทย: set the scare level by age before picking a spirit
nodes.text: The same Thai spirit can be cute or terrifying, so pick the tone from the players first. Kids 6-9: round, big-eyed, glowing friends who are lost or hungry and need help home, morning or evening light, no gore, no faces close to the camera. Teens 13-17: eerie but not gory, spooky or night lighting, slow reveals at the side of the route, never a jump scare that makes a walking player run. Adults: folklore atmosphere and story, still no blood or organs, because the scenery is low-poly and gore reads as cheap rather than scary.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Mae Nak / แม่นาค: the loyal ghost wife, a love story first
nodes.text: Mae Nak of Phra Khanong is a tale of a wife who waits for her husband even after death, so the strongest hook is love and loyalty, not horror. The catalog has her stilt house, canal banks, rowboats, a swinging cradle, a lullaby note marker and the famous long arm reaching for a dropped lime. For kids, the route can be "Help Mae Nak find the limes before dawn" with a lullaby at each checkpoint; for teens, the long arm reaching across the canal makes a great side spectacle beside a hazard. End at dawn with the portal so the story closes gently.

nodes.title: Krasue / กระสือ: the floating glowing head, toned without gore
nodes.text: The krasue is a floating woman's head trailing glowing organs, which is too graphic as told. In low-poly, show only the head and a soft glowing ribbon trail (the catalog has green-glow, pink-coil and flying-trail versions plus a Krasue Queen boss). For kids it is a shy night-light spirit that drifts over the rice fields; for teens its trail can mark where a hazard is, and the Krasue Queen works as a battle boss name in a dark theme. Keep the trail abstract light, never organs.

nodes.title: Phi Pop / ผีปอบ: never design a "find the possessed villager" game
nodes.text: In folklore the phi pop possesses a person and eats their insides, and real villagers, often older women, have been accused of being phi pop and driven out of their homes. So a game where players accuse or hunt a villager hidden in a crowd repeats a real harm. Use the catalog's old-woman and old-man phi pop as clearly supernatural, comic-grumpy spirits who steal snacks from the kitchen, and make the player return the snacks, not punish anyone.

nodes.title: Nang Tani / นางตานี: the banana-tree lady as a gentle guide
nodes.text: Nang Tani lives in wild banana trees and is usually told as a beautiful, mostly harmless spirit in green, which makes her one of the best Thai ghosts for children and families. The catalog has the Tani banana-tree lady plus young, fruiting and tattered banana clumps, a firefly tree and glow mushrooms. Build a banana grove route where she points the way: each checkpoint is a banana clump with a soft glow, and the portal is a moonlit clearing. Evening lighting keeps faces friendly; night makes the green glow pop indoors.

nodes.title: Phi Am / ผีอำ: the sleep-pressure ghost needs care with bedrooms
nodes.text: Phi Am is the spirit that sits on a sleeper's chest, the folk name for sleep paralysis, which is a real frightening experience for many people. For teens and adults, a haunted-house interior (the catalog has teak beds with mosquito nets, wardrobes ajar, rocking chairs, dust-sheet sofas and the Phi Am shadow sitter) makes a strong spooky runner indoors at night. For kids, skip the bedroom setting and show Phi Am as a sleepy heavy shadow who just wants a pillow, placed in a garden, not over a bed.

nodes.title: Pret / เปรต: the tall hungry ghost works as a "feed them" goal
nodes.text: Pret are very tall hungry ghosts with tiny mouths from Buddhist teaching about greed, and Thai children know them from temple murals. The playful, respectful angle is generosity: the catalog has tall and hunched pret, a Pret King boss, a pret-mouth target hoop and trays of throw food (rice balls, khanom krok, sticky rice). A runner where each checkpoint "feeds" a pret turns them from scary to sad-and-helped. In battle, Pret King can be a dark-theme boss name, but the line should be "send them to rest", not mockery of the teaching.

nodes.title: Phi Ta Khon / ผีตาโขน: a joyful ghost parade, not a horror theme
nodes.text: Phi Ta Khon is a festival in Dan Sai, Loei (usually around June or July), where people wear bright masks made from rice-steaming baskets and coconut-tree bases and dance through town. It is colourful, noisy and merry, so treat it as a parade theme: the catalog has a Phi Ta Khon festival mask figure and a mask jack-o-lantern. A runner that follows a parade street with banners and dancing mask figures beside the route suits families at noon or evening light, since the colours survive daylight.

nodes.title: Phi Khamot / ผีโขมด: will-o-wisps as the kindest guide lights
nodes.text: Khamot are floating lights in the dark fields that lead travellers astray in folklore. Flip it into a guide: the catalog has orb, flame and trio wisps plus firefly clusters and fog bands. A wisp hovering above each checkpoint gives first-time VR kids a target they can see from far away without reading text. The light reads only in night or spooky lighting indoors, or evening at a dim venue.

nodes.title: In battle, Thai spirits are sent to rest, not killed
nodes.text: Thai ghost stories usually end with a spirit being calmed, given merit or let go, so slashing ghosts to death feels off to many Thai players and parents. Keep the battle engine as it is (grunts, shields, beasts, a boss) but write the chapter lines and boss intro as releasing restless spirits before dawn: "Calm the wandering spirits", "Free the Pret King". The verbs change the meaning with no change to mechanics.

nodes.title: Himmapan forest / ป่าหิมพานต์: a golden mythic sky world
nodes.text: The Himmapan is the mythical forest of Thai art, full of hybrid creatures, which gives a fantasy world that is clearly Thai without touching anything sacred. The catalog has a full set: golden gates and sky portals, floating islands with golden salas and spires, lotus platforms, naga bridges, kinnaree, golden swans, white elephants and golden-leaf trees. It suits a runner as a "journey through the sky forest" or a void-floor dramatic finale, and the gold reads in daylight, so noon and morning work outdoors.

nodes.title: Naga / พญานาค: a revered guardian, use as rails and allies, not a slain boss
nodes.text: Naga serpents guard temple stairs and rivers and are honoured as protectors, especially in the Mekong region and Isan, where many people believe in them sincerely. Use naga as bridge railings, stair rails and gates (the catalog has naga-railed bridges, naga-head newels and a sweeping naga tail) and as a friendly guide in the story. If a battle needs a water serpent foe, invent a different creature (a "river wyrm" or "mud eel") with its own look rather than defeating a naga.

nodes.title: Garuda / ครุฑ: a Himmapan bird is fine, the state emblem pose is not
nodes.text: The garuda is a great half-bird hero of Himmapan art, but in Thailand a red and gold garuda with spread wings and raised arms is the royal and state emblem, seen on official buildings and documents. A game must not use that emblem look on badges, banners, prizes or as an enemy. If a creator wants a garuda, show it as a flying creature in the sky or perched far away, in a different pose and colour scheme, and never on a crest.

nodes.title: Kinnaree / กินรี: graceful bird-maidens for gates and dance moments
nodes.text: Kinnaree are half-woman half-swan dancers of grace and beauty, known from Thai classical dance. The catalog has flying kinnaree, a circling pair, a kinnaree wing gate and a bird-maiden dancer. Use them as the gatekeepers of checkpoints (wings open as you approach) and as the sensation moment for spectators. Keep the costume graceful and covered, a cultural art form, and avoid sexualised poses.

nodes.title: Singha / สิงห์: guardian lions that frame the start and finish
nodes.text: Stone singha lions guard gateways in Thai and Lanna temples and palaces, which makes them natural markers for the start and the portal. The catalog has a stone singha guardian and a winged lion guardian statue. Place a pair either side of the spawn or the finish portal, facing outwards, 1.5 m clear of the walking line. On a tactics board story they can be the two "watchers" at the edge of a courtyard, but never pieces to capture.

nodes.title: Songkran / สงกรานต์: Thai New Year water festival, 13-15 April
nodes.text: Songkran is the Thai New Year, 13 to 15 April, the hottest time of year, known for water fights in the streets (Chiang Mai's moat is famous) and the gentle custom of pouring scented water over elders' hands for blessing. In a runner, checkpoints can be "Splash station" stops along a street with water jars, buckets, flower garlands and a moat bank, hazards as slippery puddles. Show the elder blessing as a calm vignette, not a joke. Noon and morning lighting fit the bright, sunny mood.

nodes.title: Songkran in MR: the water must stay virtual
nodes.text: Creators planning a Songkran booth sometimes want real water play next to the game. Quest 3 headsets and controllers are not waterproof, and wet floors make walking players slip. Keep all water in the virtual scene, place the booth away from street water fights, and use a covered, dry floor; suggest spectators throw cheers, not water.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Loy Krathong / ลอยกระทง: float a light on the river
nodes.text: Loy Krathong falls on the full moon of the 12th Thai lunar month, usually in November, when people float krathong (banana-trunk rafts with flowers, a candle and incense) on rivers to thank the water and let go of bad luck. It is calm and pretty, so the runner fits submission and narrative: walk a riverside route, each checkpoint lights a lantern, and the portal is the water's edge where you "float your wish". Night lighting indoors makes candles glow; the catalog has lotus lanterns, lily pads, piers and a krathong lantern.

nodes.title: Yi Peng / ยี่เป็ง: Lanna lantern night in Chiang Mai
nodes.text: Yi Peng is the Lanna festival held at the same full moon as Loy Krathong, famous in Chiang Mai for hanging lanterns (khom fai), star lanterns and sky lanterns (khom loi). A lantern trail runner is the natural fit: the route winds under Lanna hexagon and star lanterns, each checkpoint lights one, and the finale releases a sky lantern above the portal for spectators to see. Sky lanterns are now restricted for fire safety, so show them as a virtual-only moment and never suggest releasing real ones at the venue.

nodes.title: Chiang Mai Flower Festival: floats and gardens, early February
nodes.text: The Chiang Mai Flower Festival takes place on the first weekend of February with a parade of flower-covered floats and big flower displays in the park, during the cool, dry season. It makes a bright daytime theme: a garden route with giant flowers, a float parade of animal shapes, bougainvillea and marigold bushes. The catalog's garden set (giant daisy and flower-head platforms, petal pennants, bluebell lamps) works with Lanna lanterns on top. Noon or morning lighting is ideal and survives outdoors.

nodes.title: Vegetarian Festival / เทศกาลกินเจ: use the food and flags, not the piercing rites
nodes.text: The Vegetarian (Jay) Festival runs nine days in the ninth Chinese lunar month (September to October), famous in Phuket and Bangkok's Chinatown, with yellow flags marked with the red character for jay, white clothing, vegetarian food stalls and firecrackers. Some processions include self-piercing by spirit mediums, which is sacred to devotees and too graphic for a game. Use the yellow-flag street food market as the theme: stalls, lanterns and a parade street, with no piercing, blood or trance figures.

nodes.title: Bun Bang Fai / บุญบั้งไฟ: Isan rocket festival, May
nodes.text: Bun Bang Fai is held in Isan (Yasothon is the best known) in May, before the rains, when villages build and launch home-made bamboo rockets to call the rain. It suits a high-energy theme: a runner through rice fields where each checkpoint "loads a rocket", and the finale launches one over the portal. The catalog has a bamboo rocket (bang fai) launcher, buffalo carts, rice granaries and sugar palms. Some parades include rude jokes and phallic props, so leave those out for family games.

nodes.title: Chinese New Year in Thailand / ตรุษจีน: red lanterns and lion dance streets
nodes.text: Chinese New Year (January or February) is big in Bangkok's Yaowarat, in Phuket and in many Thai-Chinese homes: red lanterns, gold, red envelopes, oranges, lion and dragon dances and firecrackers. A runner down a lantern-lit market street (round Chinese paper lanterns, shophouses, fruit stalls) with the dragon or lion dancers beside the route makes a cheerful family theme. Keep ancestor altars and shrines as quiet background, not interactive props.

nodes.title: After a festival date, rename the theme instead of dropping it
nodes.text: A festival theme feels stale or wrong the day after the event, but the art is still useful. Rename it: Songkran becomes a "water splash festival", Loy Krathong and Yi Peng become a "lantern river night", Christmas becomes a "winter village" after 26 December, Halloween becomes a "ghost night" or "spirit festival" after 31 October. Keep the props, change the title, story and labels, and remove the dated wording from the intro card.

nodes.title: Thai night market / ตลาดกลางคืน: stalls, lights and a winding walk
nodes.text: A Thai night market is rows of stalls under string lights, with food smoke, music and crowds, which maps neatly onto a runner: the route winds between stall vignettes and each checkpoint is a stall to visit ("Buy the meatball skewer", "Find the lantern seller"). The catalog has market stalls, sweets stalls, cloth stalls, fruit stalls with parasols, lantern posts and paper lantern strings. Night or evening lighting gives the right glow; hazards can be spilled ice or a puddle.

nodes.title: Floating market / ตลาดน้ำ: boats, canals and fruit
nodes.text: Floating markets sell fruit, noodles and flowers from small wooden boats on canals, a classic central-Thailand image. The catalog's lotus city set has bobbing longtail fruit boats, flower boats, a sampan with a frog vendor, piers with pavilions, canal banks and mooring poles. Lay the route along the canal bank with boats drifting beside it; the canal itself can be a void-floor drop in VR, or simply water scenery in MR with a plank bridge to cross. Morning lighting fits, since markets open at dawn.

nodes.title: Rice fields / ทุ่งนา: open green paddies with village life
nodes.text: Rice paddies are the heart of rural Thailand: flat green squares, raised earth paths between them, a wooden hut, buffalo, scarecrows and a rice granary. The raised paths form a natural grid, which fits a tactics board story ("cross the paddies without waking the scarecrows") as well as a calm runner. The catalog has rice granaries, buffalo carts, haystacks, scarecrows with ngob hats, sticky-rice baskets and banana trees. Morning or noon light suits daytime farm life; at night it becomes the stage for krasue and khamot stories.

nodes.title: Doi Suthep mountain feel: mist and forest, not the temple
nodes.text: Creators in Chiang Mai often want "Doi Suthep", the mountain west of the city. Its sacred temple, golden chedi and naga staircase are a pilgrimage site, so do not recreate them as a game level. Capture the mountain feel instead: misty forest, mossy boulders, winding stone steps, viewpoint over a city of lights, cool morning air. Use fog wisps beside the route, old conifers and stepping stones, and a viewpoint portal at the top facing spectators.

nodes.title: Old city moat and walls / คูเมือง: a square city with corner bastions
nodes.text: Chiang Mai's old city is a square ringed by a moat and old brick walls with gates and corner bastions, and many Thai towns have similar old walls. This shape makes a loop route around a walled square, with each gate as a checkpoint and the corner bastions as landmarks. The catalog has brick city walls, bastions with banners, a city gate, laterite plaza tiles and lamp posts. Invent the city's name (as in "Phayakburi") rather than copying a real gate's sign.

nodes.title: Lanna style / ล้านนา: northern Thai teak, kalae and star lanterns
nodes.text: Lanna is the old northern kingdom centred on Chiang Mai, with its own look: dark teak houses on stilts, crossed kalae boards on the gable tips, tung banners (long hanging flags), hexagon and star paper lanterns, woven bamboo, sticky-rice baskets and red, gold and deep green accents. In low-poly, lean on silhouettes: steep stacked roofs, long tung banners, a lantern line. It is warm and welcoming, and tourists recognise it, so it fits both a family runner and an elegant tactics courtyard.

nodes.title: Temples: distant backdrop only, never part of the action
nodes.text: Temple scenery (chedis, halls, bell towers) can set the mood of a Thai world, but it must stay respectful. Keep any temple model at the far edge of the scene as backdrop, not on the route, not inside a battle arena, not as a tactics target or board feature, and never a hazard. Prefer ruined, generic or invented structures (a ruined bell chedi in an ancient forest) over anything that looks like a real active temple, and never build an interior with altars.

nodes.title: Spirit houses and offerings: scenery to respect, never hazards
nodes.text: Most Thai homes and shops have a spirit house (san phra phum) with daily offerings, and many players treat them seriously. The catalog has spirit houses, garlands, bai si towers, incense, fruit platters and even pig-head offerings. Place them as quiet vignettes beside the route, perhaps marking the start as "the guardian of this land", but never as hazards, things to kick, targets to capture, or score pickups.

nodes.title: Yantra, amulets and takrut: keep them invented and off the floor
nodes.text: Yantra cloths, takrut scrolls and amulets are sacred to many Thai people, who wear and bless them. The catalog includes floating yantra and takrut pickups, which are acceptable when the patterns are clearly invented fantasy runes and they float at checkpoints. Do not place them on the floor to be stepped on, do not copy a real monastery's yantra design, and do not make amulets a gacha or loot reward.

nodes.title: Thai street food stall: an errand route kids and tourists love
nodes.text: Thai street food is a shared pride and an easy hook for any visitor: noodle carts, grilled meatball skewers, khanom krok in a dimpled pan, sticky rice in a woven basket, iced drinks in plastic bags. A runner where each checkpoint is "the next order" gives a clear goal and a fun finish ("Serve the hungry ghost" or "Bring dinner home"). The catalog has charcoal stoves, woks, skewers, khanom krok, sticky rice balls and coconut carts.

nodes.title: Mango sticky rice / ข้าวเหนียวมะม่วง: a gather-the-ingredients runner
nodes.text: Mango sticky rice is sweet sticky rice with coconut milk and ripe mango, a favourite in the hot season (March to May). It gives a neat story loop for kids: four checkpoints gather the parts in order (mango tree, sticky-rice basket, coconut cart, the plate), the portal is the shared dessert table. The catalog has mango trees with fruit, sticky-rice baskets, young coconuts and toke dining trays. Noon or morning light keeps the yellow and white bright.

nodes.title: Muay Thai / มวยไทย: theme the world, the engine still swings a sword
nodes.text: Muay Thai is a national pride and a natural "battle" request, but the battle engine is a sword (PC: 3-hit combo and dash; MR: the right controller is the sword), with no punches, kicks or clinch. Offer a Muay Thai camp as the world and story (ring ropes, sandbags, tyres, training camp boards) with the sword battle, or a training-camp runner where checkpoints are drills. Treat the wai khru dance and the mongkhon headband as respected traditions shown in the intro, never as hazards or loot.

nodes.title: Krabi krabong / กระบี่กระบอง: the Thai sword art fits the battle engine
nodes.text: Krabi krabong is a traditional Thai martial art with swords, staffs and shields, shown at cultural festivals and in historical dramas. It matches the battle engine honestly: the player holds a sword, shields block from the front, and a beast charges. Write the chapters as a warrior training to defend a walled old town, use forest or desert theme for a sun-baked field, and give the boss an invented name, not a real historical king or hero.

nodes.title: Elephants / ช้าง: free and gentle, no riding, no chains, no tricks
nodes.text: Elephants are the national animal of Thailand and beloved, and elephant tourism has moved away from riding, chains and circus tricks towards sanctuaries. Show elephants walking free in a forest, bathing in a river or as the gentle white elephant of Himmapan stories (the catalog has a white-elephant fountain, an island elephant and an elephant fruit merchant). Never put players on an elephant's back, never show hooks or chains, and never make an elephant a battle enemy or hazard.

nodes.title: Isan (northeast Thailand) / อีสาน: rice, festivals and khaen music
nodes.text: Isan is the large northeastern region with strong Lao-Thai culture: rice fields and sugar palms, sticky rice in woven baskets, wooden stilt houses, buffalo, khaen pipe music, mor lam songs, the Bun Bang Fai rocket festival and Phi Ta Khon in Loei. It is warm, lively and proud. Show it as cheerful and resourceful, with the music and festivals as the energy, not as "poor countryside".

nodes.title: Southern Thailand / ภาคใต้: islands, longtail boats and old towns
nodes.text: The south is limestone islands, turquoise water, white beaches, longtail boats with ribbons on the bow, coconut palms, coral reefs and Phuket's Sino-Portuguese old town shophouses in pastel colours. It fits sunny noon runners (island hopping on plank bridges), an underwater reef world, or a pastel old-town street. The south is also home to Muslim communities, so mosques are backdrop with the same care as temples, and food scenes should not assume pork everywhere.

nodes.title: Central Thailand: river life, canals and ancient brick ruins
nodes.text: Central Thailand is the Chao Phraya river plain: stilt houses over canals, floating markets, rice, and the brick ruins of old capitals with tree roots and leaning chedis. Ruined brick and laterite walls, broken pavilions and a giant bodhi tree give an "ancient lost city" feeling that is Thai without being an active temple. Keep any Buddha head in tree roots out: it is a famous real image that is sacred, not decoration.

nodes.title: Hill communities: no costumes as decoration, no "exotic" spectacle
nodes.text: Northern Thailand is home to many highland peoples (Karen, Hmong, Akha, Lahu, Lisu and others) with their own languages, dress and beliefs. Do not use their clothing, faces or rituals as costumes, enemies, scenery "natives" or tourist spectacle, and never reference neck rings or other dress as a curiosity. If a creator wants a mountain-village feel, use terraced fields, mist, bamboo bridges and generic wooden houses; if a community wants its own story told, it should be designed with them.

nodes.title: Buddha images: never props, targets, enemies or floor decor
nodes.text: Buddha images are deeply sacred in Thailand; even tattoos or decor showing the Buddha cause offence, and placing one low or near feet is disrespectful. In FortalLand a Buddha image must never appear as scenery, a checkpoint, a hazard, a tactics target, a boss or a collectible, in any genre. If a creator asks for one, explain kindly and offer a lotus, a golden bodhi tree, a lantern or an invented guardian spirit instead.

nodes.title: Monks and novices: never enemies, jokes or hazards
nodes.text: Monks are highly respected in Thai society; women traditionally avoid touching them and people bow when meeting them. A monk or novice must not be an enemy, a comic character, a hazard, a chaser or a spectator gag. Most game stories need none; if a wise helper is wanted, use an invented hermit (ruesi-like but named and dressed as a fantasy sage), an old forest spirit or a talking animal instead.

nodes.title: Royal symbols are off-limits: build an invented fantasy court
nodes.text: Royal portraits, crowns, regalia, the royal garuda, royal flags, royal barges and the names of real kings or queens are protected by Thai law and custom and must not appear as props, prizes, characters, enemies or jokes. A "kingdom", "palace" or "prince" story should use an invented realm with its own name, crest (a lotus, a star lantern, a white elephant) and fictional characters with no resemblance to real royals, and the palace architecture should be fantasy, not a copy of a real palace.

nodes.title: Head high, feet low: place respected things above foot level
nodes.text: In Thai etiquette the head is the highest part of the body and the feet the lowest, so pointing feet at, or stepping over, respected things is rude. In MR the player's feet are the main interaction with the virtual floor: hazards and floor decals sit where people step. So never put faces of elders, spirit houses, lotus symbols, national flags or sacred patterns on floor tiles or hazards; place them as raised scenery beside the route and keep the floor to neutral ground, tiles and water.

nodes.title: Castles and knights: a generic storybook kingdom
nodes.text: A castle is the easiest theme for UK players and kids everywhere: towers, keeps, gatehouses, banners and a drawbridge. The catalog has round and octagonal towers, a castle keep, gatehouse, wall bastions, a banner hall and a throne dais. It fits all three genres: a battle defending the castle gate (forest theme), a tactics board as the castle courtyard (knight piece first, naturally), or a runner from the gatehouse to the throne. Keep crests invented and avoid any famous film castle or royal family.

nodes.title: Halloween: pumpkins, witches and friendly frights, late October
nodes.text: Halloween on 31 October is big in the UK and US and growing in Thailand: pumpkins, witches, black cats, bats, skeletons and trick-or-treat sweets. The catalog has a large party set (jack-o-lanterns, cauldrons, witch hats, bat bunting, candy bowls, sheet ghosts, cute skeletons) and a witch marsh world. For kids, keep it "spooky cute" in evening light; for teens and adults, spooky or night lighting indoors. Battle fits a dark theme with sheet-ghost chapters and a witch boss.

nodes.title: Thai events: no Halloween wording from 1 November
nodes.text: For Fortal events in Thailand the team stops using the word Halloween (ฮาโลวีน) in titles, intro cards, labels and promo from 1 November, even when the event runs on into November. The ghost content itself can stay: rename it as a "ghost night", "spirit festival", "Thai ghost party" or a Loy Krathong lantern night, and replace jack-o-lantern wording with lanterns. Check the event dates first whenever a brief has a spooky or pumpkin theme.

nodes.title: Christmas: a winter village with gifts, 1-26 December
nodes.text: Christmas fits December events in the UK and Thai malls alike: snowy pines, cabins, sleighs, gifts, lantern posts with wreaths and hot cocoa. The catalog's frost vale set has penguins, polar bears, a red sleigh, a frost elk, gift piles and glowing igloos. A runner "deliver the gifts before morning" with one gift stop per checkpoint is simple and cheerful. Keep it secular and generic: an invented gift-giver or animal helpers rather than a branded Santa design, and drop the name after 26 December.

nodes.title: Bonfire Night (UK), 5 November: fireworks, not effigies
nodes.text: Bonfire Night (Guy Fawkes Night) on 5 November is a UK tradition of bonfires and fireworks in parks on cold, dark evenings. A runner across a dark field with a virtual bonfire glow and a fireworks finale over the portal fits families. The tradition includes burning a "guy" effigy, which is uncomfortable for kids and a burning human figure is not something to put in a game; show fireworks and toffee-apple stalls instead.

nodes.title: British seaside pier: boardwalk, carnival rides and gulls
nodes.text: The British seaside pier is a long boardwalk over the sea with arcades, carousels, candy floss and fish and chips. It is a perfect out-and-back or lanes runner: walk out along the pier with ride vignettes either side, and the portal at the end over the sea. The catalog's carnival set has bulb-lit boardwalks, carousels, popcorn stands, cotton-candy carts, ticket booths and ferris wheels. Noon lighting for a sunny day, evening for the bulb lights.

nodes.title: London-like city: generic big-city icons, invented names
nodes.text: A UK city theme reads quickly with a few generic icons: a clock tower, red buses, black cabs, terraced houses, a river with bridges, rain and umbrellas. Use a clock tower and a river bridge from the catalog and keep it "a London-like city" with an invented name, so it stays original and does not need landmark permissions. A rainy evening palette with street lamps suits a runner chase through streets, and the river bridge makes a great midpoint checkpoint.

nodes.title: Ancient Egypt-inspired ruins: sand, sun and scarabs
nodes.text: Desert ruins with sandstone blocks, obelisks, scarabs and sun discs make a bright adventure theme that survives daylight outdoors. The catalog's desert set has rotating sundials, scarabs rolling sand balls, sandworms, sliding stone blocks, mosaic plazas and sun banners, and the battle engine has a desert theme with the brightest base light. Use invented gods and pharaohs; avoid mummies of real people or tomb-looting framing, and do not label mixed ancient styles as Egyptian.

nodes.title: Jungle sun-temple ruins: invent the culture, do not blend real ones
nodes.text: The catalog's sun set (stepped pyramids, glyph steles, jaguar statues, macaw perches, cenote islands) is inspired by Mesoamerican ruins. Present it as an invented jungle civilisation with its own name, not as "Aztec" or "Maya", and do not mix it with Egyptian or Thai sacred art in one world. Avoid sacrifice imagery; the hook is lost jungle discovery, so discovery feelings and a winding runner fit best, with forest lighting and green glows.

nodes.title: Norse-inspired: longhouses, frost and runes, invented
nodes.text: A Norse-inspired world uses fjords, snowy pines, longhouses, forges, dragon-headed ships and runes. The catalog's frost vale, forge and dragon sets cover it, and the battle engine's ice and lava themes suit a "frost giant" or "forge dragon" story. Use invented runes and invented gods or heroes; some real runes and symbols have been used by hate groups, so do not copy runic symbols or rune lines from real sources.

nodes.title: Japanese-inspired: torii, sakura and dojo, generic and respectful
nodes.text: The catalog's ninja set has torii arches, pagoda islands, sakura trees, stone toro lanterns, koi ponds, red bridges, taiko pads and a moon-gate portal, which makes a calm or action theme. Torii and shrines are religious sites in Japan, so use torii as the gate of an invented world, not a real shrine, and never as a hazard. Avoid stereotyped accents, the rising-sun flag and recreating a famous ninja anime's headbands or villages.

nodes.title: Dinosaurs and museums: discovery with a roar
nodes.text: Dinosaurs are loved by kids in every country and work for museums, schools and malls. The library has dinosaur island creatures and jungle scenery (tree ferns, ginkgo, monkey-puzzle trees, cliffs). A museum client usually wants learning: a runner where each checkpoint is a dinosaur with a one-line fact, finishing at a big skeleton or nest. In battle, a dinosaur can be the beast, but for young kids keep dinosaurs as giants to watch, not chasers.

nodes.title: Space: stations, planets and warp portals
nodes.text: Space reads instantly at any age and suits neon or night lighting indoors. The catalog's space set has neon gantries, glass tube bridges, docking plazas, ringed planets, hologram arrows, UFO beams and a neon warp portal. Runner: a mission across a station with system checks as checkpoints; battle: neon theme with robot grunts; void floor: a walk across space for confident teens. Invent agencies, ships and aliens, and avoid real space agency logos.

nodes.title: Pirates: treasure islands and harbour towns, kid-friendly
nodes.text: Pirates suit kids and families: ships, docks, treasure chests, parrots, cannons and colonial harbour towns. The catalog has a deep pirate collection (ships, docks, fort walls, harbour towns by day and night, octopus tentacles, rocking decks). A treasure-map runner where each checkpoint is a map clue is a classic; tactics can be a ship deck board. Keep it comic adventure, invent the captain, and avoid famous film pirate looks.

nodes.title: Toy room: giant toys at shrink-ray scale
nodes.text: A toy world makes the player tiny among giant toys: spinning tops, jack-in-the-boxes, toy trains, dominoes, building-block bridges and a music-box carousel are all in the catalog. It is bright and safe for young kids and works in daylight. A tactics board as a giant chessboard on a bedroom floor is a natural fit. Keep toys generic: no famous brick, doll or figure brands.

nodes.title: Candy land: sweets, cakes and gummies
nodes.text: Candy worlds are joyful and readable for under-10s: lollipops, gummy bears, donuts, cakes, cookie stepping stones and candy-cane lamps are in the catalog. They fit birthday parties and family malls. Hazards can be sticky jam puddles; battle can be the neon or forest theme with gummy grunts. Keep the colours saturated but use red only for hazards, and avoid branded sweets.

nodes.title: Ice and frost: crystal palaces and auroras
nodes.text: Ice worlds are calm, clean and cool: ice palaces, crystal spires, frozen ponds, aurora ribbons and snowy pines. The battle engine has an ice theme for a frost-beast story, and the frost vale set brings friendly animals. Ice is a great escape theme in hot Thai months (March to May) and a natural Christmas-to-February theme in the UK. Pale blues wash out at noon outdoors, so prefer indoor or evening.

nodes.title: Music world: piano bridges and drum stages
nodes.text: A music world turns instruments into the set: piano-key bridges, guitar fretboard decks, giant snare-drum plazas, metronome arms and golden-note save stands. It suits concerts, schools and festivals, and can carry Thai flavour by adding a khaen or ranat-shaped stage prop in the story. Neon lighting gives a concert feel indoors. Avoid famous band names and song titles.

nodes.title: Farm: barns, tractors and friendly animals
nodes.text: A farm is gentle and familiar in both the UK (barns, tractors, hay bales) and Thailand (rice, buffalo, chickens). The catalog's farm set has windmills, hay bales, scarecrows, tractors, sprinklers, pecking hens and patchwork-field platforms. A morning runner "wake up the farm" is great for kindergartens and seniors, with very soft hazards. Keep animals as friends, not enemies.

nodes.title: Jungle: vines, waterfalls and hidden ruins
nodes.text: The jungle works across cultures and covers both Thai forests and adventure stories: banyan trees, bamboo, ferns, vine curtains, river stones, rock arches and waterfalls. The battle engine has a forest theme (greens and warm torchlight) for a friendly adventure. Combine with gentle wildlife (birds, monkeys) and keep elephants as calm scenery. A discovery runner with hidden vignettes behind vines suits explorers.

nodes.title: Underwater reef: coral, jellyfish and sunken ships
nodes.text: An underwater reef is magical and calming: coral arches, kelp, jellyfish lifts, giant clams, pufferfish, sunken-ship decks and a whirlpool portal are in the reef set. It fits southern Thailand stories and ocean-awareness themes for schools ("clean the reef" checkpoints). Night lighting makes glowing kelp and jellyfish shine indoors. Avoid drowning or shark-attack framing for young players.

nodes.title: Robots and factories: neon battles and conveyor runs
nodes.text: Robots are the best enemy theme for kids who should not fight "living" things: hitting a robot feels harmless. The battle engine's neon theme fits a robot factory; the robot set adds robot arms, stamping presses, conveyors, laser gates, drones and robot dogs. In a runner, a factory with sweeping lasers as hazards and "reboot the core" checkpoints gives a clear tech story. Invent the robots; avoid famous film robots.

nodes.title: Superheroes: invent the hero, never a comic-book IP
nodes.text: Kids often ask for a specific famous superhero. Explain kindly that FortalLand only makes original heroes, and offer an invented hero with a power that the engine shows well: a storm hammer, an arc shield or a nova gauntlet (all in the catalog's hero-tech set). Let the creator name the hero and pick its colours, so it feels theirs. Avoid any costume, symbol or name pattern that copies the big comic universes.

nodes.title: Thai festival calendar: which themes fit which month
nodes.text: January to February: Chinese New Year and the Chiang Mai Flower Festival (first weekend of February), in the cool season; March to May: hot season, Songkran (13-15 April), mango sticky rice and Bun Bang Fai rockets in May. June to July: Phi Ta Khon in Loei; September to October: Vegetarian Festival, rainy season (go indoors) and Halloween up to 31 October. November: Loy Krathong and Yi Peng at the full moon of the 12th lunar month, with no Halloween wording; December: Christmas in malls and the New Year countdown. Lunar festivals move every year, so check the exact dates.

nodes.title: UK calendar and daylight: which themes fit which month
nodes.text: UK seasons shape both theme and light. Winter (December to February) gets dark around 16:00, so night themes work even outdoors in late afternoon; Christmas fits 1-26 December. Spring (March to May) suits gardens and Easter-style egg hunts (keep it secular). Summer (June to August) stays light until about 21:00, so dark themes outdoors fail; seaside and festivals fit. Autumn: harvest, Halloween (31 October) and Bonfire Night (5 November).

nodes.title: Thai seasons decide indoor or outdoor play
nodes.text: Thailand has a hot season (March to May, often above 35 C), a rainy season (June to October, sudden heavy storms) and a cool, dry season (November to February), the best time for outdoor events. In the north, February to April also brings smoke haze from field burning, so outdoor play in Chiang Mai can be unhealthy then. Headsets overheat in direct sun. Use outdoor themes from November to February and plan indoor venues for the rest.

nodes.title: Themes that make good battle enemies
nodes.text: The battle engine needs foes the player is happy to hit: robots (neon), lava or forge creatures (lava), frost beasts (ice), restless spirits sent to rest (dark), mummies or sand beasts (desert), goblin-like forest critters (forest). Map grunts to small foes, shields to armoured foes and the beast to the big one: robot drones, shield bots and a mech; imps, armoured golems and a lava beast. Avoid real animals people love, real peoples, monks or sacred beings as enemies.

nodes.title: Themes that suit a tactics board
nodes.text: A 6 x 8 tactics board needs a setting where a grid feels natural: a castle courtyard with stone tiles, a marble palace plaza, a rice-paddy field of earth paths, a market of stall rows, a floating market canal grid, a toy-room floor, a ship deck. Guards become castle sentries, scarecrows, market watchmen or toy soldiers; tables become stalls or haystacks. Keep sacred places off the board: a Lanna-style pavilion courtyard is fine, a temple courtyard is not.

nodes.title: Themes that suit a runner route
nodes.text: Runner themes need a path that makes sense to walk: a lantern trail, a market street, a parade, a canal bank, a pier, a mountain path, a castle tour, a treasure map. Choose a theme whose checkpoints can be named in a sequence (stall 1 to 5, gate to throne, recipe steps). Lantern trails and markets suit night; parades, piers and farms suit noon; ghost villages suit spooky.

nodes.title: Inspired-by is fine, recreating a named IP is not
nodes.text: Creators often say "like" a famous game, film or cartoon. Being inspired by a feeling, a genre or a public-domain myth is fine; copying a named game, film, character, logo, level, costume or distinctive look is not. Thai folklore spirits, Greek myth and Himmapan creatures are traditional and free to use, but a specific film's version of them (its costume, scenes or title) is owned. Always ask what the creator loves about the reference and build that feeling in an original world.

nodes.title: Make an original twist in three moves
nodes.text: To turn a reference into something original: (1) change the who: a different species, age or role (a gecko knight instead of a famous hero), (2) change the where: move it into a Thai or invented setting (a ninja story in a Lanna rice valley), (3) change the why: a new goal (bring the lanterns home, not save the princess). Combining two unrelated themes, such as Himmapan plus space or pirates plus floating market, often gives a fresh world the library still covers.

nodes.title: No real people: celebrities, influencers, politicians or royals
nodes.text: Creators sometimes want a famous singer, footballer, YouTuber or politician in their game. Using a real person's face, name or likeness needs their permission and can be defamatory or illegal (and royals are fully off-limits in Thailand). Offer an invented character with a similar vibe (a "rock star cat", a "football robot") and let the creator design it.

nodes.title: Each battle enemy kind asks the player a different question
nodes.text: The battle engine has exactly three enemy kinds. A grunt (3 health, fast) asks "can you swing in time?", a shield (5 health, blocks hits from the front) asks "can you get to its side?", and a beast (14 health, charges with a red ring at your feet, hits for 2) asks "can you read the warning and move?". Design each chapter around which question it asks, not around a body count.

nodes.title: Chapter one is grunts only, and never a beast
nodes.text: The checker rejects a beast in chapter 1, and for good reason: the first chapter is where the player learns that a swing hits and a red ring hurts. Use 2 to 3 grunts and no rain. On PC this is a short warm-up; in MR it gives a first-time headset player time to find the controller-sword before anything charges.

nodes.title: Add one new thing per battle chapter
nodes.text: A clear ramp introduces one new element per chapter: first grunts, then shields, then the first beast, then rain, then a mix. When two new things arrive together the player cannot tell what hurt them. The last chapter before the boss is the only place where everything mixes.

nodes.title: Pick the battle chapter count from the session length
nodes.text: The engine takes 3 to 6 chapters and then adds the boss fight on its own. As a planning estimate, a chapter takes about 40 to 90 seconds and the boss 1.5 to 3 minutes, with a short pause between chapters. So 3 chapters fit a 3-5 minute event slot, 4-5 chapters fit 6-8 minutes, and 6 chapters suit 10 minutes or more for keen players. Confirm the real times in a playtest.

nodes.title: In MR a battle chapter holds at most 6 enemies
nodes.text: In MR the player stands in a real room, so the checker allows at most 6 enemies in a chapter (PC allows 9). Enemies also walk at about 60 percent of their PC speed in MR. Treat 4 as a normal MR chapter and 6 as the climax; more bodies around a real person feels crowded and makes rings hard to escape in a small room.

nodes.title: On PC a battle chapter holds at most 9 enemies, and 9 is a peak
nodes.text: A PC chapter may list up to 3 foe entries, each with 1 to 6 of one kind, with a total of at most 9. Nine is a showpiece for the last chapter before the boss, when the player has learned all three kinds. A typical PC ramp is 3, 5, 3 (with the first beast), 5 with rain, then 7-9.

nodes.title: Rain is a pressure chapter: fewer, weaker enemies under falling rings
nodes.text: When a chapter has rain, warning rings keep dropping around the player (roughly one per second) for as long as enemies are alive. That already makes the chapter hard, so pair rain with 3 to 4 grunts and no beast. Use rain once in a short game and at most twice in a long one; it reads as a story moment (a storm, a curse, falling rocks, meteors).

nodes.title: Rain in MR makes real people step often: size the room for it
nodes.text: In MR there is no dash: the player escapes a ring by stepping out of it with their own feet. Rain chapters therefore mean many quick steps. In a 3 x 3 m room or with first-time headset players, either skip rain or use it once with at most 3 grunts. In 5 x 5 m or larger it works well and looks great to spectators.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: The boss is one fixed fight: you choose only its name and intro line
nodes.text: Every battle ends with the same boss behaviour: a large crowned warrior that slams red rings at the player, calls 2 grunts every few seconds, and gets faster with extra rings once below half health. The design only sets boss.name and boss.intro. Make the name and intro pay off the story the chapters told ("The Frost Warden wakes. Break the ice crown.").

nodes.title: When the creator asks for a special boss, offer name, intro and theme
nodes.text: Creators often ask for "a giant dragon boss" or "a robot boss with lasers". The battle engine has one boss model and one behaviour. Say so kindly and offer what does change: the boss name, its intro line, the theme colours around it, and the story the chapters build toward it. A lava theme plus "The Ember Tyrant" carries much of the dragon feeling.

nodes.title: Chapter titles and lines tell the story in order
nodes.text: Each chapter has a title and one line shown when it starts. Read in order, the titles should form a story: arrive, meet resistance, face the beast, survive the storm, break in, face the boss. Keep each line one sentence, present tense, with the place and the threat ("The gate falls. Everything inside comes for you.").

nodes.title: Let each chapter line carry the hint for its new enemy
nodes.text: The line is the only text a player reads at the start of a chapter, so it doubles as the tutorial. For shields say to hit from the side, for a beast say to watch its red ring and strike after it charges, for rain say to keep moving. Players then learn the counter inside the story instead of from a rules screen.
nodes.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

nodes.title: Battle themes and the mood each one carries
nodes.text: The battle engine has six themes. dark is purple night and torches for gothic dread; ice is cold blues, calm and clean, for frost or winter stories; lava is red and orange danger for a volcano or forge. forest is greens and warm torchlight for friendly adventure; neon is magenta and cyan for an arcade or cyber party; desert is warm sand with the brightest base light, for ancient ruins or sun.

nodes.title: In MR pick the battle theme by the real light
nodes.text: In MR only the floor and the enemies are drawn; the real room stays visible. In a bright hall or daylight, dark and neon look washed out, while desert and ice (the lightest themes) stay readable. In a dim hall or after dark, neon, lava and dark glow and feel dramatic. Red rings must stay readable on the floor in every case.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: A battle ramp for kids: short, grunt-heavy, one beast late
nodes.text: For ages about 6 to 11 use 3 or 4 chapters: grunts, then shields with grunts, then one beast with 1-2 grunts, then an easy final mix. Use rain at most once and keep totals at 3-5. The player has 10 health and heals 2 after each chapter, so a gentle ramp lets most kids reach the boss, which is the moment they talk about afterwards.

nodes.title: A battle ramp for gamers: 5-6 chapters with combined threats
nodes.text: Gamers want the combinations: shields that block while a beast charges, rain over a grunt pack. Use 5 or 6 chapters, two rain chapters, and a final chapter at the cap (9 on PC, 6 in MR). The end score adds a bonus for finishing fast and for health left, so tell them that speed and clean play raise the score.
