nodes.title: MR battle needs at least 3 x 3 m of empty floor
nodes.text: The arena is fitted to the room minus about 0.5 m on each side, so a 3 x 3 m floor gives a 2 m fighting area: enough for grunts and shields, tight for a beast charge (its warning ring is about 2.8 m across). From 4 x 4 m a beast is comfortable; 5 x 5 m is the template default. Under 3 m on a side the checker only allows runner options.

nodes.title: MR battle: the controller is the sword and the feet only step
nodes.text: In MR the right controller holds the sword and a fast swing attacks; the player stands and steps, with no dash and no running. Enemies walk in slowly from the edges, and every threat is a red ring the player steps out of. Write rules and pitches around "swing and step": it is safe, and it is what spectators enjoy watching.

nodes.title: PC battle: 3-hit combo and a dash are the whole move set
nodes.text: On PC the player moves with WASD, aims with the mouse, swings a 3-hit sword combo (the third hit deals double damage and reaches further) and dashes with Space or right click, which briefly dodges attacks. That is the full kit. Good PC chapters are about using the dash to leave a red ring and the third hit to finish a shield or beast.

nodes.title: Battle has no items, no co-op and no second weapon
nodes.text: Creators often add upgrades, potions, a partner hero or a bow to a fight concept. The battle engine is one player, one sword, three enemy kinds, rain rings, one boss, health that refills by 2 after a chapter, and a score. Offer the closest real things: the heal between chapters as "rest at the campfire", score as bragging rights, spectators as the cheering party.

nodes.title: Battle score rules to write into the game card
nodes.text: Score comes from kills (grunt 50, shield 80, beast 400), 200 for each cleared chapter, and on a win a bonus for speed and for health left. Write two rules from this: "Clear a chapter to heal 2 and gain 200" and "Finish fast with health left for a higher score". It gives friends taking turns something to compare.

nodes.title: MR battle spectators watch a real sword fight with no visible enemies
nodes.text: People beside an MR battle see a person swinging, turning and stepping out of invisible rings. That is funny and dramatic, so give them a place outside the floor edge with at least 1 m extra for the swinging arm, and let them cheer each "Chapter cleared". The boss is the loudest moment; spectators can cheer the boss health going down if a screen mirrors the game.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: The shield chapter is the battle game's little puzzle
nodes.text: Shields block hits from the front, so the player must get to their side. In MR this means stepping around a slow enemy, which feels clever and is easy to read. Use 2 to 3 shields with 1 to 2 grunts as distraction; more than 4 shields becomes a wall that frustrates new players.

nodes.title: Budget the player's 10 health across the run
nodes.text: The player has 10 health, regains 2 after each chapter, and beast and boss hits cost 2 while grunt hits and rain cost 1. Many beasts or long rain chapters drain health before the boss, which ends runs at the wrong moment. Aim for a run where an average player arrives at the boss with about half health.

nodes.title: Example battle plan: forest rescue for a family day (MR, 4 x 4 m)
nodes.text: Theme forest; chapter 1 "Goblins at the gate": 3 grunts; chapter 2 "The bark shields": 2 shields, 1 grunt, line "Step around them, hit their side". Chapter 3 "The mud boar": 1 beast, 1 grunt, line "Watch the ring, step out, strike"; chapter 4 "Acorn storm": 3 grunts with rain. Boss "The Thorn King", intro "He has the fox cub. Win it back." Every MR chapter stays at 4 or fewer.

nodes.title: Each tactics piece teaches a different way of seeing the board
nodes.text: The knight jumps in an L over anything, so it teaches seeing hidden two-step paths. The bishop slides on diagonals and can only ever reach one colour, so it teaches routing around. The rook runs straight lines that tables stop, so it teaches lanes. The queen moves any way, so the board becomes a test of reading danger rather than finding a path.

nodes.title: A good tactics piece order: simple reading first, queen last
nodes.text: The rook is the easiest piece to read (straight lines) and suits board 1 for kids and newcomers; the knight suits board 1 for puzzle lovers because its jump is a fun surprise. Put the bishop in the middle and the queen on the last board or two, where freedom meets the most guards. The build task asks for the pieces to vary.

nodes.title: Give bishop boards fewer targets
nodes.text: A bishop zig-zags to reach anything, so each target costs more moves and more beats under guard pressure. Code still makes the board solvable, but 5 or 6 targets with a bishop feels slow. Use 3 to 4 targets on bishop boards and spend the extra difficulty on guards instead.

nodes.title: Pick the tactics board count from the session length
nodes.text: The engine takes 3 to 6 boards. As a planning estimate a board takes about 45 seconds to 2 minutes on PC and longer in MR, where every move is a walk and guards wait at least 3 seconds. So 3 boards fit 3-5 minutes, 4-5 boards fit 6-10 minutes, and 6 boards suit a long session for puzzle fans. Confirm in a playtest.

nodes.title: Guards ramp from at most 2 on board 1 to at most 4
nodes.text: Each board has 0 to 4 guards, and the checker rejects more than 2 on the first board. Guards are the main difficulty knob because their attacked squares change every beat. A typical ramp is 1, 2, 2, 3, 4; for kids 0 or 1 guard on board 1 lets them learn how the piece moves before anything moves back.

nodes.title: You choose how many guards, not which pieces they are
nodes.text: Code picks each guard's kind (rook, bishop or knight in rotation) and its patrol path when it builds the board. So a board story should not promise "two knights guard the vault" or "a rook patrols the hall". Describe guards by role in the story ("the night watch", "palace guards") and let the engine decide their moves.

nodes.title: Set the guard beat by who plays
nodes.text: The beat is the seconds between guard moves (1.5 to 3.5). Slower is easier: there is time to look at the red and orange squares and plan. For kids or first-time players use 3 to 3.5 s throughout; casual adults on PC 2.5 to 3 s; puzzle fans on PC can end at 1.8 to 2 s. Shorten the beat by about 0.2 to 0.3 s per board at most.

nodes.title: In MR guards move every 3 s or slower, so ramp with other knobs
nodes.text: Players walk the board in MR, so the engine never lets guards move faster than every 3 s, whatever the plan says. In MR use beats of 3 to 3.5 s and make later boards harder with more guards, more cracked squares and more targets instead of a faster beat. A plan that relies on a 2 s beat for its climax will feel flat in a headset.

nodes.title: MR board squares are fitted to the floor, up to 1 m
nodes.text: The 6 x 8 board is scaled to the room: each square is the smaller of 1 m, width / 6 and depth / 8, and never below 0.5 m. A 6 x 8 m floor gives 1 m squares; 4.5 x 6 m gives 0.75 m; 3 x 4 m gives 0.5 m, where it is hard to stand clearly on one square. The player moves by standing on a legal square for about a third of a second.

nodes.title: MR tactics: walk, never jump, and keep the board edge clear
nodes.text: A queen or rook move can cross the whole board, which in a 6 x 8 m room is several metres of walking in a headset. With a guard beat ticking, players may hurry. Tell them in the rules to walk, keep 0.6 m clear beyond the board edge, keep spectators off the board, and remember that after a hit the player walks back to the start ring.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Tactics is a race on time with a leaderboard
nodes.text: The run timer counts every board, each hit adds 5 seconds, and the player has 3 hearts. The leaderboard ranks by boards cleared, then by time, and asks for the next player's name, so it suits events where people take turns. Pitch it as "fastest clean run wins" and suggest showing the leaderboard on a screen for the queue.

nodes.title: Wrap each tactics board in one story line
nodes.text: Every board has a one-line story, and the run reads as a plot when the lines connect: sneak in, cross the hall, reach the vault, face the king. Common wraps that fit the mechanics: a heist (targets are treasures, guards are watchmen), a rescue (targets are keys taken in order), a ghost hunt (targets are spirits to catch). The rules stay chess; only the words change.

nodes.title: Tables come with seated characters: use them for indoor stories
nodes.text: Each table blocks a square (sometimes two side by side) and has cartoon characters sitting at it who cheer when you capture. That suits stories set in a cafe, library, classroom, banquet or night market. Tables also block a rook or bishop guard's line, so they make safe shadows on the board.

nodes.title: Cracked squares are fixed traps that hurt when you land
nodes.text: A cracked square costs a heart when the player lands on it; it never moves. Use 0 to 1 on early boards and 3 to 4 later, and give them a story name: thin ice, lava cracks, broken tiles, cursed stones. Because they are static, cracks reward planning rather than timing, which balances boards where guards already add timing pressure.

nodes.title: Targets set the length of a board more than its difficulty
nodes.text: Each board has 2 to 6 targets captured in number order. More targets mean more moves and more beats, so a longer board, but not much harder if guards are few. Use 3 targets early, 4 to 5 in the middle and up to 6 late, and keep target counts lower in MR where every move is a walk.

nodes.title: The king is the last target on the final board only
nodes.text: Setting king: true makes the last target of that board a king. Use it on the final board as the story climax ("Take his guards, then take him"), with the other targets as his court. A king earlier in the run spends the climax too soon, and a run without a king needs another strong final line.

nodes.title: Escalate the target piece to show rising stakes
nodes.text: target_piece sets how targets look: pawn, knight, bishop or rook. Targets do not move or fight back; the change is visual and narrative. Escalate across boards (pawns, then knights, then bishops, then rooks guarding the king) so players feel they are climbing toward the court.

nodes.title: The AI chooses numbers; code places the board and proves it solvable
nodes.text: For tactics the design gives each board a piece, a story line and counts (targets, guards, tables, cracks, beat, king). Code places everything and checks that every board can be solved. So never promise exact square positions, hand-made puzzle layouts or a specific trick in a prototype; promise the experience and the ramp.

nodes.title: Tactics teaches itself through floor colours
nodes.text: Green rings show where you can move, orange numbered pieces are targets in order, red squares are attacked now, and light orange squares will be attacked after the next guard move. Board 1 should have few guards so players learn these colours. In rules, name the colours rather than chess terms, which helps kids and people who never played chess.

nodes.title: Turn one or two tactics knobs per board, not all five
nodes.text: A tactics board has five knobs: beat, guards, cracks, tables and targets. Guards and beat change difficulty most, cracks add planning, tables can make it easier (shelter) or harder (blocked lines), and targets change length. Changing one or two per board makes the ramp readable; changing all at once makes a spike.
nodes.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

nodes.title: Tactics is not two-player chess: offer the time race instead
nodes.text: Creators often imagine players playing chess against each other or against a computer opponent. In this engine one player is a piece, guards follow patrols on a beat, and targets wait to be taken. Offer turns on the same boards with the leaderboard (fastest clean run), or friends calling hints from the side.

nodes.title: Tactics spectators become the hint crowd
nodes.text: In MR people beside the floor see a player stepping square to square and stopping to think. They cannot see the board, but with a screen mirroring the game or after watching a few runs they love to shout hints. Put the spectators along the long side, show the leaderboard there, and present it as a calm, social puzzle rather than an action game.

nodes.title: Tactics serves challenge, discovery and expression, not sensation
nodes.text: Tactics is slow and readable: the pleasure is finding a path (discovery), planning your own route (expression) and beating the clock (challenge). It is the best pick in a brief that mentions thinking, chess, puzzles, school or calm competition. It is the weakest pick for "wow", fast action or pure relaxation, so score fun honestly when the brief is sensation-led.

nodes.title: Example tactics plan: library heist for kids (MR, 5 x 7 m)
nodes.text: Board 1: rook, "Sneak past the reading tables", 3 targets, 1 guard, 2 tables, 0 cracks, beat 3.5, target pawn. Board 2: knight, "Hop over the book piles", 3 targets, 1 guard, 2 tables, 1 crack, beat 3.5, target pawn. Board 3: bishop, "Slip along the diagonals", 3 targets, 2 guards, 1 crack, beat 3.2, target knight. Board 4: queen, "Take the Librarian King's keys", 4 targets, 3 guards, 2 cracks, beat 3.0, king true, target bishop.

nodes.title: Loop routes: the safe default for small and medium rooms
nodes.text: A loop walks around the space and ends near the spawn, so the finish portal is where the queue and spectators already are. It uses the whole floor without crossing itself, which keeps the 1.2 m walking corridor simple. Use it for rooms under 4 x 4 m and as the default in 4 to 10 m spaces.

nodes.title: Zig-zag routes fill long rectangular rooms
nodes.text: A zig-zag goes back and forth across the short side while moving down the long one, so every leg is about the room width. It suits classrooms, halls and courts, and gives natural spots for hazards in the middle of each leg. Keep turns at the ends at least 0.6 m from the walls.

nodes.title: Spiral routes build to a climax at the centre
nodes.text: A spiral walks inward ring by ring, so the story naturally heads "to the heart" of something: the temple shrine, the dragon nest, the eye of the storm. Put the last checkpoint and the portal at the centre. It needs a fairly square space of about 5 x 5 m or more; in smaller rooms the inner turns get too tight.

nodes.title: Two-lane routes suit big spaces and side-by-side play
nodes.text: Two parallel lanes let two players walk the length of a large space at the same time and stay apart, which is clear for spectators along the long side. It needs over 10 x 10 m (for example the 14 x 22 m Fortal court). Keep at least 1.2 m clear for each lane plus a gap between them.

nodes.title: Hub-and-spoke routes: a central camp with trips outward
nodes.text: A hub route returns to a centre between trips to the edges, like a village square with paths to the well, the forest and the temple. Checkpoints still go in order, so alternate: spoke, hub, spoke. It fits discovery and story briefs in medium and large square spaces, and a big hero model beside the hub anchors the whole Land.

nodes.title: Out-and-back routes fit narrow spaces and corridors
nodes.text: Out-and-back walks to the far end and returns, so it suits a long narrow garden path, a corridor or a strip of a car park. The turnaround is the story climax (the summit, the treasure), and the return leg can bring new hazards. Offset the return 1.2 m or more from the outward leg where the width allows, so walkers do not meet face to face.

nodes.title: Write checkpoint labels as short verb-first story beats
nodes.text: Each checkpoint has a short label that tells the story. Write 2 to 4 words, verb first, saying what happens there: "Feed the dragon", "Light the lantern", "Wake the guardian". A label tells the player why they are walking, which turns a course into a story without any new mechanic.

nodes.title: Arrange checkpoint labels as a five-step story arc
nodes.text: With 5 to 7 checkpoints, a simple arc reads well: setup (arrive), two rising steps, a twist (something goes wrong), the climax, then the portal as the way home. Example: "Enter the temple", "Light the first candle", "Cross the spirit bridge", "The ghost awakes", "Return the bell", then the portal. Place the scenery for each step beside its checkpoint.
nodes.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

nodes.title: Checkpoint count and spacing follow the room size
nodes.text: Small spaces (under 4 x 4 m) use 4 to 5 checkpoints 1.2 to 4 m apart, and a very small room (about 2 x 3 m) only 3 to 4. Medium spaces (4 to 10 m) use 5 to 7, 1.8 to 6 m apart. Large spaces (over 10 m) use up to 10, 2.5 to 9 m apart. The layout checker enforces ranges like these, so plan within them.

nodes.title: Put hazards mid-leg, visible from the previous stop
nodes.text: Hazards are red circles on the route between stops (about 0.45 m radius in small rooms, 0.6 m medium, 0.8 m large) and must keep a gap from every checkpoint (0.4, 0.7 and 1 m). Place them in the middle of a leg so the player sees one coming after touching a checkpoint and steps around it. Give each a story name like "spirit puddle" or "lava crack".

nodes.title: Use hazards sparingly for kids, more for gamers
nodes.text: A hazard sends the player back to the last checkpoint and costs 25 points, so it doubles a leg. For kids, families and seniors use 0 to 2 hazards on short legs. For teens and gamers use about one per leg on later legs. Avoid hazards right before the portal on long legs: being sent back at the finish feels unfair.

nodes.title: Set a runner time limit from route length and walking speed
nodes.text: The time limit is optional. Estimate the route length and divide by a walking speed: about 0.5 m/s for first-time headset users, kids or seniors, and about 1 m/s for confident players, then add 50 percent for reading labels and stepping around hazards. For young kids and relaxed tours skip the time limit; the finish time bonus already rewards speed.

nodes.title: Runner online modes: race for rivals, shared floor for togetherness
nodes.text: In a race everyone walks their own copy of the Land with a live leaderboard, which suits friends and teens who want to compete. On a shared floor players see each other's avatars, which suits families and groups who want to walk the story together. Pick from the brief's play_mode and feelings: challenge points to race, fellowship to together.

nodes.title: A race in one room puts real bodies on the same route
nodes.text: Every racer walks the same route, so in one real room racers can walk into each other. Keep same-room races to large spaces (over 10 x 10 m) with a few players and staggered starts; or race across turns or different rooms, with the leaderboard comparing them. Under 4 x 4 m, do not race at all.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Void floor is dramatic but dizzying: use it with care
nodes.text: The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop with scenery below. It is a strong sensation moment for confident adults indoors, but it can make first-time headset users, kids and seniors freeze or feel unwell. Use it only with a slow walk, no time limit, no race, and say clearly at the start that the floor is solid.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Pick the runner lighting preset from the real light
nodes.text: Presets are noon, morning, evening, night, spooky, neon, studio and default. Outdoors in daylight use noon or morning, because glow and dark themes wash out. Indoors with steady light, studio or evening keep colours readable. Spooky, neon and night work best in a dark hall or after dark.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Pick a runner theme the scenery library really covers
nodes.text: The runner dresses the route with 1,900+ low-poly models: Thai ghosts and temples, fantasy worlds, dinosaurs, pirates, toys, sci-fi, candy, ice, music, farm and animated rides. Choose a theme the library covers well and say it plainly in the layout brief ("Thai temple at night with lanterns"). Decor can be marked VR only so it is hidden in MR.

nodes.title: Dress the runner as vignettes beside a clear corridor
nodes.text: Players walk the straight lines between stops, and nothing may stand within a 1.2 m corridor plus half the object's size. So scenery is grouped into small scenes beside the route (a dragon nest, a lantern stall), each tied to the checkpoint label next to it. Big pieces go to the edges and corners, small props line the route.

nodes.title: Place the portal where spectators can see the finish
nodes.text: The finish portal comes after the last checkpoint, and the finish is the moment spectators cheer. Put it on the side where people watch, with the last leg facing them. Keep the spawn clear (about 0.8 m in small rooms, 1.2 m medium, 1.5 m large) so players start without bumping into scenery.

nodes.title: Runner score rules to write into the game card
nodes.text: Score is fixed: each checkpoint +100, each hazard step -25, and the finish +300 plus a time bonus. Write the rules from this ("Touch the stones in order", "Red circles send you back", "Reach the portal fast for a bonus") and keep game.rules to 3 to 5 short lines. Do not add stars, coins or combos the engine does not count.

nodes.title: Runner has no enemies: turn a chase wish into hazards and a clock
nodes.text: When a creator wants monsters chasing players in a walking course, the runner cannot move enemies. Offer the closest real things: hazards named as the monster's traps, a time limit framed as "before the ghost wakes", spooky lighting and still scenery beside the route. If real enemies matter, propose the battle genre as another option.

nodes.title: Runner has no pickups: collecting is checkpoints in order
nodes.text: Creators often say "collect 5 gems". The runner has no inventory or free pickups, but checkpoints touched in order can be the collection: label them "Take the red gem", "Take the blue gem", and show the gems as scenery at each stop. Say plainly that they are collected in a set order.

nodes.title: Route the runner around real obstacles in the room
nodes.text: In MR the real floor is the play area, so pillars, tables or trees inside it must stay outside the walking route. Plan the route shape around them (a loop around a pillar, a zig-zag between two trees), keep 0.6 m clear of them and of the edge, and never place checkpoints or hazards against them. Mention each obstacle and its position in the layout brief.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Under 3 x 3 m in MR, all three options are runners
nodes.text: Battle and tactics need at least 3 x 3 m, so a smaller MR room gets three runner options. Each still has to differ on at least 2 of the 4 axes: vary the route (loop vs out-and-back), the loop type (story vs dodge vs tour) and the social mode. Use 3 to 5 checkpoints, small props, and no race.

nodes.title: PC runner: WASD walking, no room limits, same rules
nodes.text: On PC the runner is played with WASD, with no real room. Skip venue and size questions and use the large-space ranges freely (up to 10 checkpoints). The void floor carries far less risk on a screen, so it can be the sensation hook here, and race or shared floor work the same online.

nodes.title: A calm runner tour for seniors, young kids or relaxing briefs
nodes.text: For submission and relaxed feelings, make the runner a guided walk: no hazards or one gentle one, no time limit, morning or studio lighting, wide spacing, and labels that point at beautiful scenery ("Greet the elephants", "Ring the temple bell"). It is often the most comfortable first headset experience.

nodes.title: Give each genre the part of the brief it serves best
nodes.text: The 3 options must use 3 different genres, so let each show its strength: battle for sensation, fantasy and action challenge; tactics for thinking, planning and calm competition; runner for story, discovery and relaxed walking. Keep the same world from the brief in all three and change the verb: fight it, outwit it, explore it.

nodes.title: One brief, three genres: "Thai temple spirits" for a school group
nodes.text: Battle: "Guardian of the Temple", forest theme, 4 chapters of spirit grunts and shield-bearers, boss named "The Rain Naga". Tactics: "Temple Steps", 4 boards where the player is a rook, then knight, bishop and queen, taking candles in order past the night watch. Runner: "Lantern Night", a 6-checkpoint loop through Thai temple scenery with labels from "Light the gate lantern" to "Ring the great bell".

nodes.title: Stretch a genre with story and theme, never with new mechanics
nodes.text: What can change freely: titles, chapter and board lines, checkpoint labels, boss name and intro, theme, lighting and scenery. What cannot: the verbs. A battle cannot add shooting, a tactics board cannot add doors or keys that unlock, a runner cannot add enemies. Map each wish to the nearest real feature, say so in the option, and name the gap in risks.

nodes.title: Common wishes and the real feature that answers each
nodes.text: Shooting or magic: battle sword swings with a fiery theme; monsters to avoid: runner hazards or battle red rings; a treasure hunt or collecting: runner checkpoints or tactics targets, always in a set order. Sneaking: tactics guards and their red squares; things falling from the sky: battle rain. A giant final enemy: the battle boss with a custom name. Racing friends: runner race or the tactics leaderboard.

nodes.title: Score mr_fit by how each genre uses this floor
nodes.text: The same room fits the genres differently. A 3 x 3 m room is fine for a runner loop, tight for battle (about a 2 m fighting area) and poor for tactics (0.5 m squares). A 6 x 8 m hall fits tactics best (1 m squares) and battle well. Over 10 m the runner shines with long routes and races. Let these facts move the scores so the 3 options do not all score the same.

nodes.title: One game is one genre: do not merge battle, tactics and runner
nodes.text: Creators sometimes ask for "a walking course with sword fights, then a chess puzzle". Each genre is its own engine, so one game cannot switch between them. Offer a combination inside one genre (a battle whose chapter lines tell the journey, a runner whose labels pose riddles), or suggest a series of separate games that share one story world.

nodes.title: On PC every genre fits, so pick by feeling and player skill
nodes.text: With no room limits on PC, all three genres always fit. Battle shines for gamers and action (combo and dash), tactics for puzzle fans and classrooms (click to move, beats down to 1.5 s), runner for story and casual explorers (WASD). Choose the recommended option by the brief feelings and how used to games the players are.

nodes.title: Knight boards: the jump over tables is the joy
nodes.text: A knight moves in an L (two squares one way, one square across) and jumps over tables, guards and targets in between. Board 1 or 2 with a knight and 2 to 4 tables lets players discover that tables do not stop them, which feels like a secret. In MR one knight move is a walk of about 2.2 squares, roughly 1.1 to 2.2 m, so it stays short and safe.

nodes.title: Bishop boards: diagonal walking and one colour only
nodes.text: A bishop slides diagonally and stays on one square colour for the whole board, so half the board is unreachable. Code still places targets it can reach. In MR every diagonal square is about 1.4 times the walk of a straight square, so long bishop slides cross the room on a slant; tell players to look where they will stop before walking.

nodes.title: Rook boards: straight lines that tables cut short
nodes.text: A rook slides any distance in a straight line and stops before a table or piece. That is the easiest movement to read, so a rook with 0 to 1 guards and 1 to 2 tables makes a good first board. In MR a full rook slide can be up to 7 squares, so remind players they may stop on any green ring along the line.

nodes.title: Queen boards: many green rings, so the danger is reading
nodes.text: The queen combines rook and bishop moves, so the board shows many green rings at once. The challenge moves from "can I get there?" to "which of these squares is safe after the next beat?". Use the queen on the last one or two boards with 3 to 4 guards and 2 to 4 cracks; on PC the beat can drop to about 2 s here.

nodes.title: Teach players to check the next-move warning before stepping
nodes.text: A player loses a heart by landing on a red (attacked) square, by standing on an attacked square when guards move, or when a guard lands on them. The light orange squares show what will be attacked after the next guard move. So the winning habit is: pick a green ring that is neither red nor light orange, then move. Put this habit into the board 1 story line or a rule.

nodes.title: Tactics solo: frame the run as beating your own best time
nodes.text: The leaderboard is kept on the device that runs the game and shows the best finished time. At an event this becomes a shared ranking as people take turns on one device; at home it is a personal best to beat. Pitch solo play as a time attack ("beat your best clean run") and do not promise an online or worldwide ranking.

nodes.title: Tactics ramp templates for 3, 4 and 6 boards
nodes.text: Three boards (MR events): rook 3 targets 1 guard 1 table 0 cracks beat 3.5; knight 3 targets 2 guards 2 tables 1 crack beat 3.5; queen 4 targets 3 guards 1 table 2 cracks beat 3.0, king true. Four boards (PC casual): rook 3/1/2/0 beat 3.0; knight 3/2/2/1 beat 2.8; bishop 4/2/1/2 beat 2.6; queen 4/3/2/3 beat 2.4, king true. Six boards (PC puzzle fans): knight 3/1, bishop 4/2, rook 4/2, knight 5/3, queen 5/3, queen 5/4 with king, beats from 2.8 down to 1.8 and cracks rising 0 to 4. Numbers are targets/guards/tables/cracks.

nodes.title: Set a board's mood with the ratio of tables to cracks
nodes.text: You choose how many tables and cracks a board has, not where they go. Many tables and few cracks make a sheltered, busy room (a cafe, a library) where tables block guard lines. Few tables and many cracks make an open, dangerous field (a frozen lake, a lava floor). Match the ratio to the story line of that board.

nodes.title: Battle chapter templates for 3 and 4 chapters (PC)
nodes.text: Three chapters: grunt 3; shield 2 + grunt 2; beast 1 + grunt 3; then the boss. Four chapters: grunt 3; shield 3 + grunt 2; beast 1 + grunt 2; grunt 4 with rain; then the boss. Both stay well under the PC cap of 9 and introduce one new thing per chapter.

nodes.title: Battle chapter templates for 5 and 6 chapters (PC)
nodes.text: Five chapters: grunt 3; shield 3 + grunt 2; beast 1 + grunt 2; grunt 4 with rain; shield 2 + grunt 4 + beast 1. Six chapters: grunt 3; shield 3 + grunt 2; beast 1 + grunt 3; grunt 5 with rain; beast 2 + shield 2; shield 3 + grunt 4 + beast 2 (the full 9). Use six only for keen players and 10+ minute sessions.

nodes.title: Battle chapter templates for MR (cap of 6)
nodes.text: Three chapters: grunt 2; shield 2 + grunt 1; beast 1 + grunt 2. Four chapters: grunt 3; shield 2 + grunt 2; beast 1 + grunt 2; grunt 3 with rain. Five chapters: add shield 2 + grunt 3 + beast 1 as the final mix (exactly 6). For six chapters insert beast 1 + shield 2 + grunt 1 before the final mix, and only in rooms of 5 x 5 m or more.

nodes.title: Name the enemy kinds to fit the theme (the models stay the same)
nodes.text: The theme changes the arena colours and light, but enemies keep the same look in every theme: bony warriors with glowing eyes, a shield-bearer, and a big beast. So rename them in chapter titles and lines with names that suit bones. dark: skeleton scouts, the shield wall, the war beast, cursed rain; ice: frost dead, ice-shield knights, the snow beast, hail; lava: ash soldiers, obsidian shields, the magma beast, falling embers. forest: bramble bones, bark shields, the mud boar, acorn storm; desert: tomb guards, sun shields, the sand beast, sandstorm; neon: glitch skeletons, firewall shields, the data beast, code rain.

nodes.title: Hazard gate: two circles with a clear gap between them
nodes.text: Place two hazards side by side across a leg with a clear gap of at least 1 m between their edges, so the player walks through the middle like a gate. Frame it with a walkThrough arch or two posts beside the route and name it in the story ("the spirit gate"). It suits medium and large spaces; in small rooms one hazard is enough.

nodes.title: Hazard slalom: alternate circles along one long leg
nodes.text: On a leg of about 5 m or more, place 2 or 3 hazards alternately a little left and right of the straight line so the player weaves between them. It reads as a river of stepping stones or a field of lava cracks. Use it once per route, on the longest leg, and only for teens, adults and gamers; it is too fiddly for small kids in a headset.

nodes.title: Zig-zag pinch: a hazard on the inside of a turn
nodes.text: On a zig-zag route, place one hazard on the inside of a turn, mid-way between two checkpoints, so players who cut the corner step in it and players who walk wide pass. It rewards looking ahead without adding a new rule. Keep the wide path at least 0.6 m from the edge of the area, and use it in medium or large rooms only.

nodes.title: Escalate a ten minute challenge in clear phases
nodes.text: For a roughly 10 minute challenge, escalate in three readable phases: baseline from 0:00 to 3:30, about 30% stronger from 3:31 to 7:00, and about 50% stronger from 7:01 to 10:00. Existing units keep the stats they had when summoned, so later upgrades do not retroactively change them, and their level stays visible. The transferable lesson is to make escalation predictable and legible, whether through battle chapters or a runner route that becomes denser with hazards.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Make the climax require coordinated preparation
nodes.text: Make a spectacular finale something players earn through coordinated movement, not a single button press. In the source, an 80 mana Meteor Shower creates impact zones that a Vanguard must run over to lock the target before a wide area strike and visual transformation. Adapt the reasoning within the engine as a final sequence of ordered checkpoints before the portal, so preparation creates anticipation and the finish feels collectively earned.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Balance powerful effects with cost and counterplay
nodes.text: Pair powerful tactical effects with meaningful cost, limits, and a chance for opponents to respond. The source prices area turrets at 40 mana, an invisible stunning mine at 20 mana with a 5 second cooldown, and temporary 15 second power boosts at 50 to 60 mana. Hidden area damage plus stun can feel unfair, so in this engine prefer the visible red hazard circles and reserve dramatic moments for clearly signposted checkpoints or the portal finish.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Use a limited comeback window, not a permanent catch-up buff
nodes.text: Trigger a comeback state only when a team is in clear crisis, such as holding under 20% of the field, and end it after recovery above 25%. A strong but bounded example doubles resource regeneration from 5 to 10 per second and permits only 2 activations, giving the losing side one counterattack opportunity without erasing the leader's advantage. Make the state and its remaining uses legible so players know they must plan the counterattack rather than rely on rescue.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Build accessibility by removing systems, not only shortening rounds
nodes.text: For a fast casual mode, use a fixed 5-minute round with the winner decided only when time expires. Remove carrying, decks, mana management and armor exceptions, then give each role one immediate verb and cooldown-only skills; a frequently usable support action can have a 10-second cooldown. Add automatic pressure at a steady interval, such as every 10 seconds, so play continues even when participants do not coordinate.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Redirect territory-shooter requests to supported contests
nodes.text: Do not promise painting territory, guns, instant kills, unit summons or team territory control, because none of these engines supports them. For competition, offer an online runner race on separate copies with a live leaderboard, ordered checkpoints worth 100 each and a finish worth 300 plus a time bonus. For direct action, offer battle chapters using sword combos, dodging and a boss, and treat territory or faction war as theme and story rather than a simulated mechanic.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Let one moving frontline carry the contest
nodes.text: For a tug-of-war contest, have opposing forces seek the nearest rival and stop where they meet, so the clash itself draws a clear border instead of making players read several meters. Reward victories by advancing that border, and maintain free baseline pressure: the source releases 3 soldiers every 15 seconds without Mana. When adapting this to another engine, preserve the single readable struggle and steady rhythm rather than copying unsupported minions.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Use a slow, contested boss to break stalemates
nodes.text: Reserve a boss for the middle or late game, and gate it behind visible preparation: a full charge, delivery to a marked summon point, then a Commander resource and skill check. Make the resulting threat slow, highly visible and hard to interrupt so the opposing team has time to respond; in the source, reaching the back line repaints 90% of the field, but killing the boss awards substantial territory instead. The design lesson is a dramatic finale with counterplay and a meaningful reversal, not an automatic win button.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Make teamwork a short cross-role power window
nodes.text: Express synergy as an explicit sequence in which one role creates an opening and another exploits a temporary empowerment, rather than as a passive bonus. The source uses a 10-second window for an enlarged Vanguard to paint trails again and a 15-second window for a Striker's shots to paint the floor directly. Clearly signal activation and expiry, and give the pair an immediate shared target so the short window produces a memorable coordinated push.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Redirect shooter and territory-control wishes by their desired experience
nodes.text: A request for a VR team shooter or territory-control battle often includes rifles, revives, mana cards and floor painting, none of which this engine supports. Say that plainly, then preserve the underlying wish: battle provides sword action, dodging and staged enemies; tactics provides spatial control through ordered captures and guarded squares; an online runner race provides group competition with a live leaderboard. When presenting three options, use these as three genuinely different genres rather than three versions of the unavailable shooter.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Build combat beats around a visible opening and a quick payoff
nodes.text: A setup-and-payoff beat makes action feel cooperative and intentional: one event creates a clearly marked opening, and a quick physical response converts it into a strong result. The source uses a flashing floor marker lasting 2 to 3 seconds, a useful starting window to playtest for notice-and-respond actions. In this engine, recreate the rhythm within supported battle play through warning rings, a short dodge or reposition, then a sword response, rather than adding stuns or role abilities.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Make cooperation a visible two-step handoff
nodes.text: Build team combos so one role creates an opportunity and another completes it, rather than asking everyone to act at once. Here, damage adds a Stun Marker and a floor light tells the Vanguard where to step, while another combo grants 15 seconds of enhanced attacks. Use a conspicuous world-space cue, a clear completion action, and an immediate result so teammates can coordinate without a tutorial.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Let planning resources recover during deliberation
nodes.text: A strategic player should not become helpless while thinking: this economy generates 5 Mana per second up to a 100 cap, reaching full from empty in 20 seconds. Discarding an unwanted card refunds 15 Mana, giving players an emergency conversion from bad options into tempo. Pair steady regeneration with a capped reserve and a costly refund so recovery is possible but still requires a decision.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Guarantee a basic action inside a varied hand
nodes.text: Keep one inexpensive, dependable card permanently available, redraw it after use with only a 1-second cooldown, and add variety through nine rotation cards drawn four at a time. The example basic unit costs 5 Mana, only one second of passive income, so a bad random hand cannot remove the player's ability to participate. This structure separates reliability from variety and makes each draw easier to read.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Express unit jobs through a readable cost ladder
nodes.text: Give each unit a distinct tactical job and make its cost communicate commitment: 5 Mana for disposable lane filler, 10 for a fast raider, 20 for a self-destruct attacker, and 30 for a large territory-capturing unit. At 5 Mana per second, those costs imply roughly 1, 2, 4, and 6 seconds of saving, creating an understandable tempo ladder. Also distinguish battlefield consequences, such as whether a destroyed unit paints the floor, so players can predict the strategic effect before spending.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Build a five minute battle toward a boss climax
nodes.text: For a short action session, use a three-part arc: minutes 0:00 to 2:00 establish the core fight with simple enemies, minutes 2:00 to 4:00 raise pressure and introduce the boss confrontation, and minutes 4:00 to 5:00 become a decisive final rush. Give the ending a clear resolution rather than letting intensity simply stop. In this engine, express the arc through successive battle chapters, enemy mixes such as grunts, shields and beasts, then the boss, with rain reserved for added late pressure.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Redirect hero-skill territory control wishes
nodes.text: Requests for summoned minions, turret drops, meteor attacks, boss armies, shooting weak points, or painting territory cannot be built by these engines, even when they fit a MOBA fantasy. Offer battle for close action with a sword, dash, telegraphed danger rings, chapters and a boss, or tactics for territorial-feeling play through ordered captures, guard patterns and route planning on a 6 x 8 board. In MR, preserve real walking and safety rather than simulating a battlefield with running players.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Open with a short, spectacular movement burst
nodes.text: For a timed area-control game, make the first 3 seconds unusually generous: every crossed row changes colour, creating instant visible progress before normal play begins. A midpoint race can add a capped bonus of 1 to 3 extra rows, scaled by the arrival-time gap, but this rewards an early lead and can snowball. Keep the opening easy to understand and treat the bonus as a dramatic kickoff, not the deciding mechanic.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Make specialist roles depend on one another
nodes.text: A 3v3, 10-minute match can divide expertise across physical area control and blocking, precision ranged play, and planning or unit management. The important pattern is interdependence, not three separate minigames: the commander can only deploy the ultimate boss after the vanguard physically places a summon box. Give the team's biggest moment a visible handoff between roles so every specialist contributes to it.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Translate territory-control wishes into supported competition
nodes.text: If a creator asks for 3v3 territory control, ranged shooting, deployable turrets, or summonable units, explain that these mechanics are not available rather than reskinning them as promises. Preserve the underlying wish with a choice: timed tactics boards for planning and ordered captures, battle chapters for direct physical action, or an online runner race with a live leaderboard for group competition. Ask whether strategy, combat fantasy, or head-to-head rivalry matters most before choosing.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Make the boss a costly gamble, not a free power spike
nodes.text: Gate a climax behind a substantial resource cost, such as the source's 90 mana, and make a failed skill check consume the attempt rather than merely delay a button press. Give the boss very high durability and very slow movement so its threat is readable, then balance its huge upside with a severe, visible penalty if it dies and make a second summon unlikely. In this engine, keep only the pacing lesson: build a chapter-end boss as a slow, readable, high-stakes finale, without promising mana, summoning, territory painting or stun systems.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Converge a climactic clash on one shared objective
nodes.text: When two major threats meet, turning their collision into a distinct duel phase concentrates attention instead of splitting it across the whole field. Give everyone the same immediate objective, focus the opposing threat, and use a bounded winner reward such as the source's 20% health recovery while the loser suffers the established defeat penalty. For FortalLand, reuse only the focus and phase-change lesson in a solo boss chapter: briefly change existing boss behavior and give the player one obvious priority using sword hits, dashes, warning rings and available enemies.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Turn defense into readable vulnerabilities, not invisible math
nodes.text: Defense becomes actionable when play can change it: the source uses repeated weak-point critical hits to break armor, after which every friendly damage source benefits, and distinguishes ordinary units from structures. Keep defense classes few and visibly different, and clearly explain any zero-damage result when attack is equal to or below armor. In this engine, express the lesson through existing behaviors, such as a shield blocking frontal hits and a beast telegraphing its charge, rather than adding armor statistics, critical hits, plasma weapons or structures.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground: MR 3v3 territory control GDD v1.0

nodes.title: Translate MOBA territory skills into supported objectives
nodes.text: A request for painting team territory, summoning a 5 x 5 cannon turret on a 20-second cooldown, or clearing a 10 x 10 area with a meteor on a 30-second cooldown cannot be built directly. Preserve the intended push-and-defend tension with battle chapters containing grunts, shields and beasts, ending in a boss, or with tactics boards that require ordered target captures while avoiding guards. For a contest over progress rather than combat, use a runner race with ordered checkpoints and a live leaderboard.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground casual mode GDD, example 2 (course material)

nodes.title: Telegraph floor hazards before resolving them
nodes.text: For a grid-based survival challenge, flash threatened tiles orange for 3 seconds, then turn lava tiles red and safe tiles green so players can read the state at a glance. In the PC proof of concept, a 10 x 20 grid, a circle for the player, WASD movement and 5 HP were enough to test the loop. Awarding 10 points for avoiding lava and subtracting 10 for being hit makes every round immediately legible; tune the warning time before adding visual complexity.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

nodes.title: Prove competitive body-controlled Snake with simple PC inputs
nodes.text: A two-player Snake concept can be tested before building its LED-floor controls: mark P1 and P2 standing positions in the simulation, map P1 to WASD and P2 to the arrow keys, and show both snakes on a simulated projector screen. Eating food lengthens a snake, while hitting its own head-to-body path or another player's tail kills it, creating direct competition through shared space. This cheap setup tests whether steering, growth and collision rules are understandable and fun before investing in physical tracking.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

nodes.title: Use a fail-safe casual round for walk-in groups
nodes.text: For children, families and mixed-skill friends, teach the rules within 30 seconds and target rounds of 2 to 5 minutes. Adjust difficulty to the group, make fun more important than ranking, and let mistakes cost points rather than end the run. Confirm every success or error with immediate, distinct colour, sound or animation feedback.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

nodes.title: Split private MR action from public information
nodes.text: Keep the player's attention on physical movement, while placing shared goals, time, scores and results on a wall screen that is visible from every angle. Treat the headset view as a private layer that bystanders cannot see, so spectators need public information plus readable player reactions to follow the game. This supports the useful venue pattern of head up for information and feet down for control.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

nodes.title: Replace territory control with a visible checkpoint race
nodes.text: If a creator asks for Territory War, do not promise floor tiles that change team ownership or a percentage-controlled map. Offer the closest supported contest instead: players walk separate copies of a checkpoint course, with a live leaderboard and results on a shared screen. For a gentler group, use the same course as an individual score challenge without forced ranking.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal phygital game GDD, example 1 (course material)

nodes.title: Escalate pressure by shrinking safe choices
nodes.text: Build difficulty across rounds by reducing safe choices rather than only speeding everything up: start with about 4 safe squares, end with 1, and place later objectives farther away. On hard boards, let the safe opportunity shift so players must read and follow the pattern. In this engine, express this through guard coverage, cracked squares and ordered targets in tactics, or tighter hazard spacing between checkpoints in a runner. Never use objective distance to force running in MR.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

nodes.title: Translate HP victory into supported scoring
nodes.text: Do not promise HP totals, damage or team elimination: these engines have no general health or combat-result system. Translate 'the side with more HP wins' into supported outcomes: checkpoint +100, hazard -25, finish +300 plus a time bonus, with a leaderboard for races. For MR battle, frame victory as clearing the chapters and defeating the boss rather than comparing team HP.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

nodes.title: Put live race stakes where spectators can watch
nodes.text: A responsive floor arena becomes a group event when a big screen shows scores and time live, letting teams and onlookers follow the contest. For an online runner race, use the live leaderboard and place dodges, the last checkpoint and the portal where spectators can see players' bodies. Spectators should cheer or call hints from outside the route, never enter the play area for a task.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

nodes.title: Make the party-game goal understandable in seconds
nodes.text: The venue's broad-age party zone succeeds with games whose rules are understood within a few seconds, whether played alone or in teams. Give a new Land one immediate goal, a visible next action and instant feedback; ordered checkpoint labels can carry the story without a long briefing. Add depth through route, timing and hazard placement rather than stacking extra rules.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

nodes.title: Build one shared spectacle worth remembering
nodes.text: The 360-degree arena surrounds several players with one scene and full-view giant creatures, creating both immersion and a photo-worthy memory. Recreate that design beat with a chapter boss, a large beast or a dramatic final portal that everyone can anticipate and witness together. In MR, frame it against the real room and keep it visible to spectators instead of hiding the climax in a private UI moment.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

nodes.title: Walk-in casual play needs instant goals and soft failure
nodes.text: For families and friend groups, target a goal players understand within 30 seconds and rounds lasting 2 to 5 minutes. Let mistakes reduce score rather than end the session, reinforce every action with clear colour, sound and animation, and offer adjustable difficulty across varied bright themes. Keep rankings optional and design the same core activity for solo play or parallel group play so competition never blocks relaxed participation.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

nodes.title: Telegraph danger, then escalate movement demands
nodes.text: A readable movement round can use three distinct states: blinking orange warns for 3 to 5 seconds, green marks safety, and red confirms the hazard. Increase difficulty by shrinking the safe area from 4 grid cells toward 1, placing it progressively farther from players, and reserving a moving safe area for the hardest level. This creates a learnable rhythm before demanding faster or more sustained movement, while immediate feedback keeps failure understandable.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

nodes.title: Size movement and readability to the floor grid
nodes.text: The reference play lane is 3 by 6 metres, divided into 10 by 20 cells of 30 by 30 centimetres, with stepping detected and light feedback shown immediately. Use that cell size to judge reachable distances and safe-area capacity, and separate communication by surface: floor colour for actions, a projected wall for prompts and animation, and a monitor for score, time and results. Two identical lanes can support parallel teams without requiring everyone to share one floor.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

nodes.title: Lava Escape contrasts forgiving co-op with team survival
nodes.text: In a 90-second single-lane version for 2 to 4 players, each timely safe-zone arrival earns 10 points and standing in lava loses 10, so errors never end play. The dual-lane version instead fields 2 teams of 2 to 4, gives each team 10 HP, subtracts HP according to how many members are caught, and awards the win to the team with more HP after 90 seconds. The comparison shows how the same telegraphed activity can shift from forgiving cooperation to optional rivalry by changing scoring, not by changing its basic rules.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Design assignment: a phygital game for LED floor and projection

nodes.title: Play first, then choose a creative track
nodes.text: For a one-day school game-design event, let students sample the medium before asking them to create: allow 20 minutes for orientation, safety and grouping, two 40-minute rotations covering four play stations, then a 20-minute scored group finale. After lunch, give students a choice of game creation, AI video or art, with 105 minutes of hands-on work. This sequence builds shared references in the morning and ownership in the afternoon.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

nodes.title: End a student workshop with a visible artifact
nodes.text: Keep hands-on school groups to about 12 to 15 students so everyone can contribute. Reserve the final 40 minutes for finishing work and preparing presentations, followed by 20 minutes to screen every track's creations, award certificates and take a group photo. Give students a usable file to take back for a school portfolio; the public finale and take-home artifact make the day feel consequential rather than like an isolated demo.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

nodes.title: Short matches benefit from three genuinely different jobs
nodes.text: This casual territory-control example uses a 5 minute, 6 player 3v3 match on a 5.5 x 11.7 m LED floor, with victory going to the larger colored area when time expires. Its roles separate bodily area capture, ranged clearing, and resource planning, so players can contribute through exertion, accuracy, or judgment rather than everyone doing the same task. Use this as a role-clarity reference when discussing group play, then express the desired experience through supported battle, tactics, or runner mechanics.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground casual mode GDD, example 2 (course material)

nodes.title: Autonomous pressure keeps play moving without a leader
nodes.text: Spawning 5 soldier minions every 10 seconds gives this territory match a baseline contest even if nobody performs the Commander role. The reusable lesson is to keep the core activity moving without constant input from an organizer or strategist, so a hesitant or absent leader cannot stall everyone's fun. In this engine, preserve that principle with self-running battle enemy chapters or an individually playable runner race rather than units players must command.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal Battle Ground casual mode GDD, example 2 (course material)

nodes.title: Teach party games in ten seconds
nodes.text: For casual venue and party play, aim for a goal players can understand in about 10 seconds. Use one immediately readable objective and let the first attempt teach the interaction, rather than front-loading instructions. This keeps the game approachable for newcomers and workable for both solo sessions and group rotations.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

nodes.title: Offer privacy for celebrations and teams
nodes.text: Birthdays, private parties and company events benefit from a private play room rather than a shared public floor. Plan a hosted session with staff support throughout, so the group can focus on playing together instead of equipment or etiquette problems. Privacy is itself part of the event value, not merely a venue detail.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

nodes.title: Make breaks part of the social session
nodes.text: Schedule a comfortable regrouping point between rounds where players can have snacks and drinks while watching friends continue. Treat it as the group's meeting place, not dead time outside the experience. This supports mixed energy levels and keeps nonplaying friends and families involved.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

nodes.title: Redirect shooting requests to sword combat
nodes.text: A creator inspired by outdoor co-op shooter attractions may ask for controller guns, but the engine cannot provide shooting. Say so kindly and offer MR battle instead: the right controller is a sword, enemies approach slowly from the edges, and players step out of red warning rings before chapters culminate in a boss. This preserves action, fantasy and physical dodging without inventing firearms or team assault mechanics.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, FORTAL XR Arena catalogue 2026 (a real MR venue and its games)

nodes.title: Keep versus rounds short, symmetric, and easy to rematch
nodes.text: For a friendly head-to-head contest, start with a 60 second round so the result arrives quickly and a rematch feels effortless. Give opponents mirrored or otherwise symmetric starting positions and equivalent opportunities, then make the win condition simply who captured or scored more. If the board is mirrored, count each logical scoring cell only once rather than accidentally doubling one side's territory.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

nodes.title: Translate territory capture wishes into supported competition
nodes.text: When a creator asks to move around and capture territory, do not promise persistent cell ownership, territory control, power-ups, or combat because those mechanics are not available. Offer the closest supported fantasy: a tactics board about capturing targets in order while avoiding guards, or a runner race where players take ordered checkpoints and compare scores on a live leaderboard. Preserve the requested fast, friendly rivalry with short rounds and clear scoring rather than copying the unsupported mechanic.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

nodes.title: Reuse one core challenge across three session formats
nodes.text: Offer distinct ways to frame the same challenge rather than inventing separate mechanics: a 30-second time attack compares how much each player achieves, an endless round continues until stamina runs out, and a tournament uses a bracket for 4 to 8 players. Choose time attack for quick turns and spectators, endless for personal endurance, and a bracket when the group wants a clear overall winner.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

nodes.title: Prove the core loop before adding content
nodes.text: Build in dependency order: first prove control input, movement, and the basic scene, then add round structure such as best-of-3 logic and clear win and lose states. Polish sound, visuals, and assets only after the game is playable, and leave power-ups, obstacles, and extra modes for last. This prevents optional variety from hiding a weak or incomplete core loop.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

nodes.title: Short duel rounds keep party crowds rotating
nodes.text: For a booth or party activation, structure a head-to-head contest as best of 3, with two equal 100 m rounds and a deciding third only if needed. First to 2 round wins takes the match, keeping the full session to 2-3 minutes. Equal goals and frequent resets make the result easy to follow, give a losing player a quick comeback chance, and limit spectator waiting.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

nodes.title: Make physical effort visibly drive progress
nodes.text: When exertion is the core input, make the relationship immediate: faster movement produces faster progress, while no movement produces none. Set base speed to 0, scale acceleration with a tunable sensitivity multiplier, and smooth the result with lerp so motion stays readable rather than jittery. Keep the fantasy and on-screen progress aligned so both players and spectators can understand why someone is winning.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

nodes.title: Teach the action before a synchronized race start
nodes.text: For an instantly learned party game, wait until both players have joined and are ready, then show one animated instruction that demonstrates the core action. Follow it with a visible 3, 2, 1 countdown so neither player gains an accidental start advantage. During play, show both competitors' progress toward the same finish continuously, making the goal and changing lead readable without further explanation.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

nodes.title: Settle XR mode, venue, players, and locomotion first
nodes.text: Before designing mechanics, establish whether the experience is MR passthrough, VR, or MR with a VR fallback; whether the venue is already calibrated, an ordinary room, or a new space requiring a scan; and whether play is solo, co-located, or remote online. In MR, design for physical walking only and never promise joystick locomotion; reserve joystick movement for VR. These decisions determine the layout, multiplayer model, and fallback experience.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Pause and require deliberate resume after headset interruption
nodes.text: Treat headset removal or opening the system menu as an immediate game pause, since the player may no longer be able to see hazards or other people. Resume only after the headset is visible again and the player gives a fresh, explicit confirmation; require the previous input to be released first so a held button cannot restart play accidentally. This prevents the game from advancing while the player is disoriented or unattended.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Turn a territory-control wish into a supported race
nodes.text: A request for competitive territory capture cannot be implemented literally because the engine has no tile ownership or direct player conflict. Offer the closest supported contest: an online runner race where everyone walks or controls their own copy, touches 4 to 10 checkpoints in order, avoids hazards, and competes on a live leaderboard. Preserve the brief, party-friendly rivalry with an optional time limit and the standard score of +100 per checkpoint, -25 per hazard, and +300 for finishing plus a time bonus.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

nodes.title: Use a hard-stop one-minute party round
nodes.text: For a quick party competition, a fixed 60-second round creates urgency without demanding a long commitment, and is suitable for an audience aged 8+. Keep the timer visible, end exactly at zero instead of inventing overtime, and define the tie result explicitly so the winner announcement is never ambiguous. In a runner design, pair the time limit with a simple published scoring rule so players understand whether to prioritize checkpoints, hazard avoidance, or a fast finish.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

nodes.title: Use symmetry to keep short duels fair and legible
nodes.text: Symmetric competition makes fairness and relative progress easy to read: mirrored sides provide equivalent routes and starting conditions, while a blocked center initially separates rivals and an open center creates a more aggressive risk-versus-reward variant. If an action duplicates progress elsewhere, count each logical objective only once; the source scores just half its 10 by 6 grid for this reason. For a supported race, use identical course copies and a live leaderboard rather than implementing capture mirroring.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

nodes.title: Compose MR around the visible real venue
nodes.text: In passthrough MR, treat the real room as the backdrop: do not add a sky, cover the real floor with an opaque virtual floor, apply a full-screen tint, or float objects without a clear physical reason. Let real walls occlude virtual objects so the scene feels grounded, and keep all decorative content switchable as one group when a venue needs an unobstructed view.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Keep MR feedback clear without moving the headset view
nodes.text: Never shake or move the XR camera for impact feedback; use controller haptics and brief HUD flashes instead. Keep large flashes and dust effects at opacity 0.6 or below, and fade particles within 0.6 m of the head so they cannot obscure the player's view of real surroundings.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Scale MR creatures against real human bodies
nodes.text: Build MR scenes at 1:1 scale, with one world unit equal to one metre, and judge sizes against the player's actual body rather than a desktop screen. As a useful upper range, humanoid enemies should be no taller than about 2.1 m and bosses around 2.7 m, preserving drama without making nearby creatures overwhelmingly large.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Use short race sets with clear comeback stakes
nodes.text: For a party race session, a best-of-3 set gives players a concrete comeback arc without requiring a long campaign: announce each round winner and score, then reserve the champion celebration for the final result. A 2-1 finish feels meaningfully different from a single isolated win. In this engine, run the set as three separate races rather than promising built-in rounds, and offer replay immediately after the champion screen.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

nodes.title: Separate personal progress from shared race status
nodes.text: A head-to-head race is easiest to follow when each player has a distinct personal view, while comparative progress and the match score occupy one consistent shared location. Keep secondary measures such as depth at the side so they do not compete with the main question of who is ahead. On PC this can be left and right views with central progress; in MR, put the shared comparison on a spectator leaderboard because bystanders cannot see the virtual course.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Digging Game: phone-controlled party game GDD

nodes.title: High-contrast neon versus palette
nodes.text: For a cyberpunk competitive prototype, use a dark purple-blue background (#0a0a1a to #16213e), neon red-pink (#ff0055) for Player 1, neon cyan (#00d4ff) for Player 2, gray (#333333) for neutral elements, and neon green (#00ff9f) for UI accents. Pair uppercase, letter-spaced monospace type with restrained motion: 0.5-second screen fades, 1-second timer and player pulses, a 2-second start-button pulse, and a 3-4-second title gradient cycle. In MR, favor this dark neon treatment indoors or after dark so daylight does not wash it out.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

nodes.title: Fast competitive HUD and retry loop
nodes.text: Storyboard a short competitive game as start screen, game screen, game over, then play again. The start screen should combine mode selection, player and control previews, a rules summary, and one large start action; during a 60-second round, keep the timer and both live scores above the playfield and control hints below it. End by naming the winner, showing both scores, and offering restart, so a loss leads directly to another attempt.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

nodes.title: Redirect territory-control wishes
nodes.text: A creator asking for territory war may mean tile capture on entry, mirrored ownership, and two players sharing one keyboard; do not promise those mechanics. Offer battle chapters with distinct enemies and a boss for direct conflict, or a timed tactics board with ordered target captures and guard avoidance for spatial planning. If the real wish is score rivalry, use a race with a live leaderboard, while retaining red-versus-cyan arena styling as theme rather than unsupported territory mechanics.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Territory War: LED floor game GDD

nodes.title: Give MR players a real escape window
nodes.text: Telegraph area attacks for at least 1.3 seconds because a walking player needs roughly 1 second to move after seeing a signal. Make the warning ring match the damage area exactly, leave empty floor around it for escape, hold new attacks when the player is near a real wall or boundary, and never use knockback or forced movement. Warn about threats from behind with a screen-edge arrow and spatial audio rather than a full-screen tint.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Budget XR visuals for the worst combat frame
nodes.text: Do not base XR art direction on bloom or other post-processing, and disable shadows unless they are essential. Measure representative content before setting budgets, then test the densest case, such as a boss with all enemies and debris, and ensure no instanced batch overflows. Proven starting references are at most 40 meshes and 6k triangles for a boss, 12 draw calls for effects, and 40 monsters distributed across 8 instanced batches.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Build a desktop preview for fast design checks
nodes.text: Give every XR project a desktop preview with walking, aiming or interaction, a third-person camera, and explicit start and restart controls. Include autoplay for demos and captures, visible fps, draw-call and particle counts, opt-in invulnerability for testing only, and controls that isolate one enemy type or model. These tools make pacing, readability, and worst-case behavior inspectable without putting on a headset for every check.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: A passing build is not a playable game
nodes.text: Verify the real play flow from entry through start, actions, damage, HUD updates, turns, and restart while checking performance and errors. Inspect every real-time capture visually, because automated tests can pass while the scene is unattractive, unreadable, or effectively unplayable. Before calling work finished, state plainly which features have not yet been tested in an actual headset.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Ask one decision-changing question at a time
nodes.text: Interview the creator one question at a time, offer answer chips, and briefly explain why each answer matters. Ask when the goal is ambiguous or the answer would change the design; act when confident, stop when the brief is complete, and confirm the brief before designing. This elicits more useful preferences with less creator effort than an open prompt box.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Differentiate three options on explicit design axes
nodes.text: Offer three genuinely different games, not cosmetic variants, and make their differences explicit on axes such as core play, pacing, social fit, venue demands, and intended feelings. Give each option reasons, risks, four scores, and an AI recommendation, but let the creator choose, modify, or remix. Explicit axes reduce design fixation, while a small structured set avoids choice overload.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Approve a concrete prototype before building
nodes.text: Before building, show key art, a storyboard, the player flow, a palette, and a code-drawn level sketch, then revise from creator comments until approval. Measure time to approval and compare the finished build with the approved prototype. These checks reveal whether the prototype communicates quickly and whether implementation quietly drifts from the agreed design.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Turn intended feelings into the evaluation target
nodes.text: Record target players, context, session length, and intended feelings using the eight MDA aesthetics, then reuse those feelings as the evaluation target rather than treating them as mood words. Have persona bots walk the level and a judge check it against the brief, followed by a study with people. This tests whether the built game delivers the agreed experience, not merely whether it is valid.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Put triangle detail where players see it
nodes.text: For real-time XR art, budget about 15,000 to 25,000 triangles for a hero character, 3,000 to 6,000 for ordinary monsters, and under 250,000 for the whole scene. Spend triangles on curved silhouettes and shaded contours rather than flat surfaces, then review front, side, top and back captures before approval. This reserves detail for readable forms instead of invisible surface density.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Prototype beautiful heroes before promising them
nodes.text: A reusable low-poly toon kit is a good fit for enemy groups, bosses and scene props, but it is not a safe basis for promising a cute or beautiful game-render-quality lead.
