For friends taking turns, seat spectators along a wall or on furniture outside the route with views of dodges and the finish, and never let dim horror lighting hide real hazards.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: For a young child, settle who wears the headset
nodes.text: Quest is manufacturer-recommended for ages 10 and up, so do not treat a 5-year-old wearing it alone as the default. Explain the concern kindly, then offer concrete arrangements: child plays slowly with an adult holding their hand throughout, an adult plays while the child watches or follows, or the group switches to PC. Who actually plays changes the whole design, so resolve this before choosing mechanics.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: A tiny living room forces the runner genre
nodes.text: Measure the clear MR floor early, accepting a room comparison or a count of steps when the creator cannot give metres. MR normally needs at least 3 x 3 m for the genre range; below that, only runner fits, so all three options must be runners rather than promising battle or tactics. If an adult must walk beside or behind a child, include that accompanying movement when judging whether the route is clear.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Ask for desired feelings, then preserve fear limits
nodes.text: When a creator gives only a theme and occasion, ask them to pick 1 to 3 desired feelings, such as following a story, relaxing without fear or losing, exploration, wonder, or role-play; these choices distinguish games more usefully than decoration alone. Treat statements like "nothing scary" and "my child startles easily" as hard constraints on enemies, lighting, surprises, and failure pressure, not as a request to make a scary theme slightly milder. A cute narrative with relaxed play can satisfy both the requested theme and the child's limits.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Let young children finish gracefully
nodes.text: For a children's attraction, even a planned 3-minute session may feel too long, so keep stages short and offer an early, celebratory ending when a child is struggling. Use a cute, non-threatening boss rather than relying on fear for excitement, and preserve the child's sense of success instead of forcing a loss.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Design the booth for people walking past
nodes.text: A public attraction needs spectacle outside the headset or player screen, not just a fun game for the participant. Place visually readable highlights such as a giant mascot reveal where passersby can see the reaction, and offer a leaderboard on a booth TV to attract and involve spectators; confirm that the display connection is genuinely supported before promising it.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Keep the creator's named mascot exact
nodes.text: Treat a named mascot, colour, and branded pattern as fixed creative requirements rather than loose inspiration. Substituting another animal can make a technically improved prototype feel wrong, so echo those details in the next version and ask before changing the character's species or identity.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Adapt honestly to a tiny MR room
nodes.text: Treat a creator's estimate of 3 steps by 3 steps as roughly 2.2 x 2.2 m, below the recommended 3 x 3 m for MR walking games; 4 steps is roughly 3 m. Check whether the area can be expanded, but respect a refusal caused by booking cost or lack of alternatives. In a fixed tiny room, offer only a short, gentle story route with no startling moments, and allow extra room when a child walks hand in hand with an adult.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Make waiting spectators part of the show
nodes.text: When friends wait for one headset, design their experience as well as the player's: in passthrough they otherwise see a body walking and turning, not the virtual floor or cake. Put readable physical moments such as a dodge or finish where the group can watch, and use a TV view or leaderboard when available. Cheering and hints give the queue a role without assigning anyone a task inside the play area.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Use reliable triggers for emotional climaxes
nodes.text: Do not make a birthday climax depend on the headset somehow knowing that a child blew out a candle. A failed or ambiguous detection can turn the emotional peak into frustration, especially for a young child. Use a simple supported action such as touching the final checkpoint, or have an adult confirm the moment, so the celebration always resolves reliably.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Turn one headset into a short group race
nodes.text: One headset does not prevent a social competition: let friends take turns on the same short course and compare times or scores while the others cheer. A four-minute zombie-escape round suits club play because several people can rotate without a long wait. Ask players' ages and whether they play simultaneously or sequentially, since those answers determine space, difficulty and whether a race structure fits.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Let real lighting decide whether glow can carry the theme
nodes.text: Ask early whether the venue can be fully darkened, merely dimmed, or must stay bright before promising a lantern, neon, spooky, or night theme. Bright real light washes out dark scenes and glow; even a dimmable gym with window light needs high-contrast colours and readable scenery rather than reliance on darkness. If the room cannot get dark, keep the night-market story through props and labels but adjust the palette, or move spooky play indoors after dark.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Simplify a first VR round before adding content
nodes.text: For children trying VR for the first time, make the first 4-minute round teach through play: brief instructions, a simple ordered route, few hazards, and checkpoint labels that make the next goal obvious. Start near the low end of the engine's 4 to 10 checkpoints rather than filling the short session with navigation complexity. Avoid intense horror and startling events that could provoke running, especially in a race with teachers and classmates watching.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Deliver an NPC voice request as staged story beats
nodes.text: Do not promise spoken NPC dialogue or conversation when a creator asks for a character such as Mae Nak to talk: the engine supports neither NPC conversations nor voice chat. Offer the closest supported storytelling by putting her short lines into ordered checkpoint labels, establishing relationships on the intro card, and using scenery and lighting changes for escalating dread. This preserves character presence without inventing an unavailable mechanic.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Size a busy booth for queue flow, not maximum play
nodes.text: For a walk-in booth with long queues, choose round length and simultaneous players after measuring only the clear floor, excluding counters and other obstacles. A 4 x 4 m MR area with a corner obstruction supports about 1-2 players safely; solo rounds of roughly 3 minutes maximize throughput, while 5 minutes gives a fuller experience. Show a live leaderboard on a spectator screen so people in the queue can follow scores without entering the play area.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Redirect impossible wishes to the feeling behind them
nodes.text: When a creator requests shooting or a mascot that can answer children's questions, state the limitation clearly and offer the closest achievable experience: swordplay against slowly approaching enemies for action, or a visible mascot that welcomes players, cheers successful hits and waves at the finish for character presence. Confirm that the substitute is acceptable, then continue the interview rather than dwelling on the refusal or implying the feature exists.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Make branded action welcoming for young first-time players
nodes.text: For elementary-age children new to headsets, express the brand through visible, nonverbal details such as a brand-coloured sword and a mascot that greets and cheers. Keep the climax cute rather than frightening, and combine simple action with a visible score goal when the creator wants both excitement and competition. Capture requests made after option selection, such as sword colours and boss tone, as explicit prototype art direction.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Turn one headset into a social score race
nodes.text: When friends want to compete but share one headset, design short solo turns with a visible score or survival-time leaderboard rather than simultaneous multiplayer. Waiting friends can watch and cheer from outside the play area, but should never receive a task inside it. A wish for both scares and "who survives longest" calls for horror staging plus a score race, not necessarily cooperative play.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Convert rough room descriptions into a safe floor plan
nodes.text: When an MR creator cannot give metres, ask for an estimate in walking steps or a comparison with a familiar room, then verify it before building. Measure the floor after movable tables are cleared and record fixed obstacles such as a corner sofa. Keep routes 1.2 m wide, put nothing on real obstacles, and keep action at least 0.6 m from the area edge.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Stage MR horror with dim light and safe pressure
nodes.text: For MR horror, ask when play happens and whether the lights can be dimmed: bright daylight washes out dark scenes and glow, while controllable indoor light keeps them readable. If one startle feels too ordinary, increase dread through pacing and slow enemies approaching from behind or the edges, not by adding sudden scares that make players run. Keep startling moments away from hazards and avoid tasks that require looking up while moving quickly.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Fit a branded battle into a three-minute mall queue
nodes.text: A 4 x 4 m mall booth with a corner counter and a long queue can support a 3-minute solo MR sword battle for elementary-age visitors. Assume most children are new to VR, use immediate one-action onboarding, keep the counter out of the cleared route, and show the live leaderboard to parents and people waiting. A mascot that cannot converse can still welcome players and cheer at the start and finish. Plan VR for ages 10 and up, with close adult supervision for younger children.
nodes.source: Land Builder users and simulated creators 2026, Land Builder design sessions (creator and AI)

nodes.title: Explain follow-ups and confirm the brief before designing
nodes.text: Keep a fixed set of required design fields, but make follow-up questions adaptive and briefly explain why each non-obvious question matters. End the interview with a one-screen brief covering concept, players, group size, VR experience, intended feelings, venue or environment, session length and play mode, then require an explicit confirmation or edit. Never request personal data while trying to fill design gaps.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Set intended feelings before choosing mechanics
nodes.text: Choose the intended player experience early, using the 8 MDA aesthetics: sensation, fantasy, narrative, challenge, fellowship, discovery, expression and submission. Designers reason from mechanics toward aesthetics, but players encounter the resulting feelings first, so record the aesthetic goals before selecting a genre or mechanic. Reuse those goals later as criteria for judging generated content and alternatives, with fellowship especially relevant to group play.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Offer three genuinely different options with visible trade-offs
nodes.text: Present three options, each with a pitch, core loop, player and venue fit, risks, scores for fun, player fit, platform fit and buildability, plus one recommendation. Declare different design axes such as dominant aesthetic, core mechanic and social structure, and verify that the options differ on at least two axes so they do not collapse into one game with three skins. A small set suits non-experts comparing complex whole-game concepts, while alternatives also elicit more critical feedback and reduce fixation better than a single proposal.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Keep the creator in charge of the AI recommendation
nodes.text: The AI may recommend one option, but the creator makes the final choice and can request changes before anything is built. Explain how every score was derived rather than showing bare numbers, because scores and recommendations can induce acceptance even when the advice is wrong. Where over-reliance is a concern, ask the creator to state an initial preference before revealing the AI recommendation, while accepting that this extra step may feel less smooth.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Require fresh input after an MR interruption
nodes.text: When a player removes the headset or the session pauses, do not resume movement or attacks from a button that was already held. Wait until every control is released, then require a new press so the game cannot continue acting on its own while the player is disoriented.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Separate enemy roles by silhouette, not recoloring
nodes.text: Give each enemy type a distinct silhouette so players can read its role at a glance, and reserve palette swaps for elemental variants, teams, or skins of the same type. A small role named palette can keep colors consistent across a cast, with emissive accents limited to focal details such as eyes or a core.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Fortal XR dev guide: WebXR Quest MR rules, safety, comfort, performance

nodes.title: Compare parallel concepts before refining one
nodes.text: Develop several concepts in parallel before investing in one detailed design. Research on parallel prototyping links it to better design results, greater divergence, and increased self-efficacy, so use the creator's comparison and critique to reveal preferences. Keep each alternative quick to assess, then refine the chosen direction.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Clarify only ambiguity that changes the design
nodes.text: When a brief is vague, ask the clarification whose answer would most change the design, rather than running through a full questionnaire. Work on eliciting preferences and selectively clarifying ambiguous questions supports using dialogue to expose consequential unknowns. For low-impact gaps, state a provisional assumption and keep the conversation moving.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Use deliberate variation to counter design fixation
nodes.text: Treat polished AI-generated concepts as prompts, not as evidence that the right direction has been found. Research on generative AI and design fixation makes deliberate divergence important: vary a fundamental design dimension between proposals and ask the creator what possibility is missing. This prevents surface-level variations from masquerading as exploration.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Build the mission and route before the scenery
nodes.text: Generate a level in two stages: first turn the brief and intended feelings into a mission, ordered objectives and playable route, then dress that route with theme and scenery. This keeps decoration from determining play and makes failures easier to locate: repair the mission or route before adjusting visual layout.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Separate meaningful level design from geometric placement
nodes.text: Let the design model specify relations such as before, beside, visible from and clear of, while a solver places objects and enforces geometry. Well-formed output does not prove a meaningful or playable level, so validate semantics separately and use a path-planning agent to test reachability and walkability on the actual MR floor plan. Track schema failures, rule violations and meaning failures separately rather than treating every rejection as the same problem.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Playtest with contrasting personas and brief-based targets
nodes.text: Create 4 to 6 personas from the intended audience and play styles, such as curious child, cautious parent with child, goal-rusher and wanderer, then run at least 30 seeded simulations per persona per level. Fit walking speed and dwell time to a few real headset traces, and measure completion, session time against the brief, area coverage, idle or lost time, crowding, near-misses, boundary clearance and checkpoint reachability. Judge success against the original players, target session and intended feelings, not merely whether the level can be completed.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Measure whether generated options truly offer different games
nodes.text: Do not assume three proposals are meaningfully different because their themes differ. Plot the three options, and outputs across many briefs, on two-dimensional comparisons such as pacing against spatial spread, then check whether options separate and different briefs produce different level shapes. Use the results to revise generation toward genuinely distinct play experiences.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Preserve creator agency when scoring options
nodes.text: Let the creator rank or choose among design options before revealing the AI's preferred option, so the recommendation does not anchor their judgment. Show what each score is derived from and explicitly mark uncertain scores rather than presenting a bare number. Allow remixing, such as taking the mechanic from option B and the theme from option A, then regenerate the combined design.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Approve a complete paper prototype before building
nodes.text: After the creator picks a concept and before building, make a paper prototype with a logline, 3 design pillars, a 4 to 6 colour palette, key art, a 3 to 4 panel session storyboard, screen contents, minute-by-minute flow, and a top-down level sketch. Add 2 to 4 questions that a later playtest must answer. Revise as often as needed from creator comments, keep every version, and require the build plan to follow the approved prototype.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Do not let the first image choose the game
nodes.text: Keep the initial game options text-only so an attractive generated picture does not decide which concept the creator selects. Once prototyping begins, treat key art as a cheap visual hypothesis and drive revisions from the creator's comments rather than attachment to the first image. This preserves exploration of visual directions while letting the creator judge experience goals before production geometry.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Generate the MR route from the real venue
nodes.text: For room-scale passthrough MR, treat the real venue as visible game context and change only the floor layer. Put the venue's size, indoor or outdoor status, lighting, walls, and spectators into the design brief, then fit the route to the detected walkable floor while keeping clear of walls and using the available area. Real walking is the only locomotion, so every path and interaction must remain reachable within that actual room.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Capture the venue as structured play data
nodes.text: Before laying out an MR game, record walls, exits, obstacles, spectator zones and lighting as structured data rather than a prose description. Snap content to real planes and adapt placement to the room's physical and social context, because site conditions shape play and plane snapping makes placement faster and better. Keep real people and objects visible: this improves usability with little loss of immersion.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Give spectators a deliberate viewing plan
nodes.text: MR spectators see players' bodies but not the virtual floor, so add a spectator plan to both the brief and the build. Specify where they stand, provide a shared screen view such as a leaderboard or floor projection, and stage dodges and finishes where their reactions are easy to read. Friends and parents can cheer or call hints, but never assign them a task inside the play area.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Budget walking comfort and bystander safety
nodes.text: Real walking gives more natural movement and presence than walking-in-place or flying, so keep it but budget session length, route length, rest points and stricter limits for children; screen comfort with the SSQ when testing. Keep routes 1.2 m clear, content off real obstacles and at least 0.6 m from area edges, with no sudden scares or fast walking while looking up. Warn about nearby bystanders with combined audio and visual distance cues, which work better than either cue alone.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Let code verify geometry while the model designs meaning
nodes.text: Have the model generate layout candidates inside a schema and external validation loop rather than asking it to verify its own spatial reasoning. Build in two stages, route first and scenery second outside a computed keep-clear corridor, with code auto-fixing small geometry slips and at most 2 feedback-driven repair rounds. This division matters: LLM-only repairs reduced blocking objects only from 38 to 30 to 24, while code fixed them in one pass.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Use bots to rank levels, not replace players
nodes.text: Treat automated playtesting as decision support: correlate bot and judge predictions with real players on the same levels before trusting them. An LLM judge can score intended aesthetics plus player and venue fit, using randomized option order, several samples or models with agreement reported, length caps, and independent checking rather than unchecked self-judging. Compute safety as a hard gate from telemetry, never as an LLM opinion.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Playtest the intended feeling at the venue
nodes.text: Compare the revised level against the unrevised version with players in the actual venue, and ask directly whether they felt each intended feeling. Use PXI as the main experience scale rather than GEQ, whose factor structure did not replicate; measure sickness with SSQ before and after. In MR passthrough, interpret presence items about realness carefully, and keep questionnaires short: in-headset items can change response variance without changing means.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Make child playtests short, consented and observable
nodes.text: Obtain parental consent and the child's own assent, secure ethics approval first, and allow either to stop the session at any time. Keep sessions short, screen for sickness, use pictorial short-form questions, and include parent observation. Do not rely on an adult's consent or questionnaire responses alone to infer that a child is comfortable.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Keep the creator in control of AI recommendations
nodes.text: Make alternatives differ on explicitly declared axes and verify that difference, so the creator avoids fixation on minor variations of one idea. Explain the basis of scores and recommendations. Let the creator rank the options before revealing the AI's preferred pick, reducing over-reliance while preserving a useful recommendation.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Land Builder research notes: AI-assisted game design literature

nodes.title: Define a session policy for lost player tracking
nodes.text: For a tracked multiplayer MR session, decide in advance what happens when a required player is lost: pause the session initially, preserve their last visible position if useful, and remove them from actions, collisions, and scoring. Add a grace period only after measuring real tracking losses, rather than letting stale positions affect play. This keeps races and shared-floor sessions fair and avoids unsafe confusion around a stationary avatar.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Verify shared MR tracking with real players
nodes.text: Before promising a shared-floor MR game, test the full intended player count with independent tracked people, not bots or keyboard substitutes. Simulated fallbacks can hide a failed real-player lookup, while a healthy global signal can hide one rejected player, so monitor connection, last valid update, and position validity per player. Repeat the test after reconnects and roster changes, with explicit recovery when tracking is lost.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Design the active roster before multiplayer play
nodes.text: Define the actual active roster separately from technical capacity: for a 2 to 4 player game, give every participant a stable slot and a unique physical tracker identity. Size ready screens, play lanes and result attribution for that roster, and explicitly test three players as well as two and four so an odd-sized group does not expose silent bot substitution or layout assumptions.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Make tracking loss a fair game state
nodes.text: For each player, specify what missing, predicted and invalid position input means during play instead of treating one latest position as proof that everyone is tracked. Decide what silence does, such as pausing that player rather than registering steps or failures, and test dropout and recovery with real bodies before accepting the design.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Choose floor triggers and test bodily interference
nodes.text: Choose explicitly whether an action requires a foot press, remaining in a tracked spot for a dwell, or a test-only input; clear action state at each round and define whether LED feedback should hold. On site, test simultaneous players, path crossings, occlusions, dropouts and recovery, and record measured update rate, latency and position error rather than trusting configuration values.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Test tracked groups with simulated players disabled
nodes.text: For a tracked group game, verify every player slot with a real participant before judging movement, pacing, or lane balance. In Deepspace, slots P3 to P6 silently became bots moving at 1.7 m/s whenever a real pose was unavailable, so a full-looking six-player test could hide broken tracking. Use stable player-to-tracker assignments, check each participant individually, and keep simulated players as an explicit test mode rather than an invisible fallback.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Make tracking loss visibly fail safe
nodes.text: Treat missing, stale, or out-of-area tracking as unavailable input, not as a valid position at the nearest edge. Clamped coordinates and automatic fallback actors can make the game appear responsive while outcomes no longer match the player's body. Pause scoring and hazard consequences for that player, show a clear tracking-loss state, and resume only after their position is valid again; a connected receiver alone does not prove that every player is tracked.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Stage the boss entrance before play begins
nodes.text: Give a boss fight a short, unambiguous opening beat: the portal grows from zero to full size, the boss emerges, the portal shrinks away, and only then does play begin. A one-time entrance separates anticipation from action, makes the boss arrival memorable, and prevents players from mistaking the introduction for a moment when they should already react.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Start boss rosters equal, then tune by feel
nodes.text: For repeated boss fights, select from a boss roster with weighted randomness so encounters vary without requiring new mechanics. Start with equal weights, test each boss individually, then adjust frequencies only after learning which encounters deserve to appear more or less often; weights alter relative likelihood, not a guaranteed fraction over a few sessions.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Treat tracking loss as a participation state
nodes.text: When a player's position stops updating, freezing their avatar is not enough: scoring, hazards and other rules may still act on the stale position. Mark that player explicitly unavailable, pause or exclude their participation according to one consistent policy, and preserve their identity when tracking returns rather than silently assigning another input source. This matters most in shared-floor or competitive play, where a dropout must not create an unfair hit, score or ownership change.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Validate readiness with a fresh player action
nodes.text: A selection countdown can force a session to start, but it cannot prove that every player is present and tracked; the source's 50-second timer could force readiness without validating players. Require a fresh, attributable action such as a step, press or hold before marking each player ready, and keep that one-time readiness signal separate from continuous movement input. Revalidate a player after hardware loss instead of treating an old position or held input as consent to continue.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Build boss chapters from four waves
nodes.text: For a chaptered action game, start with four enemy waves before each boss; tuning converged on four after trying three, four, and five. You can remove pauses between waves for relentless pressure while retaining a separate stage-transition countdown and a pause after the boss dies, giving intensity a clear beginning and end.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Give respawning players three seconds of grace
nodes.text: Start with about 3 seconds of post-respawn protection, rather than 1.5 seconds, so players can reorient before taking damage again. Treat this as a playtest starting point, not a universal value: the doubled timing came from a different death model, so immediate danger, spawn position, and whether the player loses health or is destroyed all affect the right grace period.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Make shared-station turn order survive walkaways
nodes.text: When several visitors share an interactive station, establish priority in join order at each round reset and whenever the active player changes. A visitor who steps away and later returns should rejoin the queue rather than reclaim an old turn; this keeps ownership legible and prevents stale claims from blocking newcomers.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Leave room for tracking lag in walking challenges
nodes.text: For position-tracked walking games, tune interactions for delayed and smoothed movement rather than instant input: this setup caps normal UWB motion at 1.8 m/s, predicts at most 0.35 seconds ahead, and treats poses older than 1 second as stale. Use broad checkpoints and hazards, avoid rapid precision dodges, and never depend on movements finer than the 0.08 m position dead zone. Test recovery after tracking errors as well as normal play, since position jumps over 0.75 m may be rejected.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Make floor input recover from stuck sensors
nodes.text: On pressure-sensitive floors, expect debris, water, a dropped bag, or an overly sensitive sensor to report a press that never ends. Temporarily ignore a cell held longer than any intentional player stance, then restore it automatically after it goes quiet; provide a test view that distinguishes active and muted cells. Set the hold timeout well above the longest deliberate stand, and the gap tolerance above the controller repeat interval of roughly 10–170 ms, so normal packet gaps do not reset the hold.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Design foot input for repeats and sensor faults
nodes.text: A pressure floor repeats an occupied cell several times per second and provides no release event, so game actions must tolerate repeated messages rather than assume clean press and release pairs. Trigger once per footfall or deliberately accumulate dwell time, preserve each packet's arrival time, and discard stale packets because a delayed frame is indistinguishable from a new step. Temporarily mute cells that stay active longer than a real step, and show muted cells differently from fresh presses so faults are visible without becoming gameplay input.
nodes.source: Fortal Interactive 2026, Deepspace: Unity LED floor + UWB tracking game project

nodes.title: Thai temple night festival: gold, deep indigo, lantern orange
nodes.text: Palette: #1f1b4d night indigo, #d4a017 temple gold, #f28c28 lantern orange, #2e8b57 banyan green, #e0262b hazard red. Reads best indoors or after dark: the gold and lantern orange glow against indigo. In MR daylight the indigo turns grey and the gold looks flat, so switch the lighting preset to evening and lean on gold rather than glow. The hazard colour #e0262b (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Songkran water fight: splash cyan, white, sunny yellow
nodes.text: Palette: #19b5e6 splash cyan, #f7f7f2 powder white, #ffd23f sunny yellow, #ff6fa8 flower pink, #d7263d hazard red. Made for MR daylight outdoors: high-value cyan and yellow survive bright sun, and white reads as wet stone. Indoors under warm light it still works but tone the white to cream so it does not glare in the headset. The hazard colour #d7263d (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Loy Krathong lanterns: river navy, candle amber, banana-leaf green
nodes.text: Palette: #0f2a44 river navy, #ffb547 candle amber, #5c9e31 banana leaf, #f4e3b1 lotus cream, #ff3b30 hazard red. An indoor or night palette: amber lights only read against the dark navy. Outdoors at noon the amber looks like plain yellow, so for daytime venues raise the cream and green and treat the lanterns as shapes, not light. The hazard colour #ff3b30 (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Thai ghost spooky: moss green, bone white, incense purple
nodes.text: Palette: #1b2a1f night moss, #e8e2cf bone white, #6b3fa0 incense purple, #9fd36b ghost-light green, #ff2e2e hazard red. Only for indoors or after dark: the dark moss base disappears in daylight and the ghost-light green needs shadow to glow. Bone white keeps silhouettes readable so it stays fun rather than truly scary for kids. The hazard colour #ff2e2e (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Candy land: bubblegum pink, mint, lemon, chocolate
nodes.text: Palette: #ff8fc7 bubblegum, #8ef0c8 mint, #fff07a lemon, #6b3e26 chocolate, #e4002b cherry hazard. Works in both MR daylight and indoors because all tones are light and saturated. The chocolate brown gives the dark anchor that pastels need, otherwise the frame looks washed out. The hazard colour #e4002b (cherry hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Ice cave: glacier blue, frost white, deep cobalt
nodes.text: Palette: #a8e6ff glacier blue, #f2fbff frost white, #1d3f8f deep cobalt, #7a5cff aurora violet, #ff4d2e ember hazard. Indoors it looks crisp; in strong MR daylight the pale blues and white merge into one glare, so add the cobalt to big shapes (rocks, ice walls). The warm hazard is the only warm colour, which makes danger pop hard. The hazard colour #ff4d2e (ember hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Lava forge: basalt black, molten orange, iron grey
nodes.text: Palette: #1e1a1d basalt, #ff7a00 molten orange, #5a5f66 iron grey, #ffd166 spark yellow, #00c2ff cool hazard cyan. Because the whole theme is red and orange, the hazard flips to cyan so it does not drown. Strong indoors and at night; in daylight keep basalt as large ground shapes so the orange has contrast. The hazard colour #00c2ff (cool hazard cyan) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Neon city: midnight, magenta, electric cyan
nodes.text: Palette: #0b0c1f midnight, #ff2bd6 neon magenta, #17e9ff electric cyan, #a6ff00 acid lime, #ff3131 hazard red. Needs a dark room or night: neon only exists against black. In MR daylight this palette fails completely, so offer the herotech or robot daytime look instead. Separate hazard red from magenta by making hazards pulse. The hazard colour #ff3131 (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Jungle dinosaur: canopy green, mud brown, fern lime
nodes.text: Palette: #2f6b2f canopy green, #7a5230 mud brown, #b8e04a fern lime, #f2c14e amber sun, #e63946 hazard red. Good in MR daylight in a garden or park: the greens extend real grass and trees. Indoors it can feel dark, so lift with fern lime and amber. Red hazard is strongly complementary to green and reads instantly. The hazard colour #e63946 (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Pirate cove: sea teal, sand, weathered wood, sail white
nodes.text: Palette: #0f8b8d sea teal, #f2d49b sand, #8b5a2b old wood, #fafaf0 sail white, #d62828 hazard red. An all-rounder: sand and white hold up in daylight, teal and wood give depth indoors. Avoid adding red flags or barrels; keep red for hazards and use gold instead for treasure. The hazard colour #d62828 (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Toy room: primary blue, block yellow, play green, cream
nodes.text: Palette: #2b6cff block blue, #ffc93c block yellow, #3ccf6e play green, #fff6e5 nursery cream, #ff1f3d hazard red. Built for a real living room or classroom indoors: primary colours look like real toys under room light. In daylight it still reads. Classic toy red is left out so the hazard red stays unique. The hazard colour #ff1f3d (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Space station: hull white, deep space, signal orange
nodes.text: Palette: #e9eef5 hull white, #101828 deep space, #3a86ff console blue, #ff9f1c signal orange, #ff1744 hazard red. Hull white keeps it readable in daylight MR, deep space only shows under the void floor or VR-only decor. Indoors the console blue glows nicely. Keep signal orange for goals and portals and red only for danger. The hazard colour #ff1744 (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Desert ruins: dune gold, terracotta, oasis turquoise
nodes.text: Palette: #e8c07d dune gold, #c0623b terracotta, #2ec4b6 oasis turquoise, #5b4636 shadow brown, #9b5de5 curse violet hazard. Daylight friendly: warm sand tones match a sunny real floor. Terracotta is close to red, so the hazard becomes curse violet, which no desert prop uses. Indoors add turquoise accents to avoid an all-beige frame. The hazard colour #9b5de5 (curse violet hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Underwater reef: ocean blue, coral, kelp, bubble white
nodes.text: Palette: #0a4f8f ocean blue, #ff7f6e coral, #2a9d8f kelp, #e6fbff bubble white, #ffdd00 jellyfish yellow hazard. Best indoors with the night or spooky preset darkened toward blue. Coral is pinkish red, so hazards use jellyfish yellow which pops on blue. In daylight lift the blue a step or the floor looks like a dark hole. The hazard colour #ffdd00 (jellyfish yellow hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Happy farm: grass green, barn red, hay yellow, sky blue
nodes.text: Palette: #6cc04a grass, #b23a48 barn red, #f4d35e hay, #8ecae6 sky blue, #ff00a8 hazard magenta. Daylight hero: matches real gardens and lawns. A farm needs red barns, so hazards switch to magenta, which never appears on a farm, so no one confuses a barn with a warning ring. The hazard colour #ff00a8 (hazard magenta) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Music stage: stage black, spotlight gold, beat purple
nodes.text: Palette: #141414 stage black, #ffcc33 spotlight gold, #8a2be2 beat purple, #00e5a0 equalizer green, #ff2a2a hazard red. An indoor show palette, matches a hall with a crowd. In daylight swap stage black for a deep purple ground so the floor does not read as a hole. Red hazards should pulse on the beat to separate them from stage lights. The hazard colour #ff2a2a (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Haunted school: chalkboard green, locker grey, flickering yellow
nodes.text: Palette: #22372b chalkboard, #8a9099 locker grey, #f6e27f flicker yellow, #4a2c5e shadow plum, #ff3030 hazard red. Indoors only, ideally a real classroom or corridor at dusk. Desaturated base plus one flicker yellow makes it eerie without being gory. In daylight the greys blend into a real school floor, so give the path a yellow edge. The hazard colour #ff3030 (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Forest spirits: mossy teal, firefly lime, bark, mist lilac
nodes.text: Palette: #2c6e63 mossy teal, #d4ff5a firefly lime, #5a3d2b bark, #c9b8ff mist lilac, #ff4040 hazard red. Gentle and magical in both lights: fireflies glow indoors, lilac and teal stay soft in daylight. Good for calm discovery games. Keep red rare so it reads as the only unfriendly thing in the forest. The hazard colour #ff4040 (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Sky islands: cloud white, sky azure, grass lime, sunset peach
nodes.text: Palette: #ffffff cloud white, #4fb3ff azure, #9be15d island grass, #ffb38a sunset peach, #e3170a hazard red. The natural partner of the void floor: islands over a bottomless sky. Bright enough for daylight MR. Under the void floor keep hazards on solid ground and clearly red so players never confuse the drop with a hazard. The hazard colour #e3170a (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Dark arena battle: charcoal, steel blue, bone, blood-orange tells
nodes.text: Palette: #232129 charcoal, #4b6584 steel blue, #e6dfd3 bone, #7d5ba6 shadow violet, #ff3d1f warning red-orange. For the battle dark theme indoors. Enemies in bone and steel, ground in charcoal, and the feet-ring warnings in one hot red-orange. Under daylight MR lift charcoal to steel so enemies on the edges stay visible. The hazard colour #ff3d1f (warning red-orange) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Tactics board: ivory and slate squares, gold piece, guard red
nodes.text: Palette: #f1ece1 ivory square, #58606b slate square, #e0b13a player gold, #2f80ed target blue, #e5383b guard red. A board must read before it looks pretty: light and dark squares differ strongly in value, the player piece is gold, targets are blue, attacked squares are red. Works in daylight because the contrast is in value, not glow. The hazard colour #e5383b (guard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Carnival fair: carousel teal, mustard, plum, popcorn cream
nodes.text: Palette: #1aa6a6 carousel teal, #f2b134 mustard, #6a2c70 plum, #fff3d6 popcorn cream, #ff1e1e hazard red. Carnival art loves red and white stripes, which would fight the hazards, so stripes become teal and cream. Bright enough for an outdoor fair in daylight, rich under evening lights. The hazard colour #ff1e1e (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: MR daylight rule: pick high-value colours, no glow, darkest tone above 25% brightness
nodes.text: Palette: #3d5a80 daylight dark anchor, #98c1d9 soft sky, #e0fbfc pale, #ee6c4d warm accent, #d00000 hazard red. Outdoors at noon the headset passthrough is very bright, so very dark colours look grey and emissive glow vanishes. Use a dark anchor no darker than about #3d5a80 and let shape and value contrast do the work. The hazard colour #d00000 (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Chunky toy low-poly: rounded blocks, big heads, soft light
nodes.text: A friendly low-poly look with chunky proportions, very few facets and soft ambient light. Reads as safe and playful for kids, and big shapes stay legible in a headset at 2-5 m. Ready prompt_style: "chunky toy-like low-poly, rounded blocky shapes, big-headed cute characters, soft ambient light, gentle shadows, bright cheerful mood".

nodes.title: Heroic fantasy low-poly: sharp facets, rim light, epic scale
nodes.text: Sharper facets, taller silhouettes and a warm rim light give a heroic, adventure feel. Good for battle and boss moments where the enemy should feel big. Ready prompt_style: "heroic fantasy low-poly, sharp angular facets, strong warm rim light, dramatic scale, epic adventure mood".

nodes.title: Diorama tabletop low-poly: tilt-shift, clean board, miniature feel
nodes.text: Looks like a painted miniature game on a table. Ideal for tactics, where the board must read as a grid of squares and the pieces as figurines. Ready prompt_style: "miniature diorama low-poly, clean tabletop board, figurine-like pieces, soft tilt-shift depth of field, crisp grid".

nodes.title: Spooky-cute low-poly: big eyes, purple shadows, warm windows
nodes.text: Ghosts and monsters with round shapes and big eyes, lit by moonlight and warm lanterns. Spooky without real horror, safe for 6-12 year olds and families. Ready prompt_style: "spooky-cute low-poly, round friendly ghosts with big eyes, purple moonlit shadows, warm lantern glow, playful eerie mood".

nodes.title: Thai ornate low-poly: gilded roofs, naga curves simplified to facets
nodes.text: Thai temple and Himmapan forms (layered roofs, chofa, naga) reduced to bold low-poly shapes with gold accents. Keeps cultural details respectful and readable. Ready prompt_style: "Thai ornate low-poly, layered temple roofs with gold trim, simplified naga and Himmapan creatures, warm festive light, respectful cultural mood".

nodes.title: Neon synth low-poly: dark facets, emissive edges, glossy floor
nodes.text: Dark faceted shapes with glowing edge lines and a reflective floor. Strong for night rhythm or sci-fi, but only works indoors or at night in MR. Ready prompt_style: "neon synthwave low-poly, dark faceted geometry with glowing edges, glossy reflective floor, magenta and cyan light, energetic night mood".

nodes.title: Storybook low-poly: soft pastel, painterly gradients, gentle sun
nodes.text: Soft pastel colours and gentle light like a picture book. Suits narrative runners and calm discovery where the mood matters more than tension. Ready prompt_style: "storybook low-poly, soft pastel colours, gentle painterly gradients on flat facets, warm afternoon sun, calm cozy mood".

nodes.title: Arcade bold low-poly: saturated primaries, hard shadows, punchy
nodes.text: Saturated colours, hard sun shadows and simple outlines-free shapes. Reads from far away and looks great in daylight MR and on spectator screens. Ready prompt_style: "bold arcade low-poly, saturated primary colours, hard sunny shadows, simple chunky shapes, energetic competitive mood".

nodes.title: Frosted crystal low-poly: translucent-looking facets, cool light
nodes.text: Ice and crystal shapes with pale gradients and a cool blue key light. Elegant for ice or magic themes; keep one warm accent so it does not look flat. Ready prompt_style: "frosted crystal low-poly, pale icy faceted shapes, cool blue key light with a warm accent, sparkling clean mood".

nodes.title: Art style is always stylized low-poly, flat shaded: vary mood, not technique
nodes.text: Every FortalLand game uses the same 1,900+ low-poly flat-shaded models, so the prototype art must promise exactly that. Vary the mood with palette, lighting preset and silhouette size, never with realistic, painted, pixel or anime styles that the build cannot match.

nodes.title: MR key art: first-person through the headset, real room visible, only the floor changed
nodes.text: For MR the honest key art is the player view: a real room (walls, windows, people) with the game floor replacing only the real floor and low-poly objects standing on it. The code already adds the MR view line, so the prompt should describe the real room concretely (a school hall with windows, a living room sofa at the edge).

nodes.title: MR alternative: over-the-shoulder of a player in the real room
nodes.text: A third-person shot of a person wearing a headset in the real space, with the virtual floor and objects drawn around them, explains MR to people who have never tried it. Use it when the brief stresses spectators or families watching.

nodes.title: PC battle key art: low third-person behind the hero mid-combo
nodes.text: Camera 2-3 m behind and slightly above the sword hero, the boss or a beast charging in from the far side, a red warning ring on the ground between them. One clear action pose (sword swing or dash) sells the 3-hit combo and dash in one frame.

nodes.title: MR battle key art: player view, controller as sword, enemies walking in from the room edge
nodes.text: Show the player view in the real room: a low-poly sword where the right controller would be, 2-3 grunts or a shield enemy walking slowly in from the wall side, a red ring glowing at the player's feet. This is exactly what the MR battle engine does, so the picture does not overpromise.

nodes.title: Tactics key art: high three-quarter view of the whole 6 x 8 board
nodes.text: A board game sells through its board. Use a high 45-60 degree view showing the whole board, the player piece (knight, rook...) as a large figurine, 1-2 guard pieces and a glowing target square. In MR show the board lying on the real floor of the room.

nodes.title: Runner key art: looking down the route toward the portal
nodes.text: Put the camera at walking height looking along the route: a checkpoint marker close, one red hazard circle on the path, and the glowing portal at the far end framed by theme scenery. The eye travels the route the way the player will.

nodes.title: Pick the climax moment, not the start screen
nodes.text: Only one picture is drawn, so draw the storyboard climax: the boss turning, the last target captured, the portal opening. A start-of-game picture looks empty and sells nothing.

nodes.title: FLUX schnell draws text, hands and crowds badly: design around them
nodes.text: FLUX schnell is fast but garbles letters, fuses fingers and melts groups of more than 2-3 characters. Keep prompts to one hero subject, few secondary shapes, no readable signs, and hands either hidden or holding a simple object.

nodes.title: Key art prompt order: camera, subject, action, setting, light
nodes.text: The code appends the view, the low-poly style and the palette, so the prompt itself should be 1-3 sentences in this order: camera angle, main subject, what happens, setting, light. 40-90 English words is enough; longer prompts dilute the subject.

nodes.title: No HUD, score or words in the key art
nodes.text: The picture is an in-game moment without interface, so health bars, timers and titles stay out of key_art.prompt. HUD is listed separately in hud. Words in the prompt make FLUX draw fake letters, which look broken and cannot be translated.

nodes.title: MR key art must not replace the real walls or sky
nodes.text: Only the floor changes in MR, so a key art with a fantasy sky or castle walls around the player promises something the headset will never show. Big scenery should stand on the floor and be lower than the real room, or be marked VR only.

nodes.title: Titles: 1-3 words, sayable in Thai and English, one concrete image
nodes.text: A good title is short enough to shout across a venue and names one concrete thing: "Lantern Run", "Naga Gate", "Ice Knight". Thai players should be able to say the English or the Thai version without awkward sounds. Avoid generic words like "Adventure", "Quest", "World" on their own.

nodes.title: Title examples that work bilingually
nodes.text: Examples: "Krathong Glow", "Ghost Market Dash", "Knight of Ice", "Tuk-Tuk Rush", "Dino Steps", "Temple Chess". Each names the theme and hints at the verb in 2-3 words.

nodes.title: Logline: you are X, you do Y, because Z is fun
nodes.text: One sentence: who the player is, what they physically do, and the hook. "You are the last lantern keeper, walking the night river to relight 6 krathongs before the ghosts drift in." It must describe the real verb of the genre (walk, step out of rings, swing, move like a knight).

nodes.title: Pillars must be testable choices, not adjectives
nodes.text: A pillar is a rule every part must serve, so it must be able to reject ideas. "Every danger is seen 2 seconds before it hits" rejects instant traps; "Fun and exciting" rejects nothing. Write 3 pillars: one for feeling, one for play, one for the real space or players.
nodes.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

nodes.title: Derive one pillar from each top MDA feeling in the brief
nodes.text: Map the brief feelings to concrete pillars: challenge becomes "Fail fast, retry in 3 seconds"; fellowship becomes "Friends race side by side and see each other"; discovery becomes "Every checkpoint reveals a new view"; submission becomes "No way to lose, only to be faster"; narrative becomes "Each checkpoint is one line of the story".

nodes.title: Battle storyboard: first wave, mixed wave, boss, victory
nodes.text: Start: 2-3 slow grunts walk in, the player learns to swing. Middle: a shield enemy plus grunts, the player must hit from the side, rain rings fall. Climax: the boss or beast charges, the player steps out of a red ring and lands the combo. End: the arena calms, score and time shown.

nodes.title: Tactics storyboard: read the board, first capture, beat the guards, last target
nodes.text: Start: the player sees the board, their piece and 1-2 guards, and plans the first move. Middle: they capture targets in order while counting guard beats. Climax: the last target sits next to an attacked square and must be taken on the right beat. End: the board clears, time goes on the leaderboard.

nodes.title: Runner storyboard: spawn view, first hazard, final stretch, portal
nodes.text: Start: the player sees the first checkpoint and the story card. Middle: hazards appear between checkpoints, touching one sends them back. Climax: the last checkpoint and the most dramatic view (void drop, big creature). End: the portal, the score with time bonus.

nodes.title: player_does uses the body verb, not the story verb
nodes.text: Captions tell the story ("The ghost queen wakes"); player_does says what the body does ("steps left out of the red ring and swings twice"). Creators judge buildability from player_does, so keep it physical and possible.

nodes.title: Use 3 panels for 2-3 minute games, 4 for longer
nodes.text: Short sessions have no real middle: start, climax, end is honest. Games of 4 minutes or more need a middle panel to show the twist or difficulty step. Each panel needs its own beat and one must be the climax.

nodes.title: In MR put the climax where the audience can see it
nodes.text: Spectators see bodies, not the game, so the climax should be a big body action (turning to face the boss, a wide step out of a ring, walking through the portal) placed on the side nearest the audience zone.

nodes.title: Battle HUD: health, chapter, enemies left, score
nodes.text: A battle player needs four facts: how much health is left, which chapter of how many, how many enemies remain, and the score. On PC add a dash cooldown. Keep it to 4-5 items.

nodes.title: Tactics HUD: board number, targets captured, guard beat, timer
nodes.text: Tactics play is planning on a beat, so the HUD shows the board (1/5), captured targets in order (2/4), a guard beat indicator that ticks before guards move, and the race timer for the leaderboard.

nodes.title: Runner HUD: checkpoint count, score, timer, next label
nodes.text: The runner engine tracks checkpoints in order, score (+100 checkpoint, -25 hazard, +300 finish) and optional time limit. Show checkpoint 3/6, the next checkpoint label as the story line, score and timer. In a race add live position.

nodes.title: Kids HUD: 2 items, icons not numbers
nodes.text: For players under 9, show at most 2 HUD items as icons: progress (lit lanterns 3 of 6) and one danger cue. Numbers, timers and scores can live on the spectator screen for parents instead.

nodes.title: MR HUD stays low and few: nothing that needs looking up while walking
nodes.text: In passthrough the HUD floats in view, so keep it to 2-4 items near the lower edge or on the wrist. Players walking must keep their eyes on the floor. Big messages appear only when the player is standing still (start, chapter break, end).
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Runner flow, 2 minutes, 5 checkpoints
nodes.text: 0:00 story card and first view. 0:10 checkpoint 1, an easy straight. 0:30 first hazard pair. 0:50 checkpoint 3 with the best view. 1:20 tight zig-zag hazard. 1:40 last checkpoint. 1:50 portal and score. Short loops suit spaces under 4 x 4 m.

nodes.title: Runner flow, 5 minutes, 8 checkpoints with a twist
nodes.text: 0:00 intro card. 0:15 checkpoints 1-2 teach hazards. 1:30 checkpoint 3, story turn. 2:30 checkpoints 4-5, denser hazards. 3:30 the dramatic view (void floor section or big creature). 4:20 checkpoint 8. 4:40 portal, score and time bonus. 4:50 leaderboard.

nodes.title: Battle flow, 3 minutes, 3 chapters and a boss
nodes.text: 0:00 title and stance tip. 0:10 chapter 1: 3 grunts. 0:50 chapter 2: grunts plus a shield. 1:40 chapter 3: rain rings start. 2:20 boss or beast. 2:50 victory and score.

nodes.title: Battle flow, 8 minutes, 5 chapters for PC players
nodes.text: 0:00 intro. 0:20 ch1 grunts. 1:30 ch2 shields. 2:45 ch3 first beast. 4:00 ch4 rain plus mixed. 5:30 ch5 hard mix up to 9 enemies. 6:45 boss. 7:40 results. Long battles fit PC better than MR, where arms tire after about 4-5 minutes of swinging.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Tactics flow, 5 minutes, 4 boards
nodes.text: 0:00 rules card with the piece moves. 0:20 board 1: 2 targets, 1 guard. 1:20 board 2: 3 targets, 2 guards. 2:40 board 3: new piece, cracked squares. 3:50 board 4: guards on a faster beat. 4:45 time to leaderboard.

nodes.title: Tactics flow, 2 minutes, 2 boards for events
nodes.text: 0:00 show the knight move on the floor. 0:15 board 1: 2 targets, 1 guard. 1:00 board 2: 3 targets, 2 guards. 1:50 time on the leaderboard. Short and repeatable for queues at events.

nodes.title: Flow steps every 20-60 seconds, ending with results
nodes.text: Write 4-8 flow steps from 0:00 to the end, roughly every 20-60 s, including the intro card at 0:00 and the results or leaderboard as the last step. The last timestamp should match brief.session_minutes within 15 s.

nodes.title: First-time VR players: add 15-20 s of standing still at the start
nodes.text: People new to headsets need a moment to look around and trust the floor. Start the flow with 15-20 s where nothing threatens them, then introduce the first verb.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Battle sketch: arena with player start in the middle, spawn edges as danger
nodes.text: Draw a battle as shape "arena": start at the centre (0.5, 0.5), danger zones at the edges where enemies walk in (r 0.1-0.15), the boss zone on the far side, and the audience zone outside the edge where people stand.

nodes.title: Tactics sketch: board shape with start corner and goal on the far side
nodes.text: Draw tactics as shape "board": start at a near corner (about 0.2, 0.85), targets as story zones, guards as danger zones, the last target as the goal near the far side. In MR add the audience beside the long edge.

nodes.title: Runner sketch: route with 3-12 path points in walking order
nodes.text: Draw a runner as shape "route" with a path of at least 3 points (checked) in walking order, start at the first point, goal (portal) at the last, danger zones on the path between, story zones at key checkpoints. Keep points 0.08 inside the square edge for the 0.6 m safety margin.

nodes.title: MR audience zone sits outside the play area on the side the brief names
nodes.text: Put the audience zone where real spectators will be (a long wall, a doorway, chairs), just outside the play area, and bend the route or arena so the climax happens on that side. Never place audience inside the walking area.

nodes.title: PC sketches skip the audience zone
nodes.text: On PC spectators watch the screen, so there is no audience place in the level. Use the zones for start, goal or boss, danger and story only.

nodes.title: Sketch with 4-8 zones: one start, one goal or boss, the rest earn their place
nodes.text: Up to 10 zones are allowed but 4-8 read best. Every zone kind tells the creator something: start, goal or boss (both required by the check), 1-3 danger, 1-2 story, 1 audience in MR.

nodes.title: Small MR room under 4 x 4 m: one loop, big zones
nodes.text: In a living room or small classroom the sketch is a tight loop of 4-5 points with large zones (r 0.15-0.25), because a 3 m room only fits about 4 steps per side. Only runner fits below 3 m.

nodes.title: Good playtest questions are observable and specific
nodes.text: Ask what you can see happen, with a threshold: "Do 4 of 5 first-time players step out of the first red ring within 2 seconds?" Bad questions ask for opinions ("Is it fun?") that players answer politely and that do not tell you what to change.

nodes.title: Battle playtest questions
nodes.text: Examples: "Do players turn to face enemies coming from behind within 3 seconds?", "How many players get hit by the first rain ring?", "Do MR players stop swinging from arm tiredness before the boss?", "Does the shield enemy make players walk around it?"

nodes.title: Tactics playtest questions
nodes.text: Examples: "Can a first-time player say how a knight moves after board 1?", "How many players step on an attacked square on board 2?", "Do players stop and count the guard beat or rush?", "Does anyone walk off the board edge in MR?"

nodes.title: Runner playtest questions
nodes.text: Examples: "Do players find checkpoint 2 without help?", "How many hazards hit per run, and where?", "Do players read the checkpoint labels aloud?", "Does anyone hesitate at the void floor edge longer than 3 seconds?"

nodes.title: Playtest questions for kids
nodes.text: Examples: "Can a 7-year-old finish without an adult explaining?", "Does any child look scared or stop moving at the ghost?", "Do kids point and tell parents what they see?" Watch faces and bodies, kids rarely say they are confused.

nodes.title: Playtest questions for spectators and groups
nodes.text: Examples: "Do spectators cheer or call out at the climax?", "Can parents tell who is winning from the leaderboard screen?", "Do waiting players watch or look at phones?" The audience is part of the MR game.

nodes.title: Playtest questions for seniors and first-time VR players
nodes.text: Examples: "Does anyone ask to stop in the first minute?", "Do players walk at normal pace or shuffle?", "How many reach for a real wall for balance?" These reveal comfort problems before fun problems.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Bad playtest questions and their good rewrites
nodes.text: "Is it too hard?" becomes "How many tries does board 2 take?". "Is the theme cool?" becomes "Do players name the theme without being told?". "Is MR fun?" becomes "Do players look around the room in the first 30 seconds?"

nodes.title: Revising from comments: change only what was asked, keep the rest word for word
nodes.text: When the creator comments on a prototype, copy every field they did not mention unchanged and edit only the named parts. Rewriting everything makes them re-review and lose trust that their approved parts survive.

nodes.title: Follow the ripple: one change may need its linked fields updated
nodes.text: Some comments ripple: "make it night" changes palette, prompt_style and key art light; "add a boss" changes the storyboard climax, the sketch boss zone and the flow; "make it 2 minutes" shortens the flow and may drop the middle panel. Update the linked fields and nothing else.

nodes.title: When a comment asks for a mechanic the engine lacks, offer the nearest one
nodes.text: If the creator asks to "add shooting" or "let them pick up keys", keep the prototype and swap in the closest buildable thing: shooting becomes the sword or stepping out of rings; keys become checkpoints labelled "Key 1, Key 2" in order. Say so kindly in the caption.

nodes.title: Change key_art.prompt only when the look or climax changed
nodes.text: Each new key art costs a FLUX picture and the creator's attention. Rewrite key_art.prompt when the comment changes the theme, mood, palette, climax or platform; otherwise keep it identical so the same picture can be reused.

nodes.title: Revision example: "too scary for my 6-year-old"
nodes.text: Keep title, route and flow. Change art.mood to playful, prompt_style to spooky-cute, palette dark base up one step, key art to a smiling ghost, storyboard climax captions to surprise rather than threat, and add a test question about children stopping in fear.

nodes.title: Revision example: "we will play outside at noon now"
nodes.text: In MR an outdoor noon venue kills dark and neon looks. Keep the game and story; switch palette to a daylight-safe variant, lighting to noon, remove glow words from prompt_style, and redraw key art with sun and real sky visible. Mention the change in art.mood.

nodes.title: Every prototype field must tell the same game
nodes.text: Check that the logline verb appears in the storyboard, the climax appears in the key art, the HUD tracks what the flow describes, and the sketch zones match the storyboard places. A creator spots mismatches instantly and stops trusting the plan.

nodes.title: Do not let the theme stretch the genre in the prototype
nodes.text: A pirate tactics game is still a piece walking a 6 x 8 board; a dragon runner still walks checkpoints and avoids red circles. Theme dresses the engine, it does not add ships to sail or dragons to ride.

nodes.title: Battle flow, 2 minutes, MR event version with 2 chapters and a beast
nodes.text: 0:00 look around, sword appears in the right hand. 0:15 chapter 1: 3 slow grunts from one wall. 0:50 chapter 2: grunts from two sides plus rain rings. 1:25 a beast charges in as the finale. 1:50 victory and score. Short enough for queues and for arms that tire fast in MR.

nodes.title: Battle flow, 3 minutes, PC version with dash taught early
nodes.text: 0:00 hero intro and controls. 0:10 chapter 1: 4 grunts, learn the 3-hit combo. 0:45 chapter 2: 2 shields, learn to dash behind them. 1:30 chapter 3: up to 9 mixed enemies with rain. 2:20 boss. 2:50 score and time. PC players tolerate denser chapters than MR players.

nodes.title: Runner flow, 8 minutes, 10 checkpoints in 3 acts
nodes.text: 0:00 story card. 0:20 act 1, checkpoints 1-3, open easy path. 2:30 act 2, checkpoints 4-7, hazard pairs and a story turn at 5. 5:00 calm view stretch, no hazards. 5:45 act 3, checkpoints 8-10, densest hazards or void floor. 7:30 portal. 7:45 score, time bonus, leaderboard. Needs a space over 10 x 10 m or PC.

nodes.title: Tactics flow, 8 minutes, 6 boards with a new piece every 2 boards
nodes.text: 0:00 rules card. 0:20 boards 1-2 with the rook: 2 then 3 targets, 1-2 guards. 2:30 boards 3-4 with the knight, cracked squares appear. 5:00 boards 5-6 with the queen, guards on a 3 s beat and tables blocking lines. 7:30 final time, leaderboard. Good for puzzle fans on PC or a calm MR hall.

nodes.title: Classroom learning: chalk green, paper white, pencil yellow, ink blue
nodes.text: Palette: #2f5d50 chalk green, #fbfaf5 paper white, #ffcf33 pencil yellow, #2d5bd1 ink blue, #e5262f hazard red. Made for a real classroom under fluorescent light, where everything stays readable. In daylight by windows the paper white can glare, so keep it on small props and use chalk green for the ground. The hazard colour #e5262f (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Office team-building: slate, teal, warm coral, clean white
nodes.text: Palette: #3c4a5c slate, #1fa59a team teal, #ff8a65 warm coral, #f5f7fa clean white, #d7191c hazard red. A calm grown-up palette for meeting rooms and lobbies under office light. Coral is warm but clearly lighter than the hazard red, so keep it on goals and team markers. In daylight it still reads well. The hazard colour #d7191c (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Tropical beach: lagoon turquoise, white sand, palm green, sunset coral
nodes.text: Palette: #23c6c8 lagoon, #f6e7c1 white sand, #3f9b4f palm green, #ff8c69 sunset coral, #7b2cbf urchin purple hazard. Outdoor daylight friendly, like a real beach. Coral and sand are close to warm hazard colours, so hazards turn urchin purple, which stands out on sand and water alike. Indoors raise saturation a step. The hazard colour #7b2cbf (urchin purple hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Autumn harvest: maple orange, wheat gold, plum, pine
nodes.text: Palette: #d9622b maple orange, #e8c35a wheat gold, #5e2750 plum, #2e5e4e pine, #00b4d8 frost cyan hazard. Warm all over, so a red hazard would hide among leaves; hazards become frost cyan. Pine and plum give the dark anchors. Works indoors and in soft daylight; at noon lift plum toward a lighter berry. The hazard colour #00b4d8 (frost cyan hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Rainy season: storm grey, wet leaf green, umbrella yellow, puddle blue
nodes.text: Palette: #5b6770 storm grey, #4caf50 wet leaf, #ffd400 umbrella yellow, #5fa8d3 puddle blue, #ff2d2d hazard red. Moody but not dark: grey sets the weather, yellow umbrellas guide the eye. Good indoors and on overcast days; on bright noon days the grey turns flat, so lean on yellow and green shapes. The hazard colour #ff2d2d (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Chinese New Year in Thailand: lantern red, lucky gold, jade, ink black
nodes.text: Palette: #c8102e lantern red, #f2c14e lucky gold, #00a86b jade, #1c1c1c ink black, #00e5ff electric cyan hazard. The festival is red by nature, so hazards must not be red: they become electric cyan, which appears nowhere in the decor. Rich indoors and at night like Yaowarat street lights; in daylight keep ink black small and let gold and jade carry contrast. The hazard colour #00e5ff (electric cyan hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: School sports day: field green, team blue, team yellow, team purple
nodes.text: Palette: #3fa34d field green, #1e63d6 team blue, #ffcc00 team yellow, #8e44ad team purple, #ff1a1a hazard red. Thai sports days use team colours; red is kept out of the teams so it can stay the hazard. Built for outdoor fields and gyms in daylight, where saturated primaries read from the stands. The hazard colour #ff1a1a (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

nodes.title: Race or shared-floor key art: two players, side by side, one clear leader
nodes.text: For an online race or shared floor show exactly 2 player avatars or 2 headset players, one a step ahead, both heading to the same checkpoint or portal. Two figures is the most FLUX schnell draws cleanly, and a visible leader sells competition in one frame.

nodes.title: Together storyboard: shared floor where players see each other, not a team mechanic
nodes.text: On a shared floor players walk the same course and see each other's avatars, but there is no shared score or hand-off. Write beats around that: start, players gather at spawn; middle, one waits for or calls out to the other near a hazard; climax, they reach the last checkpoint together; end, both portals and both scores.

nodes.title: Race HUD adds live position; shared-floor HUD adds nothing
nodes.text: In a race each player walks their own copy, so add live position (2nd of 4) next to checkpoint count and timer, and mirror the leaderboard on a spectator screen. On a shared floor the other players are visible as avatars, so no extra HUD is needed.

nodes.title: Ask what the game is FOR before what it looks like (วัตถุประสงค์)
nodes.text: Many creators are teachers, brands, HR teams or parents who need the game to do a job. Early in the interview, ask one question: what should be different for players after they play (they know a fact order, they remember a brand, they talked to colleagues, they relaxed)? The answer picks the genre, session length and whether there is a race far more than the theme does.

nodes.title: The purpose must ride on the core loop, not on top of it
nodes.text: A purpose game works when the thing the player does again and again is itself the lesson, the message or the bonding. If the purpose lives only on the intro card while play is unrelated, players remember the play and forget the purpose. Check each option: if you deleted the theme, would the purpose still be present in what the player does?
nodes.source: Bruckman 1999, Can Educational Be Fun? (GDC); design practice

nodes.title: Ordered checkpoints teach sequences (ลำดับเหตุการณ์)
nodes.text: The runner forces checkpoints to be touched in order, so it is a natural teacher of anything that has a correct order: a life cycle, a process, a timeline, steps of an experiment. Give each checkpoint one short fact label in the true order, 4-8 stops, 1.5-3 m apart. Walking the order with the body helps it stick, and the order is the content, not decoration.

nodes.title: Life cycle walk: butterfly, frog or rice plant
nodes.text: A life cycle maps perfectly onto a loop runner. Butterfly: 'Tiny egg on a leaf', 'Caterpillar eats', 'Chrysalis rests', 'Butterfly flies', back to the leaf. Rice for Thai schools: 'Seed soaks', 'Seedling grows', 'Plant in paddy', 'Rice flowers', 'Golden harvest'. 4-6 stops in a loop, morning lighting, a big model of each stage beside its stop, hazards as hungry birds or dry cracked mud.

nodes.title: Thai history timeline by eras, not by kings
nodes.text: For Thai history, make checkpoints eras in order: 'Ban Chiang pottery', 'Sukhothai script', 'Ayutthaya trade port', 'Thonburi', 'Rattanakosin city'. Show each era with buildings, boats, crafts and markets as scenery. Do not put real royal figures, portraits or royal symbols in the game; teach through places, objects and daily life, which is also easier to show in low-poly.

nodes.title: Solar system walk: planets in order from the Sun
nodes.text: Spawn at the Sun and place 8 checkpoints, one per planet, Mercury to Neptune, so the order is learned with the feet. The real distances cannot fit any room, so space the stops evenly (1.5-3 m) and say on the intro card that the spacing is not to scale; a teacher can show real scale later.
