Night lighting indoors makes the planets pop; hazards as asteroid patches between Mars and Jupiter teach the belt's position.

nodes.title: Geography as a journey: river, regions or a trade route
nodes.text: Geography works when the route is a real journey in miniature: the Chao Phraya from the northern rivers to the Gulf, or a trip through Thailand's regions north to south. Each checkpoint is a place in travel order with a landmark-type model (mountains, rice plains, a port, islands). The room's long side can stand for north to south so players feel direction.

nodes.title: English vocabulary walk: one word per checkpoint with a picture model
nodes.text: For Thai learners of English, each checkpoint label is one English word from a topic set (fruit, jobs, weather, prepositions) and a clear model of it stands beside the stop. Order can follow a story ('Wake up', 'Brush teeth', 'Eat breakfast', 'Walk to school') so the words are used in context. Players cannot type or answer in the game, so the teacher asks the class to say the words before and after.

nodes.title: Maths through movement: tactics pieces and number-sequence labels
nodes.text: Tactics pieces are maths made visible: the rook moves in lines, the bishop in diagonals, the knight in an L of 2 and 1 squares. A board where the player must plan a capture order teaches counting squares, coordinates and planning. In a runner, checkpoint labels can be a number pattern ('2', '4', '8', '16') so the next stop is a prediction the class makes aloud before the player walks.

nodes.title: Tactics boards teach planning and algorithms
nodes.text: A tactics board is a small algorithm: a fixed set of rules, a goal (capture targets in order) and obstacles (guards on a beat, cracked squares). Solving it means planning steps ahead, testing, and fixing a plan after a mistake, which is the core of computational thinking. Ask the player to say the plan out loud before stepping, then compare plan and result in the debrief.

nodes.title: Teaching chess piece moves: one piece per board, simple to complex
nodes.text: To teach how pieces move, give one piece per board in this order: rook (lines), bishop (diagonals), queen (both), knight (the L, hardest). The first board of each piece has no guards, only targets, so the player just learns the move; the second adds one guard to show attacked squares. In MR the body learns the shape of the move, which beginners often forget on a small board.

nodes.title: Battle as metaphor: germs vs the immune system
nodes.text: The battle engine can teach a defence story: the player is a white blood cell, grunts are fast small germs, shield enemies are germs with a tough coat that must be hit from the side, the beast is a big infection, and the boss is the final wave. Chapter titles can teach stages ('The cut', 'The alarm', 'The big fight'). In the debrief, the teacher says where the metaphor is not true (cells do not use swords).

nodes.title: A battle metaphor that teaches a wrong idea
nodes.text: Metaphors stick, including the wrong parts. If recycling is taught as 'slash the plastic monsters', kids may learn that waste disappears when you hit it. Before using battle for a lesson, list what each element stands for and check one wrong lesson it could teach; if the wrong lesson is the main takeaway, choose a runner where the correct order of actions is the content instead.

nodes.title: Hazards as common wrong ideas
nodes.text: Hazards can carry labels, so they can stand for misconceptions: on a solar system walk a red circle labelled 'Sun goes round Earth', on a food chain walk 'Plants eat soil'. Stepping in one costs 25 points and sends the player back, a gentle way to mark a wrong idea without quizzes. Keep it to 2-3 such hazards and discuss them in the debrief.

nodes.title: No quizzes, typed answers or multiple choice in any engine
nodes.text: Teachers often ask for questions with answers. No engine can show a question and accept an answer, and routes are fixed, so there are no branching 'pick the right door' paths. Offer instead: the correct answer order as checkpoints, wrong ideas as labelled hazards, and the teacher asking questions out loud before and after play. The game is the experience; the quiz happens in the room.

nodes.title: Write one observable learning objective
nodes.text: A learning game needs one objective phrased as something you can see a student do afterwards: 'put the 5 rice stages in order', 'name 6 planets from the Sun', 'explain why the knight jumps'. Avoid 'understand' or 'learn about'. The objective decides the checkpoint labels, and it becomes the thing you check in the debrief.

nodes.title: Learning games by age band
nodes.text: Ages 5-7: 4-5 checkpoints, labels of 1-3 words with picture-clear models, no time limit, no tactics guards. Ages 8-10: 5-7 checkpoints, short fact labels, tactics with rook or bishop and one slow guard. Ages 11-14: up to 8-10 checkpoints, cause-and-effect labels, tactics with knight or queen, battle as a metaphor. For MR, follow the headset maker's minimum age (Meta sets 10+ for Quest, with a parent-managed account); younger classes play on PC.
nodes.source: Meta Quest safety and age guidance; design practice

nodes.title: Debrief after play: the learning happens in the talk
nodes.text: Experience becomes learning when people reflect on it. Plan a 3-5 minute debrief with three questions: What happened, in order? Why was it in that order? Where is that true in real life? Players and watchers answer together. Put the debrief in the flow of the prototype so the teacher plans time for it.

nodes.title: Give each fact at the moment it is used
nodes.text: Good games teach by putting information exactly where and when the player needs it, not in a manual first. In a learning Land, that means the fact sits on the checkpoint label the player is walking to, and the scenery beside it shows it. Keep the intro card for the story and goal only, and never put a reading wall before play.
nodes.source: Gee 2003, What Video Games Have to Teach Us About Learning and Literacy

nodes.title: Which school topics fit the engines and which do not
nodes.text: Fits well: sequences (life cycles, history eras, steps of a recipe or experiment), ordered lists (planets, food chains, journeys), movement rules and planning (tactics), defence or struggle stories (battle as metaphor). Fits poorly: open debate, reading comprehension, essays, arithmetic drills, anything that needs an answer typed or chosen. For poor fits, propose a game as the hook and keep the core task in class.

nodes.title: Class rotation: 30 students, few headsets, everyone busy
nodes.text: With 2-4 headsets and 30 students, run stations: players in the area, a watching group with a simple sheet (write the checkpoint order you see, spot the hazards), and a group doing a related paper task. Turns of 3-4 minutes and a race of 2-4 players keep the queue moving; a full class rotation takes about 30-40 minutes. Watchers see bodies, so the sheet asks about what bodies do (where did she turn back?).

nodes.title: Science fair or school project: students design the Land
nodes.text: At a science fair, the learning can be in making the game: a student team picks a process, writes the checkpoint order and hazards, and explains each design decision on a poster. Visitors play a 2-minute runner and the team explains why each stop is where it is. The AI should help the students reason (why this order, why this hazard) rather than design it all for them.

nodes.title: A museum game sends visitors back to the real objects
nodes.text: In a museum, the game should not replace the exhibits; it should make visitors look harder at them. Base each checkpoint on a real object in the nearby gallery ('Find the bronze drum'), and end the story with an invitation to go and see the real one. In MR passthrough, an exhibit visible beyond the edge of the play area can be the backdrop of the finish.

nodes.title: Heritage craft as a process walk: Lanna umbrella or lacquerware
nodes.text: Local crafts are perfect sequences. Bo Sang umbrella making: 'Cut the bamboo', 'Make the ribs', 'Stretch the saa paper', 'Paint the flowers', 'Dry in the sun'. Each stop shows the tool or the half-made object, so visitors learn the steps and the effort. Morning or noon lighting, warm wood and paper colours, one hazard as a wet paint puddle.

nodes.title: Local legends: tell them as legends, keep them respectful
nodes.text: Local legends (a guardian spirit of a mountain, a city founding tale) make great narrative runners, but players should know it is a legend, not history. Say 'the old story says' on the intro card. Use original character designs, avoid making revered spirits into enemies or hazards, and ask a local guide or museum staff to check the telling.

nodes.title: Library reading programme: walk the story of a book
nodes.text: A library can turn a book's plot into a runner: each checkpoint is a key moment in story order, and the finish invites the reader to the shelf where the book lives. Use public-domain tales or the library's own original stories, or get permission for a published book's names and look. Calm indoor lighting and 5-6 stops; kids who read the book first will recognise the order.

nodes.title: Brand activation: which success goal matters most?
nodes.text: Brand clients mean different things by success: dwell time at the booth, a photo moment people share, high throughput (players per hour), a leaderboard with prizes, or one clear message remembered. Each pulls the design a different way (throughput means 2-minute turns, dwell means watchable races, message means story labels). Ask the creator to pick the top one.

nodes.title: Booth throughput: players per hour = headsets x 60 / (turn + changeover)
nodes.text: Changeover (fit headset, 20-second brief, clean, reset) takes about 1-2 minutes. With 4 headsets, a 3-minute turn and 2-minute changeover give 4 x 60 / 5 = 48 players per hour; a 2-minute turn gives 60. If the client expects 500 players a day over 8 hours, that needs about 60 per hour, so 2-minute turns. Do this maths before choosing session length.

nodes.title: Brand look without ads inside gameplay
nodes.text: Carry the brand through the world, not through billboards: use the brand palette for the floor and props, make the finish portal area in brand colours, and design an original world that fits the brand's values (fresh, playful, premium). Avoid pop-up ads, slogans on every prop and logo text in key art. Logos belong on the booth, the queue sign and the leaderboard screen, where people read them.

nodes.title: Never make the product a hazard or an enemy
nodes.text: If a drink can is a hazard players must avoid, or a snack is an enemy to slash, the game tells players to avoid the product. Make the product the goal or the reward: a giant model at the finish, checkpoint labels that follow the product's story ('Pick the fresh leaves'), or the theme of the world. Hazards should be the problem the product solves (thirst, dull days), shown as neutral things.

nodes.title: One brand message per game
nodes.text: A 2-3 minute game can carry one message, not five. Pick one sentence the client wants remembered and build the story card (2-4 sentences) and the checkpoint labels around it, for example a coffee brand's 'from mountain farm to cup' becomes 5 stops in that order. Extra messages go on the booth, not in the game.

nodes.title: The photo moment happens outside the headset
nodes.text: Spectators and cameras see bodies, not the game, so the shareable moment is real: the player's victory pose at the finish, a friend's reaction, the leaderboard screen with their nickname. Put the finish portal where a photo spot with the brand backdrop sits behind the player, and let staff take the photo (with consent) after the turn. A screen showing the player's view helps the photo tell the story.

nodes.title: Leaderboard prizes that stay fair and keep people coming
nodes.text: A prize leaderboard draws repeat visits but can make late visitors feel they cannot win. Reset the board every hour or every session block and give a prize per block; use nicknames or team colours, never real names or phone numbers. Everyone plays the same Land with the same timeLimit so scores compare. Announce the current top score so the queue has a target.

nodes.title: Design the queue: watching is the trailer
nodes.text: The queue is where people decide to stay. Place it along the side where the players' turns and the finish are visible, show the leaderboard and a short looped video of the player's view, and give a 3-rule card people can read in 20 seconds. Pre-brief in the queue so the in-headset time is all play.

nodes.title: Staff operation plan for an event booth
nodes.text: Plan staff before the event: about 1 staff per 2 headsets to fit, brief and spot players, plus 1 person on the queue. A spotter stands at the edge to stop players drifting out of the area. Write a 3-line script for staff (welcome, the goal, the safety rule) and a reset step between turns (restart Land, wipe headset, check the floor is clear).

nodes.title: No personal data in the game, even for brand leads
nodes.text: The game should never ask for names, phone numbers, emails, schools or photos. Leaderboards use nicknames or team colours. If a brand wants leads, that happens outside the game, on the client's own form with clear consent, and is not a condition for playing. This also keeps children safe at public events.

nodes.title: Team-building: compete or cooperate? (ทีมบิลดิ้ง)
nodes.text: Ask what the HR team wants people to feel: competing teams (energy, rivalry, good for sales teams) or one team together (trust, communication, good for new or mixed teams). Race mode with a leaderboard serves rivalry; shared-floor together mode or a relay where the team's total time counts serves cooperation. A mix (teams race each other, members cooperate inside a team) suits most groups.

nodes.title: Relay of short boards: every member plays, the team total counts
nodes.text: Split the team so each person plays one 1-2 minute turn: a tactics board or a short runner section, and the team's summed time or score goes on the board. Everyone contributes once, nobody carries the team alone, and teammates outside the area can call out plans. Use 3-4 boards of rising difficulty so the team chooses who plays which.

nodes.title: Teammates outside the area become the navigators
nodes.text: There is no voice chat, so make real talking the teamwork: the player in the headset sees the world, and teammates outside see the body and the screen with the player's view, calling out 'next stop is left' or 'guard moves next beat'. Communication becomes the game. Keep callers outside the play area behind a line on the floor.

nodes.title: Mixed-ability teams: walking pace, no running, optional effort
nodes.text: Office groups mix ages, fitness levels and comfort with VR. Design for walking pace (no running in MR), checkpoints 2-3 m apart, few or slow hazards, and battle chapters without rain for the first round. Let each person choose their role: player, caller or scorekeeper. The goal is that the least sporty person enjoys it.

nodes.title: Team debrief: link the play to how the team works
nodes.text: End team-building with a 10-minute talk: What helped us? What did the callers do that worked? Where did we lose time? What would we do differently in round 3? Link one answer to real work (how we hand over tasks). Without this, it was a fun break; with it, the team names a behaviour to keep.

nodes.title: Forcing everyone into a headset
nodes.text: Some people cannot or do not want to wear a headset (motion sickness, glasses, pregnancy, anxiety, make-up). If the only way to join is to play, they sit out and the event fails its purpose. Design roles that need no headset: caller, plan writer, scorekeeper, judge of the best victory pose. Mention these roles in the options.

nodes.title: Birthday party: the birthday child is the star of the story
nodes.text: Let the birthday child choose the theme from 3 (dinosaurs, space, candy) and write the story around them ('Help the dino find the giant cake'). With 8-12 kids and 2 headsets, use 2-minute turns in pairs so everyone plays twice in an hour, and give the birthday child the first and the final run. The finish is the cake model, and the real cake comes right after.

nodes.title: Family day: grandparents and grandchildren play together
nodes.text: On a shared floor in together mode, a grandparent and a grandchild walk the same Land and see each other's avatars. Use a gentle runner: checkpoints 2.5-3 m apart, no time limit, 1-2 hazards, studio or morning light, no void floor. Labels can invite talk ('Grandma's old market', 'Feed the buffalo'), so the older player tells stories while the child leads.

nodes.title: Family game night at home on PC: take turns on a tactics board
nodes.text: On PC, a family can share one computer: tactics boards become a puzzle the family solves together, one person on the keyboard while the others plan out loud. Use 3-4 boards of rising difficulty and let a different family member drive each one. Runner Lands with WASD suit a quick turn for each person, with the time board making a friendly family challenge.

nodes.title: A calm game removes pressure: no timer, no race, few hazards
nodes.text: For relaxation (submission), take away the things that create pressure: timeLimit null, solo or together mode instead of race, 0-2 hazards placed well off the route, and no leaderboard on display. The score still exists in the engine, so say on the intro card that there is no rush. The player's own pace is the design.

nodes.title: Calm tour route: wide loop, long sightlines, gentle labels
nodes.text: A relaxation runner is a tour: a wide loop with stops 2.5-3 m apart, open sightlines so the next checkpoint is always visible, and nature or garden scenery with slow animated rides (a turning windmill, floating lanterns). Labels are gentle invitations, not orders: 'Rest by the pond', 'Watch the clouds', 'Listen to the bamboo'. Morning or evening lighting gives soft colour.

nodes.title: Gentle mood without a soundtrack setting
nodes.text: The engine's game settings have no music track, so do not promise a soundtrack. Create the calm feel visually: soft lighting presets, slow-moving scenery, open space, soft palette (sage, sand, sky blue). If the venue wants music, it can play quiet music on its own speakers in the real room, which players in passthrough hear naturally.

nodes.title: No health or therapy claims for calm games
nodes.text: A calm walk can feel restful, but the game must not claim to treat stress, anxiety, depression, pain or any condition. Describe it as 'a quiet walk in a garden world', not therapy. If a clinic or therapist uses it, they decide how it fits their practice. Avoid words like heal, cure, therapy or reduces anxiety in titles, stories and pitches.

nodes.title: Sensory-friendly sessions: predictable and easy to stop
nodes.text: For players who are sensitive to busy input (some autistic players, anxious first-timers, older adults), design for predictability: show the route from the spawn, no void floor, no sudden appearing models, soft lighting, few props, no time limit. Tell them before play that lifting the headset or saying stop ends it any time. A quiet hour at an event helps.

nodes.title: Estimate walking distance honestly from the route
nodes.text: Distance walked is about the sum of the gaps between stops: 7 checkpoints 2.5 m apart plus spawn and portal is roughly 20 m, so a single runner lap is short. A 10 x 10 m route with 10 stops 3 m apart is about 30-35 m. One step is about 0.75 m, so 1,000 steps needs about 750 m, which is many rounds. Frame runner fitness as gentle movement, not a workout.

nodes.title: Movement goals in MR still mean walking, never running
nodes.text: In passthrough MR, running risks collisions and falls even in a cleared space, and headsets slip. Effort comes from more walking, turning, stepping out of rings, squatting to see low details, and arm swings in battle, not speed. Set time limits generous enough that a brisk walk wins.
nodes.source: Meta VR comfort and MR design guidelines; design practice

nodes.title: MR battle as interval movement: chapters are sets, gaps are rest
nodes.text: Battle in MR is the most physical genre: the controller is the sword and red rings make players step. Treat each chapter as a set of 45-90 seconds and the gap between chapters as rest. Add rain rings in middle chapters for extra stepping, and keep the boss short. A 3-4 chapter game makes about 5 minutes of real movement.

nodes.title: Active play safety: heat, sweat, breaks and spotters
nodes.text: Active headset play warms people fast. Keep active turns to 5-10 minutes, offer water, add breaks between rounds, and use wipeable face covers. Outdoors at noon in Thailand, heat and glare add up, so prefer evenings or shade. A spotter watches the area edge, and swinging arms need 1 m of clear space around each player.
nodes.source: Meta VR comfort and safety guidelines; design practice

nodes.title: No step counting, heart rate or calorie tracking
nodes.text: The engines track checkpoints, hazards, time and score, not steps, heart rate or calories. Do not promise fitness stats in the HUD. If the purpose is a step goal, use the score and finish time as the progress measure, and suggest players use their own phone or watch if they want steps.

nodes.title: Chiang Mai city promotion: a journey through the old city
nodes.text: A tourism runner can walk the old city as a journey: 'Enter at Tha Phae Gate', 'Cross the moat', 'Lanna wooden house', 'Sunday walking street', 'Khao soi stall', 'Lanterns over the river'. Use Lanna-style buildings, the moat and lanterns as scenery, and the mountain on the skyline as a silhouette. Keep temples as respectful backdrop scenery, never checkpoints to stomp or hazards.

nodes.title: A tourism game is a teaser for the real place
nodes.text: The purpose of a tourism game is that players want to go. Show a short taste of 5-6 places, not the whole city, and end the story with a real-world invitation ('The lanterns are real: see them at the river tonight'). Staff can hand a paper map after the turn. A game that feels complete leaves no reason to visit.

nodes.title: International visitors: picture-first, very short labels
nodes.text: Tourist booths get visitors who read neither Thai nor much English. The game text is in one lang (th or en), so make labels 1-3 words, choose English for mixed tourist crowds, and let the scenery carry the meaning (a lantern, a noodle bowl, a gate). Staff demonstrate with gestures, and the 3 rules have pictures on the booth sign.

nodes.title: Festival booth: Yi Peng and Loy Krathong evening walk
nodes.text: During Yi Peng and Loy Krathong in Chiang Mai, an evening booth can run a lantern and krathong walk: 5 checkpoints in festival order ('Fold the banana leaf', 'Add flowers and candle', 'Light the lantern', 'Make a wish', 'Float on the river'), evening or night lighting, water and lantern scenery. Outdoor at night, glow reads well. 2-minute turns for big crowds.

nodes.title: Fair competition: everyone plays the identical Land
nodes.text: Competition is only fair if every player faces the same thing. Use one fixed Land, the same timeLimit and the same lighting for all heats, and do not change the layout during the event. Tactics boards are already built and proven solvable by code, so every board has a fair answer. Change only between event days, and announce it.

nodes.title: Repeatable skill: practice run, then scored runs
nodes.text: Competitive games need a skill that grows with tries: a route with a faster line around hazards, or a tactics board with a shorter capture path. Give first-timers one practice run that is not scored, then 2-3 scored runs with the best counting. This keeps the board about skill, not about who already played before.

nodes.title: Event tournament: heats of 2-6 racers, then a final
nodes.text: In race mode each player walks their own copy of the Land with a live leaderboard, so heats of 2-6 run side by side if the space allows. Run 3-minute heats through the day, keep a top-scores board, and hold a final at a fixed time when the crowd is biggest. The final is the spectator moment: put the finish portals on the crowd side.

nodes.title: Wheelchair users in MR: wide route, gentle turns, larger stops
nodes.text: A seated player in a wheelchair can play an MR runner because the headset tracks their position as they roll. Make the route at least 1.5 m wide with no tight turns, stops 2.5-3 m apart, few hazards placed away from the turning circle, and a smooth floor without cables. Tactics squares of 1 m are tight for wheelchairs; prefer the runner or a PC game.

nodes.title: Seated play default: offer PC as a full version, not a lesser one
nodes.text: When players must stay seated (bed-bound, limited stamina, a hospital ward, an office desk), PC is the natural platform: all three genres work with mouse and keyboard. Present it as the full game, with the same story and Land, so seated players are not given a smaller experience.

nodes.title: Low vision and colour blindness: contrast and shapes
nodes.text: Hazards are red circles, so pick a ground colour that is not red, brown or green (sand, pale grey, blue) so they stand out for red-green colour blind players. Use studio or noon lighting indoors, large and simple scenery shapes, and checkpoints with clear tall markers nearby. Avoid fog, night or neon when players have low vision.

nodes.title: Simple language for labels, rules and story
nodes.text: Write for the weakest reader in the group (young kids, second-language players, people with learning disabilities): labels of 2-4 words, verb first ('Find the boat'), rules of 3 short lines, story of 2-3 short sentences with everyday words. Picture-clear scenery repeats what the label says, so reading is a help, not a gate.

nodes.title: Special education class: one small success, repeated
nodes.text: For a special education class, aim for a guaranteed success: a short runner of 4 checkpoints in a 4 x 4 m space, no hazards or one well off the route, no time limit, bright lighting and a big friendly finish. A teacher or aide stays at the edge and can talk the student through. Playing the same Land twice builds confidence; the second run is often the joyful one.

nodes.title: Playtest a learning game: can they do the objective after?
nodes.text: Check learning, not just enjoyment. After play, give players the checkpoint facts on paper cards shuffled and ask them to put them in order (2 minutes); compare with a group who did not play, or with a quick check before play. Also watch: do players read labels aloud, do watchers argue about the order? If they enjoy it but cannot order the cards, the facts are decoration.

nodes.title: Playtest a brand activation: count, time and watch
nodes.text: Measure what the client cares about: players per hour, average queue length, how long passers-by stop to watch (dwell), photos taken at the photo spot, repeat players, and whether players can say the brand message in one sentence afterwards. Count over a fixed 30 minutes and compare with the throughput maths.

nodes.title: Playtest team-building: watch the talking, not the score
nodes.text: For a team game the evidence is communication: how often teammates call to the player, whether quiet members speak, whether the team changes its plan between rounds, and whether everyone had a role. Note laughter and high-fives. A great score with silent teammates means the game did not do its job.

nodes.title: Playtest a calm game: do players slow down and look around?
nodes.text: Signs of a working relaxation game: players walk slower on the second half than the first, stop to look at scenery, turn their heads, and take the headset off smiling rather than rushing out. Ask one question after: on 1-5, how calm do you feel now compared to before? If players hurry to the portal, something (a timer, a hazard, the score) is still pushing them.

nodes.title: Playtest active play: effort, safety and willingness to repeat
nodes.text: For movement games, observe minutes of active play, how many chapters or rounds players finish, near-misses at the area edge, and whether players want another go. A simple effort question after play (on 1-10, how hard did that feel?) shows if it is too easy or too much. Any near-miss with a wall or another player means the layout needs more clearance.

nodes.title: Playtest tourism and museum games: do they go to the real thing?
nodes.text: The best evidence that a museum or tourism game worked is behaviour after the headset: visitors walk to the related exhibit, ask staff where the real place is, take a map, or name a place they want to visit. Count these over a session. If visitors leave the booth and go elsewhere, the game was a ride, not a doorway.

nodes.title: Playtest a competition: is it fair and worth repeating?
nodes.text: Check that scores spread out (not everyone the same, not one runaway winner), that newcomers improve on their second run, and that nobody complains a heat was unfair. Watch return rate: do players rejoin the queue to beat their score? Many ties mean the course needs a skill line; one dominant player with huge gaps means a beginner board is needed.

nodes.title: Playtest family and inclusive games: did everyone play and enjoy?
nodes.text: For families, parties and accessibility briefs, success is inclusion: every person who wanted to play finished at least once, the youngest and oldest both smiled, helpers (parents, aides) needed to step in rarely, and nobody was left watching all session. Note who needed help and where on the route; that spot needs a wider path, a simpler label or a removed hazard.

nodes.title: In MR the player sees the real place, only the floor is replaced
nodes.text: Quest 3 passthrough shows the real walls, people, sky and light; the engine only swaps the floor for the Land's ground and stands models on it at 1:1 scale. Design every option as a layer on top of a real place, not as a sealed virtual world. Ask what is around the floor, because that is half of what the player will see.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Everything stands at real 1:1 scale on the real floor
nodes.text: A 1 m model in the Land is 1 m tall in the room, next to real furniture and people. A 4 m dragon in a 3 m high living room clips through the ceiling visually, while the same dragon on a car park looks huge and right. Size hero pieces against the real ceiling height and the floor size, not against an imagined world.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Use the real walls as the edge of the world
nodes.text: Players can see the real walls, so make them part of the fiction: the fortress wall, the edge of the island, the end of the map. Place the route so it turns before the walls with at least 0.6 m to spare, and put low edge scenery near the walls so the change from virtual floor to real wall feels intended.

nodes.title: A real skyline or garden becomes the backdrop for free
nodes.text: On a rooftop, car park or garden the real sky, trees and buildings fill the view above the floor. Pick themes that agree with them: a city skyline suits sci-fi or heroes, trees suit forest, dinosaurs or farm, open sky suits pirates or islands. Put the finish portal so players face the best view when they arrive.

nodes.title: Turn the real crowd into the in-game audience
nodes.text: In a hall or at an event, the people standing around are visible in passthrough. Frame them as the arena audience, the villagers or the race fans. The story can say the crowd is watching your trial, which makes cheers feel part of the game and makes players perform for them.

nodes.title: The void floor is dramatic but makes people dizzy
nodes.text: The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop with scenery below. It is a strong wow moment but triggers fear of heights, slower walking and discomfort, especially for first-time VR players and seniors. Use it for short, slow sections with confident adults, never for kids or races.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Mark backdrop pieces VR only so they vanish in MR
nodes.text: Decor can be flagged VR only so it is hidden in MR and shown only in full VR. Use it for walls, ceilings, skies and tall backdrops that would otherwise float through the real room or block the view of real walls and people. Floor-level scenery stays visible on both.

nodes.title: There is no joystick movement in MR, the route must fit the real floor
nodes.text: In MR players move only by walking, so the whole route, every checkpoint and the portal must lie inside the real empty floor. A creator who wants a long journey gets it through loops, zig-zags and story labels, not distance. Offer a spiral or out-and-back route instead of teleporting or scrolling worlds.

nodes.title: Living room: small, furniture, 1-2 players
nodes.text: A typical cleared living room gives 3 x 3 to 4 x 5 m of floor, with sofas, tables and a TV at the edges and warm indoor light. It fits 1-2 players, a short loop of 4-5 checkpoints and small props. Family members watch from the sofa. Cosy themes (toys, candy, farm, small dragons) fit better than epic battles.

nodes.title: Classroom: desks to move, a class watching
nodes.text: A classroom is about 7 x 8 m but desks fill it; after pushing them aside the clear floor is often 4 x 6 m. Light is steady fluorescent, good for colour. 1-3 students play while 25-35 watch, so turn taking and spectator moments matter more than length. Learning themes (Thai history, planets, animals) with checkpoint labels as facts work well.

nodes.title: Hall or function room: big, indoor, good for groups
nodes.text: A school or hotel hall often gives 12 x 20 m or more of clear floor with steady light and sometimes a stage. It supports races of up to 6 players, long routes and two lanes. Lights can often be dimmed, which makes spooky and neon themes possible. Spectators stand along the sides or sit on the stage.

nodes.title: Sports hall or gym: court lines, echo, wide floor
nodes.text: A gym or futsal court gives 15 x 25 m or more of flat floor with painted lines. Light is bright and even. Basketball hoops and wall bars stand at the edges, and benches give spectators a clear view. It suits races, sports or hero themes and long routes.

nodes.title: Garden or lawn: daylight, trees, uneven ground
nodes.text: A garden offers 5 x 8 m up to large lawns, but grass is uneven, there are trees, paths and garden furniture, and daylight washes out glow. Players walk slower on grass. Bright themes (farm, dinosaurs, pirates, candy) fit; dark or neon themes do not. Trees inside the floor must be listed as obstacles and the route kept away from them.

nodes.title: Car park: huge and flat, but traffic and sun
nodes.text: An empty car park gives 20 x 30 m or more of flat hard floor, ideal for long routes, two lanes and 6-player races. The risks are cars, kerbs, drains, strong sun and heat. Only use it when it is closed to traffic. Big hero pieces read well against open sky.

nodes.title: Rooftop: skyline view, wind and edges
nodes.text: A rooftop gives a dramatic city skyline but has parapets, vents, wind and sun. Keep the route at least 2 m from any roof edge or low railing, much more than the usual 0.6 m, because a player stepping back cannot see what is behind. Sci-fi, heroes or night city themes work best in the evening.

nodes.title: Mall atrium: crowds, bright light, passers-by
nodes.text: A mall atrium offers about 8 x 12 m with bright mixed light, shiny floors, escalators and a constant crowd of passers-by. It is good for brand events and showing off, but people may walk into the area. Put a barrier or staff around it, keep plays short (2-3 minutes) and design big visible moments for the crowd.

nodes.title: Event booth: 3 x 3 to 6 x 6 m and a fast queue
nodes.text: Exhibition booths usually give 3 x 3, 3 x 6 or 6 x 6 m of floor with strong show lighting and noise. Most players are first-time VR and want a quick taste, so 90 seconds to 3 minutes per play with a clear goal works best. The booth lives on throughput and on how fun it looks from the aisle.

nodes.title: Fortal court: 14 x 22 m, steady light, 2-6 players
nodes.text: The Fortal court (XR Arena, Chiang Mai) is an indoor 14 x 22 m floor with walls on all sides, painted court lines, 4 doors along one long wall and steady indoor light. Staff and families watch along one long side and a wall screen can show the leaderboard. It fits long routes, races, two lanes and spooky or neon themes.

nodes.title: Under 3 x 3 m only the runner genre fits
nodes.text: If either side of the MR space is under 3 m, battle and tactics do not fit: enemies need room to walk in from the edges and the 6 x 8 board needs squares a person can step on. All 3 options must then be runners that differ in theme, route and feeling instead. The builder checks this.

nodes.title: Under 4 x 4 m: 1-2 players, a short loop, no race
nodes.text: A floor under 4 x 4 m is a small play area: plan 1-2 players, a short loop of 4-5 checkpoints and small props. A live race needs parallel space and does not fit, so offer a solo time attack with a leaderboard instead. From about 3.7 m on the shortest side the builder's small rules apply (3-6 checkpoints, 1.2-4 m between stops, 8-30 objects); below that the tiny-room rules take over.

nodes.title: 4 x 4 to 10 x 10 m: 1-4 players, loops and zig-zags
nodes.text: Medium floors such as a cleared classroom or a small hall fit 1-4 players, loops or zig-zags and 5-7 checkpoints. When the usable side is 5-10 m the builder expects 1.8-6 m between stops, a 1.2 m clear circle around the spawn and 15-50 objects. Shared floor play works well with 2-3 players.

nodes.title: Over 10 x 10 m: up to 6 players, long routes, races
nodes.text: When the usable side is 10 m or more (for example the 14 x 22 m Fortal court) the builder uses large rules: 4-10 checkpoints 2.5-9 m apart, a 1.5 m clear circle around the spawn and 20-80 objects. This is where races, two lanes and hub-and-spoke routes shine. Fill the space with 3-12 vignettes so long walks do not feel empty.

nodes.title: Judge size by the shortest side minus 1.2 m
nodes.text: The builder measures the usable floor as the shortest side minus 0.6 m on each edge. A 4 x 8 m space is really 2.8 m usable, which counts as small, not medium. Always reason from the shortest side, because the route must turn inside it.

nodes.title: A shortest side under 3.7 m triggers the tiny-room rules
nodes.text: The builder subtracts the 0.6 m edge margin on both sides, so any floor whose shortest side is under about 3.7 m has less than 2.5 m usable and gets tiny rules: 3-4 checkpoints, stops spaced about 45 percent of the usable side (at least 0.5 m), hazard radius 0.35 m, a 0.6 m spawn circle, 2-4 vignettes and 8-20 objects. A 3.5 x 5 m bedroom is tiny, not small. Plan a tight circuit where the story labels and one hero piece carry the experience.

nodes.title: Keep everything at least 0.6 m from the edge of the floor
nodes.text: Players overshoot targets, swing arms and step backwards. Keep checkpoints, hazards, the portal and the route at least 0.6 m inside the edge of the measured floor, and more next to glass, stairs or roof edges. The builder applies 0.6 m by default.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Keep a 1.2 m corridor clear along the walking route
nodes.text: Players walk the straight lines from spawn through the checkpoints in order to the portal. No object may stand within 0.6 m plus half its footprint of those lines, which gives a 1.2 m corridor. Arches and gates can sit on the line only if marked walkThrough. This keeps players from flinching at virtual props they think are solid.

nodes.title: Real obstacles inside the floor must stay off the route
nodes.text: A pillar, tree or table inside the floor is a real thing players can hit. List it in obstacles, keep the route and markers well away from it (at least 0.6 m plus a margin) and consider dressing it with a virtual piece of the same footprint, such as a rock around a pillar, so it reads as part of the world.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Convert paces to metres: 1 pace is about 0.75 m
nodes.text: Many creators do not know the size in metres. Ask them to walk the empty floor and count normal steps: 1 adult pace is about 0.75 m (a child's pace is shorter, about 0.5 m). 6 paces by 8 paces is about 4.5 x 6 m. Round down, never up.

nodes.title: If the size is unknown, assume a small floor and say so
nodes.text: If the creator cannot give the size even in paces, assume the safe case: a 3 x 3 m floor indoors, 1-2 players, a short loop. Write the assumption into the brief and tell the creator the game can scale up if they later measure a bigger space. Guessing big risks routes that run into walls.

nodes.title: Ask for the empty floor, not the room
nodes.text: Rooms include furniture; the play area is only the floor that is clear. Ask how big the empty floor you can walk on is, and offer quick choices such as about 3 x 3 m, 5 x 5 m, 10 x 10 m or bigger, and I will count my steps. The answer changes genre, player count and route, so it is required for a space venue.

nodes.title: Space checkpoints so players walk, not shuffle
nodes.text: Stops too close together make players shuffle in place; too far apart and the walk feels empty. The builder checks 1.2-4 m between stops on small floors, 1.8-6 m on medium and 2.5-9 m on large. Aim for the middle of the range and vary it so the route has rhythm.

nodes.title: Hazards sit on the route but leave room to step around
nodes.text: Hazards are red circles that send the player back to the last checkpoint. In MR the player must see them early and step around them without leaving the corridor. Keep hazards at least the builder's gap from each other (0.4 m small, 0.7 m medium, 1 m large floors) and away from the edge, so the dodge is never toward a wall.

nodes.title: Keep the spawn clear so players start calmly
nodes.text: Players put the headset on at the spawn and take a moment to adjust. The builder keeps a clear circle around it: 0.8 m on small floors, 1.2 m medium, 1.5 m large. Put the spawn near the entrance and the staff side so helpers can reach players quickly.

nodes.title: Bright daylight washes out glow and dark themes
nodes.text: In sun, passthrough is bright and virtual glow, neon and dark colours look faded. Outdoors in daylight choose bright, saturated themes with strong silhouettes and the noon or morning preset. Save spooky and neon for indoors or after dark.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Steady indoor light keeps colours readable
nodes.text: Halls, classrooms and the Fortal court have even artificial light, so most themes read well. The studio or default presets match it; spooky and neon work if the room lights can be dimmed. Ask whether the lights can be changed, because it opens darker themes.

nodes.title: After dark, spooky, neon and night presets shine
nodes.text: Outdoors after sunset or in a dimmed hall, glow and dark palettes pop and spooky or neon themes feel strong. But passthrough gets grainy in low light and players see real obstacles less well, so keep some room light on, widen clearances and slow the pace.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Default lighting preset by venue
nodes.text: Garden or car park at midday: noon. Morning outdoor events: morning. Sunset rooftop or garden: evening. Living room or classroom with lights on: default or studio. Hall or court with dimmable lights: spooky or neon for dark themes, studio otherwise. Outdoors after dark: night. Pick the preset that agrees with the real light the player will see.

nodes.title: Ask when it will be played, not only where
nodes.text: The same garden is a bright dino park at 11:00 and a ghost trail at 19:00. Ask the time of day for any venue with windows or open sky; it decides the lighting preset and which themes are possible. Offer quick choices: morning, midday, evening, night, indoors without windows.

nodes.title: Sun patches from windows fade colours on part of the route
nodes.text: A room can have even light except where sunlight falls through a window, and that patch moves over the day. Inside it, virtual colours and hazard circles fade while the rest of the route looks fine, so a player can walk into a hazard they did not see. Ask where the sun falls at play time and keep hazards and checkpoints out of that patch, or close the curtains.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Design for walking, never running
nodes.text: Players in headsets misjudge real distances and may miss small real objects. Time limits and races must be beatable at a brisk walk. In battle the player steps out of rings, never sprints. Write walk, do not run into the rules of every race.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: No sudden scares that make people run
nodes.text: A jump scare makes people step back or bolt, and in MR that can mean a wall or a person. Build horror with slow dread: dim light, Thai ghost scenery seen from far away, story labels. Keep scary pieces beside the route and visible early, never popping up in front of a player.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: No tasks that need looking up while walking fast
nodes.text: Looking up while walking hides the floor and real obstacles and causes trips. Put checkpoint labels and targets at chest to eye height. Tall scenery is fine to admire while standing still at a checkpoint.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Offer a seated or standing-still way to play
nodes.text: Some players cannot or should not walk around: limited mobility, some seniors, a tiny room. The PC platform serves seated players, and in MR battle the player mostly stands in place and steps out of rings. Mention the alternative so the creator can include everyone.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Avoid motion sickness: the floor must stay still
nodes.text: In MR the player walks for real, so the main sickness risks are a bottomless floor and anything that moves the world instead of the player. Keep the floor stable, avoid the void floor for sensitive players, and use animated rides as scenery, never as something players stand on. Fast spins to find the next checkpoint also cause discomfort, so keep the next stop roughly ahead.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Default session length: about 4 minutes in MR
nodes.text: Most MR walking plays feel complete in 3-5 minutes and stay comfortable. First-time players and events want 2-3 minutes; a home game with keen adults can run 8-10 minutes across chapters. If the creator does not say, use 4 minutes and write it into the brief.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Plan rest breaks between chapters for long sessions
nodes.text: Heat, headset weight and eye strain build up over time, faster in warm venues. If the whole experience runs over 10 minutes, split it into chapters of 3-4 minutes with a short break in which the player can lift the headset or sit down. In battle, the chapter by chapter structure gives natural break points before the boss; in runner, the intro card of a second Land can act as one.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Quest 3 is heavy for small children: keep their plays short
nodes.text: The headset weighs around half a kilo, which is a lot for a young child's neck, and the fit is loose on small faces. For kids 6-9 keep plays to 2-3 minutes, avoid long periods of looking down, and have a helper adjust the strap. Check the manufacturer's age guidance for the venue.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: At events plan hygiene and turnover between players
nodes.text: Each change of player needs wiping the face pad, fitting the strap and a short briefing, about 60-90 seconds. Plan the play length and throughput around it. Disposable face covers and a second headset that alternates keep the queue moving.

nodes.title: Hot outdoor venues overheat players and headsets
nodes.text: In midday Thai sun, headsets overheat and players sweat into the face pad, and sunlight falling into the lenses can damage the screens. Prefer shade, morning or evening times, and outdoor plays of 2-3 minutes. Store headsets lens-down in the shade between players.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Draw the headset boundary on the floor that was measured
nodes.text: The game only knows the size the creator gave; on site, the safety net is the boundary drawn in the headset. Tell the creator to clear the floor first, then draw the boundary on that same floor, so the Land, its 0.6 m margin and the boundary all match. If the drawn boundary is smaller than the brief, rebuild with the smaller size rather than playing past it.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: One spotter watches the floor during group plays
nodes.text: On a shared floor players see each other's avatars but still misjudge distance, and real people may wander in. One staff member or parent stands at the edge with a clear view of the whole floor, ready to call stop. Design routes that flow in one direction so players never walk toward each other head-on.

nodes.title: Kids 6-9: short, bright, forgiving, few words
nodes.text: Young children read slowly, scare easily and tire fast. Use 2-3 minute plays, 4-6 checkpoints with labels of 2-4 words, few hazards, no time limit or a generous one, bright high-contrast colours and friendly themes (animals, candy, toys). In tactics use slow guards (4 s or more) or a board with one guard.

nodes.title: Kids 10-12: give real challenge and a score to beat
nodes.text: Older children want to win and to beat their friends. They read short sentences, handle hazards and a time limit, and love leaderboards. Mild spooky themes such as cute Thai ghosts work. Keep plays 3-4 minutes and let the challenge rise across checkpoints.

nodes.title: Teens: competition, style and showing off
nodes.text: Teens care about looking cool to the friends watching and beating each other. Races, leaderboards, neon and hero themes, tactics guards at 3 s and battle bosses fit. Keep text short and let them restart quickly.

nodes.title: Adults at home or with friends: longer, harder, a bit of nostalgia
nodes.text: Adults who choose to play (a game night, a team outing, a birthday) are past the novelty and want a real game: 6-10 minutes across chapters, a time limit that bites, a leaderboard among friends. Themes that call back to childhood (pirates, dinosaurs, toys) or local legends land well. They are self-conscious in front of colleagues, so avoid poses or moves that look silly and let the competition be the show.

nodes.title: Seniors: steady floor, slow pace, large clear text
nodes.text: Older players may have balance or vision limits. Keep the floor stable (no void), no time limit or a generous one, wide corridors, large high-contrast labels and calm themes (temples, gardens, history). Offer the PC version for anyone unsteady on their feet.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Mixed-age families: one route, two levels of challenge
nodes.text: A family group can have a 6 year old and a grandparent at once. Design for the youngest: short, bright, safe. Older players chase the time bonus and avoid hazard penalties while kids simply finish. Shared floor play lets a parent walk beside a child.

nodes.title: First-time VR players need a calm first minute
nodes.text: First-timers spend the first 30-60 seconds looking around and checking that the floor is really there. Put the first checkpoint close and in plain view, no hazards before it, and save the wow for the second half. Keep the intro card to 2 sentences.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Experienced gamers want depth and mastery
nodes.text: Players used to VR or games read the rules fast and look for mastery. Give tighter time limits, denser hazards, tactics boards with 3 s guards and a strict capture order, or battle chapters mixing shield and beast enemies with rain. The leaderboard keeps them replaying.

nodes.title: School classes: many turns, everyone watches
nodes.text: With 30 students and 1-2 headsets, the game is mostly watched. Plays of about 2 minutes, a class leaderboard on a projector and checkpoint labels that teach a fact give the watchers a role: they learn and cheer. Use team names so turns feel fair and no personal data is shown.

nodes.title: Tourists: local culture, little text, quick to understand
nodes.text: Tourists may not read Thai and often play only once. Use visual storytelling and very short labels, Thai temples, ghosts or local legends as scenery, and a 2-3 minute play. The experience should be photo worthy for the friends watching.

nodes.title: Limited mobility: smaller loops, no stepping tasks, or PC
nodes.text: For wheelchair users or people who cannot walk far, long MR routes and battle ring dodges exclude them. Offer the PC platform, or a small runner loop with wide flat corridors of 1.5 m and no hazards that need side steps. Ask what they need without asking for medical details.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Keep in-headset text short: labels under 5 words
nodes.text: Text in a headset is harder to read than on a phone, and walking players only glance at it. Keep checkpoint labels to 2-5 words, the goal to one line and the story card to 2-4 short sentences. Young players and tourists need even less.

nodes.title: High contrast colours for markers, more for kids and seniors
nodes.text: Markers must read against both the virtual floor and the real light. Hazards are red, so keep the floor palette away from red and orange. Pair light floors with dark props or the reverse, and avoid low-contrast palettes for kids, seniors and daylight venues.

nodes.title: Tactics guard beat by player: 4-5 s for kids, 3 s for gamers
nodes.text: In tactics guards move every 3 s or slower. Walking onto a square in MR takes time, so for kids, seniors and first-timers use 4-5 s per beat and few guards; gamers and teens can handle 3 s. A beat that is too fast turns planning into panic and tempts people to rush.

nodes.title: Set time limits from walking speed and player type
nodes.text: Estimate the walk: a brisk adult covers about 1 m per second plus a few seconds at each checkpoint. Give kids and first-timers about double that walking time, adults 1.5 times, gamers 1.2 times. Or leave the limit off and let the time bonus reward speed.

nodes.title: Spectators see bodies, not the game
nodes.text: People watching from the side see players walk, turn, step and react, but not the virtual floor. Design moments with visible body language: a sidestep around a hazard, a pause at a checkpoint, arms raised at the portal. A screen with the leaderboard gives them the rest.

nodes.title: Put key moments on the spectator side
nodes.text: Find where people stand and place a hazard dodge and the finish portal on that side, 1.5-3 m from them and inside the edge margin. They then see faces and reactions instead of backs. The layout brief must say which side the spectators are on.

nodes.title: Show the race leaderboard on a screen
nodes.text: A TV or projector with the live leaderboard turns watchers into fans and gives the queue a reason to stay. Place it where spectators and the queue can both see it, not where players in headsets walk toward it.

nodes.title: Let parents and friends cheer and call out hints
nodes.text: Spectators can shout left or one more. Design moments where a hint helps: a checkpoint behind a prop, a hazard the player has not noticed yet. This creates fellowship without any spectator task inside the area.

nodes.title: Never give spectators a task inside the play area
nodes.text: Anyone standing on the floor is a real obstacle that players cannot see as part of the game. Spectator roles stay outside the edge: cheering, watching the screen, choosing the next player.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Entertain the queue at events
nodes.text: At booths the queue is the next set of players and the crowd that draws others in. Show the leaderboard or a looping trailer on a screen and let the queue watch players react. A short 2-3 minute play keeps the wait short.

nodes.title: Race or shared floor: pick by space and goal
nodes.text: In a race each player walks their own copy and sees a live leaderboard; in a shared floor players see each other's avatars. Races feel competitive, but players on the same real floor can still collide, so they need a large floor or players taking turns. Shared floor suits families and teamwork.

nodes.title: Cap players at once by area: about 8 square metres each
nodes.text: When several people share one real floor (a shared-floor game or a simultaneous race), each walking player needs about 6-10 square metres to move without bumping into others. Divide the floor area by 8 and round down, then cap at 6: a 4 x 5 m floor fits 2, a 7 x 7 m floor fits 6 on paper but 4 is safer with hazards to dodge. More people than that means turns, not a bigger group.

nodes.title: Two mirrored lanes for a fair side-by-side race
nodes.text: On floors over about 8 m wide, split the floor into two mirrored lanes with at least a 1 m gap so two players race at once without crossing. Spectators love seeing them side by side, and mirrored lanes keep the race fair.

nodes.title: Turns plus an all-day leaderboard replace live races at busy events
nodes.text: When more people want to play than the floor can hold, let them play one or two at a time and compete on a leaderboard that runs all day. A player who finished can come back to see if they still lead, and the next player knows the score to beat before putting the headset on. Reset the board at a fixed time and announce the leader.

nodes.title: Estimate throughput: players per hour
nodes.text: Players per hour = 60 / (play minutes + changeover minutes) x headsets. A 3 minute play with a 1.5 minute changeover on 2 headsets gives about 26 players per hour. Use this to set the play length the event can afford.

nodes.title: On PC skip every question about the real room
nodes.text: A PC game has no real floor, so do not ask about size, surroundings, obstacles or venue, and do not set venue, width_m, depth_m or indoor. Spend those questions on players, feelings and session instead.

nodes.title: On PC, friends watch the screen, not the body
nodes.text: PC spectators see the same screen as the player, so they understand everything that happens. Loud visual feedback on hits, checkpoints and the finish makes watching fun, and hot-seat turns with a leaderboard work well for friends.

nodes.title: PC players expect WASD, mouse look and quick restarts
nodes.text: On PC the runner is played with WASD and battle uses a third person sword with a 3-hit combo and a dash. Players expect standard controls, instant restarts and tighter challenge than in MR, because nobody walks a real floor. Routes can be longer and hazards denser than in MR.

nodes.title: Ideas too intense for MR belong on PC
nodes.text: On PC nobody walks a real floor, so a fast pace, darker and scarier themes, dense hazards and dramatic heights are safe. When the creator wants something that breaks an MR safety rule (sprinting, jump scares, a long void walk), say why it is unsafe in a headset and offer PC as the home for that idea, or a gentle MR version alongside it.

nodes.title: Loud venues drown out game sound: make every cue visual
nodes.text: Events, malls, gyms and halls are loud, and music or a crowd covers headset audio. Any cue that matters (a hazard, the next checkpoint, the time running out) must also be visible: the red hazard circle, the checkpoint label, the timer. Treat sound as a bonus layer, and remember the crowd can be the soundtrack: cheering at the finish is part of the show.

nodes.title: Rain and wind outdoors need a covered fallback
nodes.text: Quest headsets are not waterproof, and wet grass or tiles become slippery. Wind blows hair into faces, moves loose decorations and can push light barriers onto the floor. For any outdoor plan ask about a covered fallback (a tent, a porch, an indoor room) and design a version of the Land that fits it.

nodes.title: The real floor surface changes how fast players can walk
nodes.text: Players feel the real floor under the virtual one. Smooth tiles and court floors allow a brisk walk; carpet is safe but rugs with edges catch feet; grass is uneven and slower; polished stone can be slippery in socks. Ask what the floor is, remove rugs and cables, and lengthen time limits on grass or carpet.

nodes.title: Low light, mirrors and glass walls can break headset tracking
nodes.text: The headset tracks itself with its cameras. Very dark rooms, large mirrors, glass walls, and plain featureless floors or walls can make it lose its place, so the virtual floor drifts or freezes. Keep the room moderately lit, cover big mirrors, and keep the route away from glass walls, which players also may not see in passthrough.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Young kids play with a parent at the edge or as a second player
nodes.text: A child of 6-9 often wants a parent close. Either the parent stands at the edge as the spotter and calls out hints, or the parent wears a second headset and plays on a shared floor beside the child. A parent walking on the floor without a headset is a real obstacle the child may not expect, so avoid that.

nodes.title: Wheelchair users in MR need wide turns and labels at seated eye height
nodes.text: A wheelchair needs about 1.5 m to turn around, so make the corridor at least 1.5 m wide and leave a 1.5 m circle at each checkpoint and at sharp turns. A seated player's eyes are about 1.2 m above the floor, so keep labels and targets low. Choose a smooth hard floor, no hazards that need side steps, and no void floor.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Temples, schools and museums need respectful themes
nodes.text: In a temple ground, a school or a museum, the theme must fit the place: no ghosts or horror on temple grounds, no violence-themed battle in a primary school, quiet play near prayer halls or classrooms in session. Ask the host about rules on photos, shoes, sound and opening times, and lean on discovery and narrative themes that tell the place's own story.

nodes.title: Stairs, stage edges and ponds near the floor need extra margin
nodes.text: The 0.6 m edge margin assumes a flat wall or open floor beyond the edge. If the floor ends at stairs, a stage edge, a pond, a pool or a balcony, keep everything at least 2 m away from that side and point the route away from it, because a player stepping backwards cannot see it.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Give every player a 30 second safety briefing
nodes.text: Before the headset goes on, tell each player three things: walk, do not run; the boundary will appear if you get close to the edge; take the headset off or raise a hand to stop. At events the intro card can repeat walk, do not run in the rules list. It costs 30 seconds and prevents most accidents.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: At home, close the doors and keep pets and small children off the floor
nodes.text: In a living room the risks are not the walls but things that move: a dog, a toddler, a sibling walking through, a door that opens into the floor. Ask the creator to close doors, keep pets out and agree that nobody crosses the floor during play. Put the spawn on the side away from the door.

nodes.title: Start from a one-sentence premise: you are X, you must Y, before Z
nodes.text: Before writing any label, chapter or board line, write the premise as one sentence with a role, an action and a stake: "You are the last lantern carrier and must relight 6 shrines before the ghosts wake." Every other line in the game should trace back to it. If the premise needs two sentences, the story is too big for a 1-8 minute play.
nodes.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

nodes.title: Split checkpoints into three acts: arrive, trouble, triumph
nodes.text: Map the checkpoint count onto a short three-act shape. With 4 checkpoints use 1-2-1, with 6 use 2-2-2, with 8 use 2-4-2, with 10 use 3-4-3. Act 1 labels set up the world and the task ("Enter the reef"), act 2 labels raise trouble ("Swim past the eels"), act 3 labels pay off ("Wake the pearl queen"). The portal is the curtain call, not a fourth act.

nodes.title: Quest chain: each checkpoint makes the next one possible
nodes.text: A quest chain links stops by cause: "Wake the bell keeper", "Ring the old bell", "Open the river gate", "Free the boats". Nothing is carried or unlocked by the engine; the checkpoint order already forces the sequence, so the words only need to imply that each step leads to the next. This makes 5-7 checkpoints feel like one task instead of a list.

nodes.title: Rescue structure: find each captive, then go home through the portal
nodes.text: Rescue is the easiest story to read: each checkpoint is someone or something freed ("Free the first kitten"), hazards are what holds them (thorns, a curse ring, fire), and the portal is home. Put a still model of each captive beside its checkpoint so the label points at something visible. For kids use animals or toys; for adults use villagers or spirits.

nodes.title: Escape structure: the place is closing, the portal is the only way out
nodes.text: In an escape the danger is behind you and the portal is the exit. Labels count down places passed ("Out of the cell", "Past the kitchen", "Up the stairs", "The last door") and hazards are the closing threat (lava, alarm rings). A time limit fits naturally ("before the volcano blows"), so set timeLimit and mention it once in the story. Escape suits challenge, sensation and races.

nodes.title: Delivery structure: you carry something precious from start to finish
nodes.text: A delivery story gives one object the whole journey: a lantern flame, a letter, a dragon egg. The object exists only in words (the engine has no carrying), so state it on the intro card ("You carry the last warm ember") and let labels be the stops on the way ("Shelter from the snow", "Cross the frozen lake", "Reach the cold village"). The portal is the handover.

nodes.title: Collection structure: a numbered set the player completes
nodes.text: Collection works when the set has a clear count and a reason: "5 lost stars to put back in the sky". Touching a checkpoint is the collecting, so labels can repeat a pattern on purpose ("Star 1: the well", "Star 2: the windmill"). Give the set a payoff in the last label or goal ("Light up the sky"). Kids love counting up, and the HUD already shows checkpoint progress.

nodes.title: Tour structure: each checkpoint is one sight with one fact or feeling
nodes.text: A tour treats checkpoints as stops on a guided walk: "See the floating market", "Visit the spirit house", "Watch the elephants bathe". Each label names the sight and the vignette beside it shows it. Add no threat words; use hazards lightly as natural obstacles (puddles, sleeping dogs). Tours suit tourists, seniors, educators and brands showing a place.

nodes.title: Mystery with a reveal at the end: a clue in each label, the answer in the last
nodes.text: A short mystery plants a question on the intro card ("Who stole the moon?") and lets each label add a clue the scenery shows ("Follow the silver footprints", "Check the empty nest"). The last checkpoint label gives the answer ("The owl kept it for her chicks"). The reveal must sit in the last label (or the boss intro in battle), because the engine has no ending screen to write on.

nodes.title: Battle arc across chapters: outskirts, defences, heart, boss
nodes.text: Across 3-6 chapters let the place move inward: chapter 1 at the edge ("The Frozen Pass"), middle chapters at the defences ("The Shield Wall", "The Hunting Grounds"), the last chapter at the boss's door ("Below the Throne"), then the boss. Moving through named places makes the fight feel like a journey even though the arena itself does not change.

nodes.title: Give each enemy kind a story meaning and name it in its chapter line
nodes.text: The engine has three foes, so the words decide who they are. Grunts are fast and weak: a swarm (imps, ice sprites, sand rats). Shields block from the front: a wall of guards (stone soldiers, palace guards). Beasts are big chargers: the boss's pet (a lava hound, a forest boar). Rain is a sky threat: hail, falling embers, a curse. Mention the main foe in its chapter line ("Stone guards lock shields at the gate") so players know what is coming. Re-check after choosing foes: falling danger only when rain is true, a big creature only when a beast is in that chapter.

nodes.title: Tactics arc across boards: the piece changes because the story does
nodes.text: Boards should vary the piece, and each change needs a story reason: start as a knight sneaking in ("Leap the garden walls"), become a rook in the long halls ("Charge the straight corridors"), a bishop in the chapel ("Slip along the diagonal pews"), and end as the queen ("Take back the throne"). The piece change reads as growth or disguise, not as a rule change.

nodes.title: The boss is the story payoff: name it twice before it appears
nodes.text: A boss lands when players already know it. Name it on the intro card ("the Ash King sleeps under the mountain"), hint at it in a middle chapter line ("His hounds smell you"), then let boss.intro deliver ("The Ash King rises. End this."). A boss who appears without warning feels like a random big enemy, not an ending.

nodes.title: Label length: English 2-5 words, Thai about 6-16 characters
nodes.text: English labels read best at 2-5 words and under about 24 characters ("Ring the old bell"). Thai has no spaces between words, so count characters: aim for about 6-16 Thai characters ("ตีระฆังเก่า", "จุดเทียนดวงแรก"). Thai labels over about 20 characters blur in a headset while walking. If a label needs a comma, it is two labels.

nodes.title: Thai labels start with the verb too, and drop the pronoun
nodes.text: Thai naturally puts the verb first in commands, so labels should read like a friend telling you what to do: "ปลุกยักษ์วัด", "ข้ามสะพานหมอก", "ช่วยลูกเป็ด". Drop "คุณ", "เรา" and "จง"; they make the label long and stiff. Good: "จุดตะเกียง". Bad: "คุณจะต้องจุดตะเกียงให้สว่าง".

nodes.title: Numbered progress in labels when the set repeats: "Bell 2", "Last bell"
nodes.text: When checkpoints are a set (bells, stars, lanterns), a number in the label tells players how far they are: "Bell 1: the gate", "Bell 2: the pond", "Last bell: the tower". In Thai: "ระฆังที่ 1 ประตูวัด", "ระฆังสุดท้าย บนหอ". Use Arabic digits so every player reads them fast, and name the final one "Last" or "สุดท้าย" to signal the climax.

nodes.title: Checkpoint labels: bad drafts and good rewrites
nodes.text: Bad "Checkpoint 2" becomes "Cross the rope bridge". Bad "Now you must find the very old ancient lantern" becomes "Find the old lantern". Bad "Talk to the monk" becomes "Visit the monk" (no dialogue). Bad "Pick up the key" becomes "Reach the key stone" (no carrying). Bad Thai "ท่านจงเสด็จไปยังศาลา" becomes "ไปที่ศาลา". Bad "Zone C" becomes "Into the bamboo".

nodes.title: Safe label verbs: actions done just by arriving
nodes.text: A checkpoint is touched by walking into it, so the best verbs happen on arrival: reach, enter, cross, visit, light, wake, ring, free, find, greet, bless, see, pass. In Thai: ไปถึง, เข้า, ข้าม, ไปหา, จุด, ปลุก, ตี (ระฆัง), ปล่อย, หา, ไหว้, ดู. Avoid verbs that need hands, buttons or speech: pick up, throw, open with a key, talk, ask, buy, build, shoot.

nodes.title: Six labels starting with "Find" read like a shopping list
nodes.text: When every label opens with the same verb ("Find the cat", "Find the hat", "Find the bat"), players stop reading after the second. Unless it is a deliberate numbered set, vary the verb so each stop has its own moment: "Spot the cat", "Wake the owl", "Cross the creek", "Free the fox". In Thai, rotate between หา, ปลุก, ข้าม, ช่วย, จุด.

nodes.title: There is no ending screen: land the ending on the last label
nodes.text: The game card has no finish-message field, and the portal only ends the run with the score. So the story's ending must live in the last checkpoint label ("Return the moon to the sky") and in what the goal line promised. Make the last label the resolution, not another errand, and give the portal a meaning on the intro card ("then the gate takes you home").

nodes.title: Intro card in 4 short sentences: world, you, trouble, go
nodes.text: The story field is 2-4 sentences read once before play. A reliable shape: 1) the world ("The river spirits lost their lights."), 2) who you are ("You are the lantern child."), 3) the trouble and the stake ("The ghosts wake at midnight."), 4) the call to action ("Light 5 lanterns and get home."). With only 2 sentences, merge 1+2 and 3+4. Keep each sentence under about 15 words.

nodes.title: Goal, story and labels must agree on the numbers and the final thing
nodes.text: If the goal says "Light 5 lanterns" there must be 5 lantern labels, and the story must not say "6 shrines". If the boss is "the Frost Warden" on the card, boss.name must match exactly. Players trust the card; a mismatch reads as a bug. Check counts and names across goal, story, labels, chapter lines, board stories (against the targets and guards of each board) and boss before submitting.

nodes.title: Rules list: 3-4 items, one plain verb each, in play order
nodes.text: The schema allows up to 8 rules for a runner and 6 for PC battle and tactics, but players read 3-4. Order them as played: what to do, what to avoid, how to finish. Runner example: "Walk to the glowing points in order", "Red circles send you back", "Step into the gate to finish". Use plain mechanic words, with at most a story word in brackets.

nodes.title: Write rules in plain words with the story word beside them
nodes.text: Rules must be understood by everyone, so lead with the mechanic and add the fiction once: "Do not step in red circles (the lava pools)", "Capture targets in order (the stolen jewels)", "Step out of the red rings (the dragon's fire)". Thai: "อย่าเหยียบวงแดง (บ่อลาวา)". The story word carries the theme; the plain words keep the rule clear.

nodes.title: In MR, one rule is always about walking safely
nodes.text: Walking players in a real room need one safety rule on the card: "Walk, do not run", or for battle "Step, do not jump". Thai: "เดินนะ ห้ามวิ่ง". Put it second or third, not first, so it is read without opening the card like a warning sign. It matters most in races, which make people speed up.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Rule lists that work for each genre
nodes.text: Runner: "Walk to the points in order", "Red circles send you back", "Finish at the gate". Battle on PC: "Click to swing, 3 hits make a combo", "Dash out of red rings", "Clear every chapter, then beat the boss". Battle in MR: "Swing your right controller like a sword", "Step out of red rings", "Beat the boss". Tactics: "Move like your chess piece", "Capture targets in order", "Never stop on a square a guard attacks".

nodes.title: Chapter title 1-3 words; chapter line one sentence under 12 words
nodes.text: Titles are names of places or moments ("The Ash Road", "Ember Storm", "ถ้ำลาวา"); lines are one present-tense sentence about what happens now ("The road splits and the hounds come running."). Thai lines stay under about 30 characters: "ฝนไฟตกลงมา หลบให้ทัน". The line shows as a chapter starts, mid-action, so it must read in 2 seconds.

nodes.title: Boss names: a title plus one strong noun, easy to shout
nodes.text: Good boss names are 2-4 words that say what the boss rules or is made of: "The Ash King", "Frost Warden", "Mother of Thorns", "ราชาเถ้าถ่าน", "เจ้าแม่น้ำแข็ง". Players and spectators should be able to shout it. Avoid apostrophes, invented syllables and names that only work in one language if the game may be made in the other.

nodes.title: Boss intro: what wakes, then what you must do, in 1-2 short sentences
nodes.text: boss.intro is the climax line. Write it as an event and a call: "The Ash King rises from the ember throne. Break his crown." Thai: "ราชาเถ้าถ่านตื่นแล้ว ล้มมันให้ได้". Use 5-15 words. The boss fight is fixed (ring slams, summoned grunts, faster below half health), so promise a fight, not a special attack.

nodes.title: Board story: one line under 12 words naming the targets and the guards
nodes.text: A tactics board line says what the targets and guards are in story terms: "Steal the 3 crowns before the night watch turns." Thai: "ขโมยมงกุฎ 3 ชิ้น ก่อนยามหันมา". Mention a target count only if it matches the board's targets number. Use the piece's nature when it helps ("Leap the hedges, rider").

nodes.title: Give each chess piece a role that matches how it moves
nodes.text: The piece the player is should feel like a character: knight = a rider or a frog that jumps over things, bishop = a monk or a shadow sliding on diagonals, rook = a battering cart or a castle golem charging in straight lines, queen = the hero, free in every direction. Write the role into the board story ("As the monk, slip along the diagonal halls").

nodes.title: Save the king for the last board and call it the climax
nodes.text: Setting king: true on the final board makes the last target a king, a natural climax: "Corner the Rat King in his hall." Earlier boards build toward it ("His guards are getting nervous"). Thai: "ต้อนราชาหนูให้จนมุม". The intro card can name the king from the start so the last board pays it off.

nodes.title: A time limit needs a story reason: before sunrise, before the tide
nodes.text: If timeLimit is set, say why in the story ("Get out before the volcano wakes", "ก่อนพระอาทิตย์ขึ้น") and state the minutes once in the goal or rules ("You have 3 minutes"). A clock with a reason feels like tension; a clock without one feels like a test. For submission or young kids, prefer no time limit and no clock words.

nodes.title: Thai: write like a friendly person speaking, not a textbook
nodes.text: Use everyday polite spoken Thai: "ไปช่วยลูกช้างกัน", "ระวังวงแดงนะ". Avoid formal written words that feel like an exam or a government notice: "ปฏิบัติภารกิจ", "ดำเนินการ", "กรุณาหลีกเลี่ยง". Avoid royal register (ราชาศัพท์) entirely unless the creator asks for a royal story, and even then keep it respectful and short.

nodes.title: Thai pronouns: drop them, or use "เรา" for warmth
nodes.text: Thai sentences work without a subject, so most lines need no pronoun: "จุดตะเกียงให้ครบ 5 ดวง".
