When the intro card needs one, "คุณ" is neutral for adults and "เรา" makes kids and families feel included ("เราต้องช่วยลูกเต่ากลับบ้าน"). Avoid "ท่าน" (stiff) and "เจ้า" (old period drama, unless the theme is fantasy), and never use rude pronouns.

nodes.title: Thai for kids 6-10: short common words, no heavy Pali or Sanskrit vocabulary
nodes.text: Children read slowly in a headset. Use words they know: "ผี" not "วิญญาณ", "ยักษ์" not "อสุรกาย", "ช่วย" not "กอบกู้", "บ้าน" not "ที่พำนัก". Keep lines to about 10-20 characters and add playful sound words sparingly ("ว้าว", "ปุ๊ง!"). Friendly creature names beat scary ones: "ผีน้อยขี้เหงา" works, while a folklore ghost famous for gore may frighten young kids.

nodes.title: Thai loanwords: keep the common ones, avoid long transliterated names
nodes.text: Some English words are normal Thai: บอส, ด่าน, เกม, ทีม. But transliterated names like "เดอะ ฟรอสต์ วอร์เดน" are hard to read and sound awkward; give a Thai name with meaning instead ("ผู้คุมน้ำแข็ง"). Prefer "จุด" over "เช็คพอยต์", "ภารกิจ" over "มิชชั่น", "คะแนน" over "พอยต์". Brand and product names stay in their official form.

nodes.title: Thai particles: none in labels, light ones on the intro card
nodes.text: ครับ and ค่ะ give the game's voice a gender and add length, so leave them out of labels, chapter lines and rules. On the intro card and goal, a light นะ, เลย or กัน adds warmth: "ไปช่วยกันเลย!", "ระวังวงแดงนะ". Do not stack them ("นะคะจ๊ะ"). Use even fewer for teens and adults.

nodes.title: Thai lines with a balanced rhythm or internal rhyme stick
nodes.text: Thai ears love two balanced halves and a sound echo (สัมผัส): "ข้ามสะพาน ผ่านม่านหมอก", "จุดเทียน เวียนรอบเจดีย์", "หนีให้ไว ไฟไล่หลัง". Use it on the intro card, the goal or 1-2 key labels, not everywhere, and only while the line stays short. A rhyme that forces a strange word is worse than no rhyme.

nodes.title: Thai sacred places and objects get respectful verbs only
nodes.text: Temples, Buddha images, spirit houses, monks and the royal family must never be enemies, hazards, tactics targets or things to break, steal or kick. Use respectful verbs: "ไหว้ศาลพระภูมิ", "จุดธูปที่วัด", "ไปกราบพระ". Folk spirits can be playful opponents; sacred objects are places of safety or blessing in the story.

nodes.title: English for UK audiences: British spelling and words, plain sentences
nodes.text: When lang = en and the players are in the UK, use British spelling and words: colour, centre, metre, sweets (not candy), queue, torch (not flashlight), mum. Keep sentences short and literal; UK families respond well to gentle understatement and dry humour ("The dragon is mildly annoyed."). Avoid American sports metaphors and dollar signs.

nodes.title: Switching language: rewrite the line, do not translate word for word
nodes.text: A label that works in English may be long or flat in Thai, and Thai rhymes vanish in English. When the same game is made in both languages, keep the meaning, the count and the names, then write each line fresh: "Ring the old bell" becomes "ตีระฆังเก่า", "Cross the misty bridge" becomes "ข้ามสะพานหมอก". Puns and rhymes are rewritten as new ones or dropped.

nodes.title: Voice for kids 6-10: warm, playful, clear, one idea per line
nodes.text: Kids follow concrete, kind tasks: helping animals, finding friends, waking sleepy giants. Use exclamations warmly but sparingly ("Help the baby turtles home!"), make villains silly rather than evil ("the Grumpy Snow Troll"), and keep every line one idea. Parents often read the card aloud, so it must sound good spoken.

nodes.title: Voice for teens: confident, a little dangerous, never talking down
nodes.text: Teens switch off at baby words and over-explaining. Write short, cool lines with real stakes: "Nobody leaves the fog. Except you." Labels can be terse ("Past the hounds", "Don't look back"). Mild menace and dry jokes work; cute mascots and "Great job!" do not. Make the challenge explicit: time, rank, the leaderboard.

nodes.title: Voice for families: sayable aloud, so parents can cheer and hint
nodes.text: In MR, parents watch from the side and call out. Labels with a clear, shoutable noun let them join in ("Go to the bell!", "The duck, the duck!"). Keep scares mild, make humour work on two levels (a pun for parents, a silly image for kids) and use "together" words when play is together. Avoid anything a parent would have to explain afterwards.

nodes.title: Voice for adults: atmosphere and wit, still short
nodes.text: Adults enjoy tone: dread, irony, nostalgia, a mystery. Lines can carry mood words ("The tide brings back what it took.") and boss names can be grim ("The Drowned Abbot"). They still read in a headset, so length limits do not change. Adults at events are often first-time VR players too, so keep the rules plain even when the story is rich.

nodes.title: Voice for brands: the product is the hero object, not ad copy
nodes.text: A brand game reads like a story, not a banner. Make the product or mascot a visible hero object (the golden bottle at the summit, the mascot to free) and use the brand name at most in the title and on the intro card. Labels stay story beats ("Climb to the golden bottle"), never slogans. Follow the brand's words-to-avoid exactly and make no health or price claims.

nodes.title: Voice for educators: one true idea per label, the story carries the lesson
nodes.text: In a school game each checkpoint can teach one simple fact through its label and scenery: "Visit Mars, the red planet", "Find the coral that feeds the fish". Keep facts short, true and checkable; if unsure, use a story label instead. The intro card frames learning as a mission ("Your rocket must visit 5 planets"), not a test.

nodes.title: Voice for first-time VR players: reassure, then invite
nodes.text: Newcomers worry about the headset more than the game. The intro card can open calmly ("Look around. The floor has changed, the room has not.") and the rules should say plainly what touching and finishing look like. Keep the first label easy and close ("Step to the first light") so the first success comes within seconds.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Fantasy: name the role and give it a title
nodes.text: Fantasy (being someone else) lives in the role words. Open the card with a titled role ("You are the Ember Knight", "เราคือผู้ถือตะเกียงคนสุดท้าย") and let labels be the role's duties ("Guard the shrine"). The boss should be the role's natural enemy. A role without a title is just "the player".

nodes.title: Submission (relaxing): soft verbs, no threats, no clocks
nodes.text: A relaxing game uses calm verbs (wander, visit, light, rest) and gentle images (lanterns on water, a sleepy cat, falling petals). Leave out timeLimit, alarm words and villains. Hazards, if any, become gentle things to step around (puddles, sleeping frogs). The intro card can invite rather than command: "Take a slow walk through the lantern garden."

nodes.title: Discovery: hint, do not spoil
nodes.text: Discovery labels promise without giving away: "Follow the glow", "Behind the waterfall", "Peek into the old well". The scenery beside that checkpoint delivers the surprise. The intro card should say there are secrets to see, not list them. Keep at least one surprise vignette that no label mentions.

nodes.title: Fellowship words must not promise teamwork the engine lacks
nodes.text: A shared floor lets players see each other's avatars and a race ranks them; there are no shared tasks, hand-offs or team scores. So write "together" as a shared journey ("Walk the ghost road together"), not as cooperation ("Lift the gate together", "One player holds the lamp"). Spectator cheering is real fellowship in MR: invite it on the card.

nodes.title: Sensation: short punchy lines and sensory nouns
nodes.text: Sensation games sell the wow, so text should be brief and physical: "Lava below. Steady steps.", "Into the storm!", "สะพานลอยฟ้า ค่อยๆ เดิน". Pair the words with the strongest visual at that checkpoint (void floor, giant models, neon). One exclamation mark per line at most.

nodes.title: Use second person "you are" and keep the player silent
nodes.text: Story text speaks to the player as "you" and gives them a role: "You are the night ranger." The player character never speaks, so never write lines for them ("I must hurry!") and never quote other characters as if they talk back. First- or third-person narration ("The hero walked...") distances players who are physically walking the route.

nodes.title: Pick a role that fits the genre's main verb
nodes.text: Runner roles walk and visit: lantern carrier, ghost hunter on patrol, courier, explorer, pilgrim, rescuer. Battle roles fight with a sword and dodge: knight, temple guardian, ice ranger, monster hunter. Tactics roles are the piece: a jumping rider (knight), a sliding monk (bishop), a charging cart (rook), the queen. A ghost hunter in a runner "checks the haunted spots"; in battle she "cuts down the ghosts".

nodes.title: Show a character's wish through the label, not through speech
nodes.text: Characters cannot talk, but the label can carry what they want: "Bring Grandma her lost cat", "Wake the sleepy giant for the harvest", "พาลูกช้างไปหาแม่". Place the character model beside the checkpoint so players connect the want to a face. One clear want per character, and at most 2-3 named characters in a short game.

nodes.title: Vignettes tell what happened: show the aftermath beside the label
nodes.text: Scenery tells story without words when it shows a result: a tipped cart and spilled fruit beside "Follow the thief's trail", broken lanterns beside "Relight the path", a sleeping dragon beside "Tiptoe past the dragon". In the layout brief, name the vignette for each labelled checkpoint so the words and the picture say the same thing.
nodes.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

nodes.title: Make the goal visible from the spawn: a landmark that pulls players in
nodes.text: Place the story's goal as the tallest or brightest model, seen from the start: the tower with the last bell, the volcano, the moon gate. The intro card names it ("Reach the moon gate"), and players see the promise the whole walk. In MR keep it inside the play area and away from real walls so it stays in view.

nodes.title: The lighting preset and the story must say the same time and mood
nodes.text: A Land has one lighting preset, so the story must fit it: night or spooky with midnight ghosts, morning with a journey starting, evening with lanterns and going home, neon with a future city, noon with bright festivals. Do not write "the sun sets as you walk"; the light will not change. In MR daylight, avoid stories that need darkness.

nodes.title: Give red circles a red fiction: fire, lava, curse, alarm
nodes.text: Runner hazards always look like red circles and battle warnings are red rings, so name them as something red or warning: lava pools, fire pits, curse rings, alarm zones, angry ant nests, dragon fire. Water or ice names fight the colour. Use one hazard name across the card, the rules and the layout brief ("lava pools" everywhere).

nodes.title: In MR, write the real room into the story
nodes.text: Players see the real walls, windows and people, so the story should explain them: the walls are "the castle walls", the crowd is "the villagers watching", the window light is "the moon outside". One sentence on the intro card is enough: "The villagers watch from the hall. Show them the ghosts are gone." This turns the real room from a distraction into part of the world.

nodes.title: Void floor needs a story reason: a bridge, a sky island, a cliff path
nodes.text: The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop, which is dramatic and dizzy. Justify it in words so it feels intended: "The bridge over the abyss", "Islands in the clouds", "สะพานข้ามเหว". Keep labels calm and reassuring on void sections ("Steady steps"), and never write lines that dare players to jump or look down while walking fast.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Story props that a label names cannot be VR-only
nodes.text: Decor marked "VR only" is hidden in MR. If a label points at a prop ("Wake the dragon"), that prop must be visible in MR, or the label points at empty floor. Use VR-only decor for background mood (sky, far walls, extra trees) and keep every story prop named by a label as normal scenery.

nodes.title: Humour: about one joke in every 3-4 lines, carried by the nouns
nodes.text: Humour lands best in silly nouns and situations, not in wordplay that must be read twice: "Wake the snoring goat", "the Grumpy Cabbage King", "ปลุกแพะนอนกรน". Use about one funny line per 3-4 lines so the story still moves; a joke on every label tires players. Put the biggest laugh on the boss name or the last label.

nodes.title: Wonder: build up with small sights, end on one big one
nodes.text: Wonder needs contrast. Let early labels be small and close ("Follow the fireflies"), then reveal a big sight with a big word near the end ("Under the sky whale"). Pair the wonder label with the largest model or the void floor. If every label says "amazing", nothing is.

nodes.title: Mild scare: dread in words and light, never sudden shocks
nodes.text: In MR, sudden scares make people run into real walls, so scare with mood, not jumps. Words do the work: "Something follows the lanterns", "Do not wake her". Use spooky or night lighting indoors, slow-reveal ghost models beside labels and a warm, safe ending ("Back to the light"). For kids, let the scary thing turn out friendly or silly by the last label.
nodes.source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Heroism: raise the stakes one step each chapter or board
nodes.text: Heroism grows when each step matters more: chapter 1 saves a farm, chapter 3 the town, the boss the kingdom. State the stake in a few words in each line ("The village is next.") and give the player the credit in the final line ("Only you stand at the gate."). Do not open at maximum stakes; there is nowhere left to go.

nodes.title: Worked runner card (English, families): The Lantern River
nodes.text: Story: "The river spirits lost their lights. You are the lantern child. Light 5 lanterns before the mist covers the river, then cross home." Goal: "Light 5 lanterns, then step through the moon gate." Rules: "Walk to the lanterns in order", "Walk, do not run", "Red circles are fire pits: they send you back", "Finish at the moon gate". Labels: "Lantern 1: the jetty", "Lantern 2: the reeds", "Past the sleeping frog", "Lantern 3: the old boat", "Lantern 4: the willow", "Last lantern: the bridge".

nodes.title: Worked runner card (Thai, school kids): rescue the baby elephants
nodes.text: Story: "ลูกช้าง 4 ตัวหลงป่าตอนพายุมา เราคือผู้พิทักษ์ป่าตัวน้อย ไปพาลูกช้างกลับหาแม่กันเลย!" Goal: "ช่วยลูกช้างครบ 4 ตัว แล้วเดินเข้าประตูป่า" Rules: "เดินไปตามจุดที่เรืองแสงทีละจุด", "เดินนะ ห้ามวิ่ง", "อย่าเหยียบวงแดง (รังมดแดง)". Labels: "ข้ามลำธาร", "ช่วยลูกช้างตัวแรก", "ลอดใต้ต้นไทร", "ช่วยตัวที่ 2", "ช่วยตัวที่ 3", "ช่วยตัวสุดท้าย".

nodes.title: Worked battle text (lava theme, teens): from chapters to boss
nodes.text: Story: "The Ash King woke under the mountain and his hounds took the road. You are the last ember knight. Fight up the mountain and end him." Chapters: "The Ash Road" / "Imps pour out of the cracks." (grunts); "The Shield Gate" / "Stone guards lock shields. Hit them from the side." (shields + grunts); "Ember Storm" / "Fire falls from the sky. Keep moving." (rain); "The Hound Pit" / "His hounds smell you." (beast + grunts). Boss: "The Ash King" / "The Ash King rises from his throne. Break his crown."

nodes.title: Worked tactics text (heist, adults): The Moonstone Job
nodes.text: Story: "Five moonstones sit in the duke's palace and his night watch never sleeps. You are the thief who becomes whatever the job needs. Take the stones in order and do not get caught." Boards: knight "Leap the garden hedges and take 2 stones."; rook "Charge down the long hall before the watch turns."; bishop "Slip along the chapel diagonals."; queen with king "The duke himself. Corner him for the last stone."

nodes.title: Worked MR battle text (Thai, families, forest): the firefly forest
nodes.text: Story: "ป่าหิ่งห้อยโดนเงามืดบุก เราคือองครักษ์ป่า ดาบอยู่ในมือขวาแล้ว ปกป้องหิ่งห้อยไว้ให้ได้!" Chapters (at most 6 foes each in MR): "ชายป่า" / "เงาตัวเล็กวิ่งเข้ามา"; "กำแพงโล่" / "ทหารเงาถือโล่ ฟันด้านข้างนะ"; "ฝนหนาม" / "หนามตกจากฟ้า ก้าวหลบให้ทัน". Boss: "ราชาเงามืด" / "ราชาเงามืดมาแล้ว ไล่มันออกไปจากป่า!" Rules include "ก้าวออกจากวงแดง ไม่ต้องวิ่ง".

nodes.title: Labels that promise mechanics: open, carry, shoot, choose
nodes.text: Writers slip in verbs from other games: "Open the chest", "Carry the egg to the nest", "Shoot the target", "Choose your path". The engine only knows touching checkpoints in order, so players try the action and nothing happens. Rewrite as arrivals: "Reach the chest", "Visit the nest", "Pass the targets", and give a single route with no choices.

nodes.title: Generic names ("Dark Lord", "Magic Forest") make the game forgettable
nodes.text: Names are the cheapest way to make a world feel specific. Replace "Dark Lord" with "the Rust Abbot", "Magic Forest" with "Whisper Woods", "ป่ามหัศจรรย์" with "ป่าหิ่งห้อย". Make each name concrete (a material, an animal, a sound, a local place) and tie it to the theme and palette.

nodes.title: Pick the aesthetic first, then the mechanics
nodes.text: MDA says the designer builds mechanics, which create dynamics at play time, which the player feels as aesthetics; the player experiences it in the reverse order. So decide the target feeling from the brief first, then choose the genre and the knobs (enemy kinds, guard count, checkpoint labels) that produce it. If the brief has no feeling, infer one from the players and venue and write it down as an assumption.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Sensation: spectacle the body feels
nodes.text: Sensation is pleasure of the senses: light, scale, motion and sound. In battle it comes from a big beast walking in, falling rain rings and a named boss reveal; in runner from the void floor, a dramatic lighting preset and hero scenery placed at the turn where the view opens; in tactics it is weakest, so carry it with theme and lighting. Put the biggest visual reveal at a moment when the player is standing still, not mid-dodge.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Fantasy: give the player a role, not just a theme
nodes.text: Fantasy is being someone else. The role must match what the body does: in MR battle the controller IS the sword, so "you are the last knight of the temple" fits the real swing; in tactics the player IS the chess piece, so "you are the knight sent to free the captives" fits walking L-shaped moves; in runner the player is a traveller, courier or explorer. Write the role into the intro story and echo it in labels so the fantasy holds from first to last second.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Narrative: tell the story through ordered beats
nodes.text: Our engines have no dialogue, so story lives in the intro card (2-4 sentences), checkpoint labels touched in order, chapter titles and lines in battle, and each board's story line in tactics. Treat these as a beat sheet: setup, rising stakes, turn, climax, resolution. A 6-checkpoint runner can carry a complete three-act story if each label is a verb phrase that moves the plot.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Challenge: an obstacle the player can master
nodes.text: Challenge is pleasure in overcoming a hard thing through skill. In battle it comes from mixing enemy kinds (shield forces flanking, beast forces stepping aside) and adding rain; in tactics from more guards, a faster beat and longer capture orders; in runner from tighter hazard spacing and a time limit. Challenge needs a visible score or time, a fair failure and a reason to try again.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Fellowship: design moments that are shared
nodes.text: Fellowship is play as a social framework. The engine gives three tools: race mode (everyone walks their own copy, live leaderboard), shared floor (players see each other's avatars) and spectators who see bodies, not the game. There is no voice chat or co-op mechanic, so fellowship comes from shared timing, comparing scores, cheering and calling hints. Put dodges and the finish where watchers can see them.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Discovery: reward looking around
nodes.text: Discovery is the pleasure of exploring and finding. In runner, use a hub or spiral route where vignettes sit beside the path and each checkpoint reveals a new view; in tactics, discovery is finding the capture path a piece can take, which each new piece reopens; in battle it is weakest. Pace reveals so something new appears every 20-40 seconds, and keep the walking line clear so looking around is safe.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Expression: let the player's style show
nodes.text: Expression is self-discovery and showing off. The engine has no building or customisation in play, so expression comes from how a player solves things: their capture route in tactics, their line through hazards in runner, their swing style in battle seen by spectators. Make solutions plural (more than one valid path) and make the performance visible to watchers or a leaderboard.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Submission: easy, calm, low-stakes fun
nodes.text: Submission is play as pastime: relaxing, no pressure. Use a runner with no time limit, few hazards (0-2, far from the line), a soft lighting preset such as morning or evening, and a loop route that returns near the start. In battle use only grunts in small numbers and no rain; in tactics use 0 guards and 2-3 targets. Failure should cost little.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: At most 3 feelings, and one leads
nodes.text: A design can serve 2-3 aesthetics, but one must be primary and decide trade-offs. Rank them: primary sets the genre and loop, secondary sets theme and story, third is a seasoning (lighting or spectator moment). When two knobs disagree, the primary wins. The options axes field holds only the primary, so choose it deliberately.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Feeling pairs that reinforce each other
nodes.text: Some aesthetics share mechanics and amplify each other: fantasy + sensation (a role plus spectacle, natural for battle), challenge + fellowship (a race with a leaderboard), discovery + narrative (a runner where each checkpoint reveals the next story beat), challenge + expression (tactics with several valid paths). Prefer these pairs when the brief allows a choice.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Challenge and submission pull in opposite directions
nodes.text: Challenge needs stakes, pressure and failure; submission needs calm and low cost of failure. One option cannot maximise both. If the brief lists both (common for "families"), split them: make the first half calm and the last chapter or board the challenge, or give the challenge only to those who opt into the race while the default is untimed.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research

nodes.title: Racing makes players skip the story
nodes.text: In race mode players optimise for time, so they ignore labels, scenery and the intro card. Narrative and discovery suffer. If the brief wants story and competition, keep the story in very short labels (3-5 words) read at a glance, or choose a solo or shared-floor mode for the story option and keep the race for a different option.

nodes.title: Tight time limits kill exploration
nodes.text: Discovery needs dwell time. A time limit under about 30 seconds per checkpoint turns looking around into wasted time. For a discovery option, set timeLimit to null or generous (at least 45 s per checkpoint), and give the time bonus only as an optional extra.

nodes.title: Keep challenge just ahead of skill
nodes.text: Flow happens when challenge matches skill and both rise together; too hard causes anxiety, too easy causes boredom. Skill grows during a session, so difficulty must climb too. Our engines have no adaptive difficulty, so the ramp is authored: each chapter, board or checkpoint stretch should be a little harder than the last, with the first one easy enough for the least experienced player in the brief.
nodes.source: Csikszentmihalyi 1990, Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience

nodes.title: Default battle chapter ramp
nodes.text: A safe 4-chapter battle in MR: chapter 1 is 2-3 grunts (learn the swing and ring-dodge), chapter 2 adds 1-2 shields (learn to hit from the side), chapter 3 adds rain with mixed grunts and shields, chapter 4 introduces 1 beast, then the boss. Stay at or under 6 enemies per chapter in MR (9 on PC). The engine rejects a beast in chapter 1.

nodes.title: Default tactics board ramp
nodes.text: Start board 1 with 0-1 guards, 2-3 targets and a slow beat (3-3.5 s); the engine rejects more than 2 guards on board 1. Then add one guard or one crack per board, lengthen the capture order to 4-5 and, on PC, tighten the beat toward 2 s. In MR keep the beat at 3 s or slower on every board because the player walks. Change the piece type every 1-2 boards so the player relearns movement.

nodes.title: Default runner hazard ramp
nodes.text: Keep the stretch from spawn to checkpoint 1 and 2 free of hazards so players learn to walk in the headset and read the checkpoint order. Introduce a single hazard that is easy to see after checkpoint 2, then raise the count toward the last third, and keep the final stretch into the portal clear for a clean, visible finish. Hazards send players back to the last checkpoint, so later hazards cost more and should be fairer.

nodes.title: Sawtooth difficulty: rest after every peak
nodes.text: Difficulty should climb in a sawtooth, not a straight line: each hard stage is followed by a slightly easier one that lets the player use their new skill with confidence, then the next peak is higher. In battle, follow a rain chapter with a smaller chapter before the boss; in tactics, follow a 3-guard board with a 2-guard board using a new piece.
nodes.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

nodes.title: There is no adaptive difficulty, so design the curve
nodes.text: Creators often ask for "easy for kids, hard for adults" in one game. The engine has no difficulty setting or dynamic adjustment. Offer instead: an authored ramp where the first half suits beginners, an optional race for those who want stakes, or separate options tuned for different groups.

nodes.title: The first 30 seconds teach the one verb
nodes.text: In the first 30 seconds the player should do the core action once and succeed. In MR battle: one or two slow grunts and a single red ring. In tactics: a first target reachable in one move. In runner: the first checkpoint visible from the spawn, 1.5-3 m away. Headset newcomers spend their first moments adjusting to passthrough, so nothing in that window should punish them.

nodes.title: The first stage is the tutorial
nodes.text: There is no separate tutorial screen, and players will not read long rules in a headset. Teach by putting the player in a stage where the right action is obvious and the wrong one is cheap. Each later stage adds exactly one new element the player meets first in a safe form (a single shield, a single crack, a single hazard) before it appears under pressure.
nodes.source: Koster 2004, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

nodes.title: Rule of threes: introduce, develop, twist
nodes.text: Use each new element three times: once alone so it is learned, once combined with something known so it is practised, and once in a twist or under pressure so it is mastered. A 4-chapter battle fits one new element per chapter with its three uses spread across the next chapters. Also cap lists at three: 3 pillars, 3 rules, 3 feelings.

nodes.title: Competence: let players feel themselves improve
nodes.text: Self-determination research on games found that feeling competent strongly predicts enjoyment. Show progress (score, captured targets, chapter count), give clear success feedback, and make failure understandable so the next try is better. A short game that can be replayed and beaten faster serves competence better than a long one that is finished once.
nodes.source: Ryan, Rigby & Przybylski 2006, The Motivational Pull of Video Games (PENS/SDT)

nodes.title: Autonomy: real choices inside a fixed structure
nodes.text: Autonomy is the feeling of acting by choice. Our runner checkpoints are touched in order and tactics targets are captured in order, so autonomy must come from how, not what: the path between checkpoints, the moment to cross a guard's line, the route through a board, or the pace of a calm walk. Leave space between stops for two reasonable lines and say in the rules that any path is allowed.
nodes.source: Ryan, Rigby & Przybylski 2006, The Motivational Pull of Video Games (PENS/SDT)

nodes.title: Relatedness: connect players to each other and to watchers
nodes.text: Relatedness is feeling connected to others. In our engines it comes from race mode (comparing on a live leaderboard), shared floor (seeing each other), spectators cheering at visible moments, and a story that casts the group as one side. Even a solo game gains relatedness if the finish faces the audience and the score can be compared afterwards.
nodes.source: Ryan, Rigby & Przybylski 2006, The Motivational Pull of Video Games (PENS/SDT)

nodes.title: Read which need the players lack most
nodes.text: Different players arrive missing different needs. First-time VR players and small kids mostly need competence: a sure first win. Gamers and adults need autonomy: choices that matter. Families, classes and friends need relatedness: shared moments and comparison. Use the brief's players field to pick which need the recommended option should serve first.
nodes.source: Ryan, Rigby & Przybylski 2006, The Motivational Pull of Video Games (PENS/SDT)

nodes.title: Agon: fair competition
nodes.text: Agon is competition where skill decides. It needs equal starting conditions and a clear measure. Race mode gives every player their own identical copy of the course plus a live leaderboard; tactics races on time with a leaderboard. Agon options suit gamers, teens and events with a screen.

nodes.title: Alea (chance) is weak in our engines
nodes.text: Alea is play where chance decides: dice, loot, random draws. Our engines are authored and deterministic, with no random rewards or loot. If a creator wants luck or surprise, offer surprise through design instead: a reveal around a turn, a new piece each board, a boss with a dramatic intro, or rain chapters that add unpredictability of position. Say honestly that results depend on skill.

nodes.title: Mimicry: playing a part with the whole body
nodes.text: Mimicry is make-believe, being someone else. MR is strong here because the body really moves: swinging the controller as a sword, walking as a chess piece, travelling a path as a pilgrim. Choose the role that matches the real motion and let spectators see the performance. This is Caillois' frame for the MDA fantasy aesthetic.

nodes.title: Ilinx: vertigo, used with care
nodes.text: Ilinx is the pleasure of disturbed perception: dizziness, height, speed. The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop, and a spiral route adds turning. It is the strongest wow in MR but can frighten or unsettle newcomers. Use it for teens and gamers, keep walking slow, avoid it for seniors and very young kids, and never combine it with a tight time limit.

nodes.title: Map 3 options to 3 different play types
nodes.text: An easy way to make 3 options genuinely different is to let each lead with a different Caillois play type: one agon (a race or timed board), one mimicry (a role-heavy battle), one ilinx or calm paidia-style free play (a void-floor runner or a relaxed tour). This also fits the rule that the 3 options use 3 different genres.

nodes.title: Fun is learning a pattern
nodes.text: Koster argues that fun is the brain mastering a pattern, and boredom arrives when nothing is left to learn. Each chapter, board or stretch should contain something new to grasp: a new enemy kind, a new piece, a new hazard layout. When the pattern is fully mastered, end the game or change the pattern.
nodes.source: Koster 2004, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

nodes.title: Stop before it becomes a grind
nodes.text: Players remember a game that ends while they still want more. Prefer 3-4 strong stages over 6 thin ones. The engines allow up to 6 chapters or boards; use 5-6 only when the session is 8 minutes or more and each one teaches something new.
nodes.source: Koster 2004, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

nodes.title: Name the core loop in one line with one verb
nodes.text: The core loop is what the player does again and again. If it cannot be said in one line with one main verb, it is not clear enough to build or to choose between. Good: "read the ring, step out, swing at the nearest enemy". Bad: "explore, fight, collect and solve puzzles". The options schema requires each option to have its own core loop.

nodes.title: The native core loop of each genre
nodes.text: Battle: watch enemies walk in, step out of red rings, swing to defeat them, survive the chapter. Tactics: read where guards attack, plan a legal move for your piece, walk onto the square, capture the next target. Runner: spot the next checkpoint, choose a line, avoid hazards, touch it. Theme and story change the meaning of the loop, not the loop itself. Start from the native loop and only reframe it.

nodes.title: Nest loops at three time scales
nodes.text: A satisfying game has a moment loop (seconds: a step, a swing), a stage loop (a minute: clear a chapter, solve a board, reach a checkpoint) and a session loop (the whole play: beat the boss, finish the last board, reach the portal, then compare score). Make sure each has a clear end signal and that the session loop invites a replay.

nodes.title: Risk and reward in the runner score
nodes.text: The runner scores +100 per checkpoint, -25 per hazard and +300 plus a time bonus at the finish. A hazard also sends the player back to the last checkpoint, which costs time. So the real risk is time, and the reward is a shorter line. Place one or two hazards beside the shortest line between checkpoints so a bold player can save seconds and a careful player can walk around.

nodes.title: Risk and reward on the tactics board
nodes.text: In tactics, guards attack squares on a beat. A short route through squares that are safe only between beats rewards timing; a longer route around attacked squares is safe but slower in a time race. Cracked squares and tables block paths and create those trade-offs. Design at least one board where the fastest path needs timing and a slower safe path exists.

nodes.title: A choice is meaningful only if its result is visible and matters later
nodes.text: Salen and Zimmerman describe meaningful play as actions whose outcomes are discernible (the player sees what happened) and integrated (it affects what comes next). Check every choice in the design: does the player see the result, and does it change score, time or position later? If not, it is decoration, not a choice.

nodes.title: A dominant strategy erases the choice
nodes.text: If one line or tactic is always best, every player does it and the choice disappears. In runner, a hazard nobody needs to go near; in tactics, a route that is both shortest and safest; in battle, standing in one corner where rings never fall. Look for the always-best answer in each stage and add a cost to it.

nodes.title: Response: feedback must feel instant
nodes.text: Swink describes game feel as real-time control, simulated space and polish. In MR the control is the player's own body, so the game must answer each action at once: a swing that hits, a checkpoint that lights the moment it is touched, a ring that clearly marks danger before it lands. A slow or missing response feels like the game ignored the player.

nodes.title: Juice comes from the engine, the designer controls staging
nodes.text: The engines already provide their own hit and pickup effects; the designer cannot add new particles, screen shake or custom sounds through the build plan. The designer's juice levers are staging: lighting preset, hero scenery at key moments, animated rides, the boss intro line, chapter titles, and where the finish sits relative to the audience. Promise polish through those, not through new effects.

nodes.title: Failure must be readable and fair
nodes.text: Players accept failure when they see why it happened and that they could have avoided it. Red rings warn before they land; guards attack on a regular beat; hazards are red circles on the route. Never place a hazard where it cannot be seen in time, never put a guard's attack on the square the player must land on with no alternative, and keep MR beats slow enough to react while walking.

nodes.title: Give short, mid and long goals at once
nodes.text: Players stay engaged when a goal is always close: short (the next checkpoint, the next enemy, the next target, seconds away), mid (finish this chapter or board, about a minute) and long (beat the boss, reach the portal, top the leaderboard). The HUD and labels should always show the short goal; the intro card states the long one.

nodes.title: Write the goal line as one action and one end state
nodes.text: The game card goal is read once, often in a headset. Make it one sentence with the action and the end state: "Free the 4 captives, then reach the gate", "Survive 4 chapters and defeat the Ash King", "Capture the targets in order before the guards catch you". Numbers help players plan.

nodes.title: Alternate tension and release
nodes.text: Interest curves rise and fall: a hook, a dip, rising peaks, the climax, then a short resolution. In battle, a chapter is tension and the gap before the next chapter title is release; in tactics, a hard board is tension and the next board's opening is release; in runner, hazard stretches are tension and open views at checkpoints are release. Plan release points as deliberately as peaks.
nodes.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

nodes.title: Place the climax in the last 20 percent
nodes.text: The climax should come near the end, after the player has learned everything it tests: the boss after the last chapter, the final board with the king or the most guards, the last checkpoint stretch before the portal. In MR, stage it where spectators can see it. Keep one short beat after it (the portal, the score) so it lands.
nodes.source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

nodes.title: An ending feels earned when it uses what was learned
nodes.text: Endings feel earned when the final challenge combines skills the player built and the story pays off the opening promise. Make the last chapter mix the enemy kinds already met, the last board use the hardest piece the player already knows, and the last checkpoint label answer the intro story ("Return the lantern to the temple"). Reaching the portal or defeating the boss then means something.

nodes.title: Fill the 8 formal elements before options
nodes.text: Fullerton lists the formal elements every game has: players, objectives, procedures, rules, resources, conflict, boundaries and outcome. For a vague brief, check each one and fill the gaps with explicit defaults: players from group_size, objective from the genre, procedures from the native loop, boundaries from the venue size. If a missing element would change the options, ask; otherwise default and say so.

nodes.title: Defaults for players and objectives
nodes.text: Players: in MR under 4 x 4 m, 1-2 at once; 4-10 m, 1-4; over 10 m, up to 6. Interaction pattern follows play_mode: solo, race (multilateral competition on separate copies) or together (shared floor). Objective by genre: battle is defeat the boss after the chapters, tactics is capture targets in order on each board, runner is reach the portal after all checkpoints. Reframe the objective with story but keep the underlying form.

nodes.title: Procedures are what players do, rules are what limits them
nodes.text: Procedures are the actions (walk, swing, step out of rings, move as a piece). Rules limit them and define consequences (a hazard sends you back, a guard's attacked square is forbidden, targets must be taken in order). In the rules list, write the 2-4 limits a player could not guess from the scene, in the player's language, and skip procedures they learn by doing.

nodes.title: Resources and boundaries in a walking game
nodes.text: Resources are what players manage: time (time limit, time bonus), health in battle, position and safe squares in tactics, and score. Boundaries are the edges of play: in MR the real floor minus 0.6 m from its edge, which also sets how many checkpoints fit (small rooms 3-6, medium 4-8, large 4-10). Name the scarce resource in each option; if nothing is scarce, there is no tension.

nodes.title: Define conflict and outcome explicitly
nodes.text: Conflict is what stops the player reaching the goal: enemies and rain in battle, guards and cracks in tactics, hazards and the clock in runner. Outcome is how it ends: win or lose, or a ranked score. Single-player walks with no conflict are tours, which is fine for submission but say so. Ranked outcomes (score, time) suit races; win or lose suits battle.

nodes.title: Make options differ on at least 2 of 4 axes
nodes.text: Each option sits on four axes: aesthetic (main MDA feeling), loop (explore, collect, race, story, escape, tour, dodge), social (solo, race, together) and route (loop, spiral, zigzag, lanes, hub, out-and-back). Any two options must differ on at least 2 axes and must use different genres. Choose the axis values first, then write the option, so difference is designed in rather than hoped for.

nodes.title: Avoid 3 skins of one idea
nodes.text: Design fixation makes designers repeat the first idea with surface changes, such as the same course themed as jungle, space and candy. These are not real options because the creator's decision does not change the game. A real choice changes what the player does, how it feels, or who they play with. If the core loops read the same with theme words removed, rewrite.

nodes.title: Score options honestly and use the whole scale
nodes.text: Scores (fun, mr_fit, players_fit, buildability, 1-5) are only useful if they differ and are tied to brief facts. A 5 means nothing to improve; most options should have at least one 3 or below. Each score_why must cite a fact (floor size, light, player age). Set confidence to low when the option depends on something untested, such as void floor with newcomers.

nodes.title: Recommend the option that serves the primary feeling and the players
nodes.text: Recommend the option that best serves the brief's top feeling for the stated players in the real venue, not the most ambitious one. Tie-breaks: fits the venue and light better, safer for the least experienced player, simpler to build well. Say in one sentence which brief fact decided it. The creator chooses first, so the recommendation is a mirror, not a command.

nodes.title: Span the risk range: one safe, one bold
nodes.text: A good set of 3 options spans risk: one safe option that clearly fits the brief, one bold option that stretches it (an unusual genre for the theme, a void floor, a race for a calm brief), and one in between. The bold option makes the creator think and often improves the final choice even when not picked. Mark the bold option's confidence honestly.

nodes.title: A 1-minute session
nodes.text: One minute suits queues, booths and young kids. Use a runner with 4 checkpoints close together, or a battle with 3 short chapters of 2-3 grunts plus a boss; tactics needs more time per board, so use only 3 boards with 2 targets and 0-1 guard. The intro card must be 1-2 sentences. Consider timeLimit 60 s for a race.

nodes.title: A 3-minute session
nodes.text: Three minutes is the default for events and first-time VR. Runner: 5-6 checkpoints with 2-4 hazards. Battle: 3-4 chapters with the boss. Tactics: 3-4 boards. There is room for one climax and one breather. For a race, timeLimit around 180 s gives a time bonus target.

nodes.title: A 5-minute session
nodes.text: Five minutes fits a full arc with a sawtooth curve. Runner: 6-8 checkpoints in a medium or large space with a story told through every label. Battle: 4-5 chapters with rain introduced mid-way. Tactics: 4-5 boards with 2 piece changes. Headset comfort is fine at this length for most players.

nodes.title: A 10-minute session
nodes.text: Ten minutes is long for walking MR: fatigue, battery and headset comfort matter, and seniors or kids may tire. Use the maximum stages (6 chapters or boards, 8-10 checkpoints only in a large space), add clear release beats, and keep the climax near minute 8. On PC this length is comfortable. If the space is small, warn that a long walk will loop repeatedly.

nodes.title: Replay through time attack and the leaderboard
nodes.text: The cheapest replay value is improvement: a fixed course and a clock. The runner time bonus and the tactics time race with a leaderboard both give players a reason to try again and beat their own time or a friend's. Keep the course short (1-3 minutes) so a retry costs little, and show the leaderboard where the queue can see it.

nodes.title: Replay through variety across stages
nodes.text: When players should come back for more content rather than a better time, vary the stages: different pieces and guard layouts across tactics boards, different enemy mixes and rain across battle chapters, varied views and vignettes along a runner route. Variety within one session also keeps first-time play fresh. Persistent unlocks are not available, so variety must live inside the game.

nodes.title: Design means turning open questions into decided facts
nodes.text: Every brief field starts as unknown, and the interview exists to move as many fields as possible to decided before options are proposed. A field is decided when the engine could act on it without guessing: a number of metres, a play mode, a list of MDA feelings, a lighting preset. Treat each question as buying certainty on the field that would change the design most. Whatever is still open at the end must be written down as an assumption, not hidden.

nodes.title: Ask the question whose answer splits the options most
nodes.text: The best next question is the one where different answers would lead to clearly different game concepts. Platform and MR floor size split everything (genre list, route, player count), so they come first. Player age splits theme and difficulty. Colour preference or checkpoint names rarely change the concept, so do not spend a question on them. If every plausible answer leads to the same 3 options, skip the question and use a default.

nodes.title: Spend the 4-7 question budget on facts that cannot be defaulted
nodes.text: Treat the interview as a budget: about 4-7 questions, never more than 9. Platform, players, feelings and (MR) floor size each need a question unless already answered; that is usually 4-5. The 1-3 remaining questions go to whichever optional field has no safe default for this creator, such as spectators at an event or brand rules for a sponsor. Session length, lighting and difficulty almost always fall back to defaults instead.

nodes.title: One question per turn, with one decision inside it
nodes.text: Each turn asks exactly one question so the creator can answer by tapping a choice. Combining 'how many players and how old' makes choices impossible to list and answers hard to read. If two facts form one measurement, such as floor width and depth, ask them together with size choices like '3 x 3 m', '5 x 5 m', '10 x 10 m or more'.

nodes.title: Give 3-6 choices that are distinct and cover the likely answers
nodes.text: Tappable choices are the main way novice creators answer, so they must be distinct and together cover most real answers. Each choice should lead to a different design, otherwise merge them. Include a middle choice and, when a default exists, a 'not sure, pick for me' choice. The creator can still type freely, so the list does not need to be exhaustive.

nodes.title: Use multi-select only when several answers can be true at once
nodes.text: Set multi to true for feelings (top 1-3 MDA aesthetics), surroundings and constraints, because several can apply together. Set multi to false for platform, floor size, play mode, session length and age band, because one answer drives the design. For feelings, say 'pick up to 3' in the question, since picking all 8 tells you nothing.

nodes.title: The why-line teaches one design idea in one sentence
nodes.text: Each question carries a one-line why that tells the creator what the answer will change, so they learn how designers think. Good why-lines name a consequence: 'Floor size decides how many checkpoints fit and whether a race is safe.' Bad why-lines restate the question or flatter. Over 5 questions the creator should learn that space, players and feelings drive a design.

nodes.title: Never ask for names, schools, photos, phone numbers or addresses
nodes.text: Many creators are children or teachers, and personal data is not needed to design a game. Ask for age bands and group types ('7-10 year olds', 'a school class of 30'), never a school or child's name. If the creator volunteers personal details, do not copy them into the brief; keep only the design fact. Describe a venue by kind and size ('a classroom 8 x 6 m'), not its address.

nodes.title: Stop asking once platform, concept, players, feelings and the MR floor are decided
nodes.text: The interview is done when platform, concept, players, feelings and, for MR, floor size and indoor or outdoor are known. Session length, play mode, lighting and constraints may be defaulted. Continuing past this point costs patience and rarely changes the 3 options. A good interview ends in 4-7 questions; at 9 you must stop and default the rest.

nodes.title: Read the brief back in 2-3 sentences that expose assumptions
nodes.text: The summary is the last cheap chance to catch a misunderstanding. Restate what the creator said in their words, then name what you assumed, for example 'I assumed about 3 minutes per play and a solo game; tell me if you want a race.' A creator corrects a wrong assumption far more easily when it is named than when it is buried. Keep it short so it is actually read.

nodes.title: 'Make it fun' or 'สนุกๆ' means the feelings are still unknown
nodes.text: 'Fun' is not a design goal because every MDA aesthetic is fun to someone. Treat it as an empty feelings field and ask which kind of fun with plain choices: 'a hard challenge', 'a story', 'exploring and finding secrets', 'racing friends', 'relaxing and easy'. Ask for the top 1-3. Different picks lead to different genres, so this question has high value.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA; Koster, A Theory of Fun

nodes.title: Missing group size: ask how many play at the same time
nodes.text: Group size decides play mode (solo, race, together), route width and, in MR, whether the floor is big enough. Creators often say 'kids' or 'my friends' without a number, or confuse total visitors with players at once. Ask 'How many people play at the same time?' with choices 1, 2, 3-4, 5-6. For events, total visitors affect session length, not group size.

nodes.title: MR floor size is never guessed: ask in metres or paces
nodes.text: In MR the empty floor is the whole game board; its size decides genre (under 3 x 3 m only runner fits), checkpoint count and player count. Ask for the width and depth of the empty floor, not the whole room. Offer choices like 'small room 3 x 3 m', 'classroom 6 x 8 m', 'hall 10 x 10 m or more', and accept paces (1 pace is about 0.75 m). If the creator does not know, ask them to pace it.

nodes.title: Scary but for 5-year-olds: offer spooky-cute, not fear
nodes.text: A wish for 'scary' with players under about 8 is a conflict between feeling and audience. Resolve it toward the audience: a spooky-cute theme (friendly ghosts, glowing lanterns, cartoon pumpkins), evening rather than spooky lighting, no sudden scares, and labels that make the child the brave hero. Name the trade-off openly and offer a slightly spookier option for older siblings.
nodes.source: Meta VR comfort and MR design guidelines; design practice

nodes.title: Relaxing but challenging: shape the session, do not average it
nodes.text: When a creator picks both submission and challenge, medium difficulty everywhere often satisfies neither. Give a calm opening and a harder ending, or let one of the three options lean each way. In a runner, the first 3 checkpoints can be hazard-free and the last 2 dense with hazards and a time bonus. Ask which feeling should win if only one could.

nodes.title: A race wish in a small MR room: offer timed turns with a leaderboard
nodes.text: Several players walking fast in under 4 x 4 m is unsafe, but the feeling behind a race is usually competition, not a shared floor. Offer the online race where each player walks their own copy, one at a time in the room, with a live leaderboard on a screen for friends watching. It keeps competition and fellowship while only one person walks.
nodes.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; FortalLand engine

nodes.title: Shooting wish: offer the sword arena or a dodge course
nodes.text: No genre can shoot. When a creator asks for guns, blasters or shooting, look for the feeling underneath: action and power. Offer battle, where in MR the right controller is the sword and enemies walk in from the edges, or a runner where hazards are 'laser beams' to dodge. Say clearly 'there is no shooting, but you can slash with a sword', so the creator is not surprised later.

nodes.title: NPC conversation wish: tell the story through the intro card and checkpoint labels
nodes.text: There are no NPC conversations or dialogue choices. A creator who wants to 'talk to the villagers' usually wants narrative. Offer the story on the intro card, checkpoint labels written as story beats ('Wake the old monk', 'Return the lantern'), and a character model placed at each checkpoint as a silent storyteller. State the limit and the alternative in one line.

nodes.title: Inventory or crafting wish: turn collecting into ordered checkpoints
nodes.text: The engine has no inventory and no crafting. 'Collect ingredients and cook' becomes checkpoints touched in order with labels like 'Pick the mango', 'Grab the sticky rice', 'Cook at the stove', and the +100 per checkpoint shows progress. Be honest that items are not held or combined; the labels tell it.

nodes.title: Flying, driving or joystick movement in MR: the player walks
nodes.text: In MR players move only with their own legs. A wish to fly a dragon can become a void floor with scenery far below so walking feels like gliding above it; driving can become a racetrack walked on foot. Mention comfort: void floors are dramatic and dizzy, so avoid them for first-time VR players and young kids. If free movement is essential, suggest the PC platform.
nodes.source: Meta VR comfort guidelines; FortalLand engine

nodes.title: Voice chat or team messaging: use the shared floor and the real room
nodes.text: There is no voice chat or in-game messaging. In MR players share the real room, so they can simply talk and point, and the shared floor mode shows each other's avatars. For players in different places, offer a race with a live leaderboard. Fellowship then comes from real people nearby, which MR does better than chat.

nodes.title: Players building or decorating during play: put expression elsewhere
nodes.text: Players cannot place objects or build during play. Expression can come from tactics boards where players plan their own path, from chasing a personal best on a leaderboard, or from the creator designing the land itself. If the creator is a kid who wants to build, point out that they are the builder: the game they design is their creation.

nodes.title: Hidden assumption: spectators can see the game
nodes.text: Creators often imagine parents watching the dragon, but in MR people outside the headset see only bodies walking and reacting. Surface this when spectators are mentioned and plan for it: a leaderboard on a wall screen, a key dodge near the audience side, and the finish portal where the crowd can cheer. Write the spectator plan into the brief.

nodes.title: Hidden assumption: a dark theme will look dark outdoors at noon
nodes.text: Creators picture night or neon themes but plan to play in a sunny garden. Passthrough shows real daylight, which washes out glow and dark scenes. When the theme is dark and the venue is outdoors, ask the time of day. In daytime, offer a bright version of the theme (sunny temple fair instead of haunted temple) or suggest playing indoors or after dark.
nodes.source: FortalLand engine; Meta MR design guidelines

nodes.title: Hidden assumption: the whole room is empty floor
nodes.text: People give the room size, not the empty floor. A 5 x 5 m living room with a sofa and table may have only 3 x 3 m clear. After size, ask about obstacles with choices like 'nothing inside', 'a table or sofa', 'a pillar', 'trees'. Write obstacles into the brief and keep the 1.2 m walking route and 0.6 m edge margin around them.
nodes.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; FortalLand engine

nodes.title: Hidden assumption: the creator is the player
nodes.text: A creator describing what they like may be designing for someone else entirely: a parent for a 6-year-old, a teacher for a class, an organiser for strangers. Before feelings, make sure you know who plays; if the creator says 'I love hard games' but players are first-time families, design for the families and mention the gap. If the creator is the player, preferences and audience are the same and one question is saved.

nodes.title: 'Adventure' or 'ผจญภัย': story, exploring, or danger
nodes.text: 'Adventure' can mean a story journey (narrative: a quest told through checkpoint labels), exploring a world (discovery: hub and spokes, hidden scenery), or facing danger (challenge: hazards, or chapters and a boss in battle). Ask 'What is the best moment of the adventure?' with choices 'finding secret places', 'a story with an ending', 'beating a big monster'. That single answer picks the genre lean.

nodes.title: 'Challenge' or 'ท้าทาย': body skill, speed, or thinking
nodes.text: A challenge can be body skill (battle: stepping out of red rings, slashing enemies), speed (a timed runner with a leaderboard), or thinking (a tactics board solved in order while avoiding guards). Ask 'What should be hard?' with choices 'moving and dodging', 'beating the clock or friends', 'figuring out the right path'. Each answer points to a different genre.

nodes.title: 'Cute' or 'น่ารัก': the look, the mood, or easy play
nodes.text: 'Cute' can describe the art (candy, toys, round animals, pastel palette), the mood (gentle, nothing scary), or a hidden request for easy play for small kids. Ask 'Cute like...?' with choices 'candy and toys', 'baby animals and farm', 'soft and easy to play'. The art reading changes theme only; the easy reading changes hazards and session length, so it matters which one.

nodes.title: 'Epic' or 'อลังการ': scale, a boss climax, or spectacle
nodes.text: 'Epic' usually means big scale (huge scenery models, a long route, the void floor drop), a climax (battle chapters ending in a boss), or wow visuals (dramatic lighting). Ask 'What makes it epic for you?' with choices 'giant monsters and places', 'a big final boss', 'wow light and views'. Check the venue: void floors and night lighting need indoor or dark conditions and experienced players.

nodes.title: 'Exciting' or 'ตื่นเต้น': speed, suspense, or surprise
nodes.text: Excitement can come from speed (time limit, race, dense hazards), suspense (spooky lighting, a slow approach to a boss), or surprise (scenery revealed around corners). Ask 'Exciting like...?' with choices 'racing the clock', 'creepy and tense', 'surprises around every corner'. In MR there are no sudden scares that make people run, so suspense must stay walkable.
nodes.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; design practice

nodes.title: 'Scary' or 'น่ากลัว': spooky-fun, tense, or real horror
nodes.text: Ask how scary with choices 'spooky but fun', 'creepy and tense', 'really scary (teens and adults only)'. The answer sets lighting (evening, spooky or night), which ghost models are used, and whether hazards are framed as threats. Combine with age: real horror is only for teens and adults, and even then no sudden scares in MR because players may run.
nodes.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; design practice

nodes.title: 'Easy' or 'ง่ายๆ': easy to play, easy to understand, or quick to make
nodes.text: 'Easy' can mean low difficulty (few hazards, no time limit), rules a first-timer understands in 10 seconds, or a quick project for the creator. Ask 'Easy for whom?' with choices 'players who never used VR', 'very young kids', 'I want to finish quickly'. Difficulty readings change hazards; the quick-project reading suggests fewer checkpoints and a simple loop.

nodes.title: 'Like Minecraft' or 'like Roblox': find which part they mean
nodes.text: Naming a famous game is a shortcut, not a spec, and those games use mechanics the engine lacks (building, shooting, open worlds). Ask 'What part of it do you love most?' with choices tied to buildable features: 'the blocky look', 'racing friends', 'exploring', 'fighting monsters'. Never copy names, characters or logos; borrow the feeling and a theme family.

nodes.title: 'Educational' or 'ได้ความรู้' / 'สื่อการสอน': facts, a sequence, or planning skill
nodes.text: Teachers ask for learning games. Readings: facts shown at checkpoint labels and the intro card, a process walked in order such as the water cycle (checkpoints as steps), or logical thinking (tactics boards). Ask 'What should students remember or be able to do?' with choices 'some facts', 'steps in the right order', 'think and plan'.

nodes.title: 'Thai style' or 'แบบไทยๆ': temple, village, folklore, or festival
nodes.text: Thai style can mean temple and palace architecture, village and farm life, folklore and ghosts, or festivals like Loy Krathong and Songkran. Ask 'Which Thai world?' with those four choices. Each picks a different model set and mood, and temples and ghosts bring cultural care rules.

nodes.title: 'Wow' or 'ว้าว' is sensation: views, light, or scale
nodes.text: A creator wanting wow wants the sensation aesthetic. The engine delivers it through scale (huge scenery), light (neon, evening, night presets) and the void floor drop. Ask 'What should make players say wow?' with choices 'a huge creature or building', 'glowing lights', 'the floor dropping away'. Check light conditions: glow needs indoors or night.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA; design practice

nodes.title: 'Play together' or 'เล่นด้วยกัน': race, shared floor, or taking turns
nodes.text: Together can mean competing (online race with a leaderboard), sharing one space and seeing each other (shared floor with avatars), or a family taking turns while the others watch. Ask 'How should they play together?' with choices 'race each other', 'walk the same world at once', 'take turns and cheer'. The answer sets play_mode and safety spacing.

nodes.title: Default session length: 3 minutes at events, 5 at home or in class
nodes.text: If session length is not given, use about 3 minutes for events and pop-ups where a queue waits, and 5 minutes for homes, classrooms and private play. First-time VR players and kids under 8 do best with short headset sessions. State it: 'I assumed about 3 minutes so the queue keeps moving; tell me if players can stay longer.'
nodes.source: Meta VR comfort guidelines; design practice

nodes.title: Default play mode follows group size and floor size
nodes.text: If play mode is unknown: one player means solo; 2-4 players on an MR floor over 4 x 4 m means together (shared floor), or race if challenge was picked with fellowship; any group on a floor under 4 x 4 m means solo turns with a leaderboard. On PC, solo unless friends were mentioned. State the choice so the creator can switch it.

nodes.title: Default lighting: match the real light, not the theme wish
nodes.text: If lighting was not discussed, choose from the venue: outdoors in daytime use noon or morning, indoors with steady light use default or studio, an indoor dark hall or evening event can use spooky, neon or night. Mention it only if it conflicts with the theme. On PC, pick the preset that best fits the theme mood.

nodes.title: Default difficulty: gentle start, one harder peak
nodes.text: When difficulty is not specified, assume first-timers: the first 1-2 checkpoints or the first chapter have no hazards, hazards are spaced so a walking adult can step around them, and one climax is harder. For gamers or teens who picked challenge, raise hazard density and add a time limit. State 'I made it gentle at first; it is easy to make harder later.'

nodes.title: Default constraints: comfort and safety rules always apply
nodes.text: If the creator lists no constraints, still write the standing ones into the brief: no sudden scares, a clear 1.2 m route, 0.6 m from the edge, nothing that needs looking up while walking fast, and no void floor for first-time players unless asked. Add age-based ones such as no real horror under 13. The creator should not have to ask for safety.
nodes.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; FortalLand engine

nodes.title: Default VR experience: first-time for public, schools and families
nodes.text: If VR experience was not asked, assume first-time for events, schools, families and seniors, and some experience only for gamers or a creator who owns a Quest. First-time means short sessions, simple rules and no void floor. It is a safe default because experienced players still enjoy a clear game, while beginners suffer in a hard one.

nodes.title: Missing concept: propose a theme from feelings and players, not a blank
nodes.text: Some creators know who plays and how it should feel but have no theme ('anything is fine'). Do not spend more questions; pick 3 different themes from the model library that suit the players and feelings and let each option carry one. The option pick then resolves the theme. Say the themes were AI suggestions.

nodes.title: Never default the platform
nodes.text: MR and PC are different games: MR needs a real floor, walking and passthrough rules; PC has mouse and keyboard and no room. Guessing wrong wastes the whole design. If the creator has not said, ask in the first or second question with choices 'Quest headset walking a real floor', 'computer game', 'not sure'. If 'not sure', explain the difference in one line and ask again.

nodes.title: Never default MR floor size, indoor or outdoor, or obstacles
nodes.text: Real-space facts are safety facts: a guessed size can place a route through a wall or a table. Width, depth and indoor must come from the creator, and obstacles must be asked, with 'nothing inside' as a choice. If the creator cannot answer now, keep the brief open and say the game cannot be laid out until they measure or pace it.
nodes.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; FortalLand engine

nodes.title: State each assumption as value, reason and how to change it
nodes.text: Assumptions are only useful if the creator can see and override them. Use one short form: 'I assumed 3 minutes because it is an event; tell me if players can stay longer.' Put it in the summary and repeat key ones in the prototype flow. Never present an assumption as something the creator said.

nodes.title: Track who decided each item: said, chose, inferred, or assumed
nodes.text: Each brief value has a source: the creator said it in their own words, the creator chose it from offered choices, the AI inferred it from a card or a related answer, or the AI assumed a default. Said values are firmest; chosen values are firm but shaped by the choice list; inferred and assumed values must be shown back for confirmation. Never overwrite a said value with an inference.

nodes.title: Confidence: high when stated, medium when inferred, low when assumed
nodes.text: Use three levels. High: the creator stated or chose it and it fits the rest. Medium: inferred from a strong clue (a school class implies 7-12 year olds and many players). Low: a default with no clue. Option confidence should drop when key fields are low, and low fields are the first things to check in the prototype test_questions.

nodes.title: Infer a field only from a strong clue, and say so
nodes.text: Some answers imply others: 'my 6-year-old's birthday party' implies kids, families, first-time VR and watching parents. Fill these in as inferred and mention them in the next why-line or the summary instead of asking separately. Do not infer from weak clues, such as guessing age from a theme; adults love dinosaurs too.

nodes.title: Each option names the assumption it depends on most
nodes.text: If an option only works under an assumed fact, say so in its risks: 'Assumes 4 players at once; with 6 the route gets crowded.' The creator then picks with eyes open and sees which uncertainty matters. Options built on firm facts can carry higher confidence.

nodes.title: Show remaining assumptions inside the prototype so comments can fix them
nodes.text: The prototype is where the creator sees the game, so remaining uncertainty should be visible there: the assumed session length in the flow ('0:00' to '3:00'), the assumed play mode in the HUD (leaderboard or not), and the riskiest assumption in test_questions. A creator who sees a 3:00 finish will say if they wanted 10 minutes.

nodes.title: Leave low-stakes uncertainty for prototype comments
nodes.text: Not everything must be settled in the interview. Cosmetic choices (palette, checkpoint names, music mood, exact theme details) are cheaper to settle by showing a prototype and letting the creator react, and reactions to a picture are more reliable than answers to abstract questions. Keep the interview for facts that change the genre or the safety of the layout.
nodes.source: Fullerton, Game Design Workshop; design practice

nodes.title: The creator decides; the AI mirrors and recommends
nodes.text: The AI proposes and argues but never overrides a creator decision except for safety and engine limits. If the creator picks the option the AI scored lower, build it well. If a choice conflicts with safety (6 walkers in a small room), explain once, offer the safe version, then follow their decision within what is safe.

nodes.title: When revising, say what changed and what stayed
nodes.text: After a creator comment, the revised prototype should say in one line what changed and confirm what was kept: 'Made the boss bigger and the lighting neon; kept the route, story and 3-minute flow.' This keeps decisions traceable and reassures the creator that unmentioned parts were not lost.

nodes.title: For an impossible wish, find the feeling and offer the closest buildable thing
nodes.text: Every impossible request hides a feeling: shooting means power and action, flying means freedom and wow, NPC chat means story. Name the limit in one line, then offer 1-2 buildable ways to reach the same feeling. The creator keeps the heart of their idea, and trust grows because nothing is promised that cannot be built.
nodes.source: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek 2004, MDA; design practice

nodes.title: When wishes conflict, resolve in order: safety, audience, venue, feeling, theme
nodes.text: Safety rules always win, then the audience's needs (age, VR experience), then what the real venue allows (size, light), then the chosen feelings, then theme details. Example: a neon theme in an outdoor noon garden for kids keeps the kids safe, uses a daylight version of the theme, and keeps the feeling. Explain which wish bent so the creator can change it.

nodes.title: Many players, small floor: rotate players, never shrink safety margins
nodes.text: A class of 30 with a 4 x 4 m clear floor cannot have everyone walking. Offer 1-2 players at a time, 2-3 minute sessions, and the rest watching a leaderboard or cheering. Do not shrink the 1.2 m route or the 0.6 m edge margin to fit more people.

nodes.title: A long story in a 3-minute session: tell it in 5 beats
nodes.text: Creators sometimes want an epic saga for an event booth. Compress it: a 2-4 sentence intro card, 5-7 checkpoint labels as story beats, and a finish that pays off the setup. Offer a longer home version with 8-10 checkpoints if the story matters more than queue speed.

nodes.title: Do not hide uncertainty behind 3 skins of one idea
nodes.text: When the brief is thin, it is tempting to give three similar options. That hides the open question. Instead let each option take a different reading of the uncertain part (adventure as discovery, as narrative, as challenge), in 3 different genres. The creator's pick then resolves the uncertainty.

nodes.title: Brand wants the product everywhere, players want a game: one hero moment
nodes.text: Brand creators may ask for the product on every checkpoint. Too much placement turns a game into an ad and players disengage. Offer one hero moment (the product as the finish portal setting or the boss arena centrepiece) plus brand colours in the palette. Explain the trade-off and let the brand choose.

nodes.title: Novice creator: plain words, examples in choices, no jargon
nodes.text: Most creators have never designed a game. Use everyday words ('race friends', not 'fellowship'), put concrete examples inside choices, and keep why-lines short. Offer a 'pick for me' choice on non-safety questions. Novices answer pictures and examples better than abstract categories.
nodes.source: Fullerton, Game Design Workshop; design practice

nodes.title: Experienced creator: accept precise specs, ask only the gaps
nodes.text: A creator who speaks in mechanics and numbers ('6 checkpoints, 90 second limit, race mode') has already resolved much uncertainty. Accept their values, skip covered questions, and spend the rest on venue and audience facts they may have missed, often spectators and obstacles. Show trade-offs directly and use the terms they use.

nodes.title: Kid creator designing for themselves: short, playful, decisive
nodes.text: Children often design for themselves and friends. Keep questions very short, use playful choices, accept big imagination and map it to buildable pieces. For MR, phrase floor and safety questions so a grown-up can help ('Ask a grown-up to count steps across the room').

nodes.title: Teacher creator: ask the learning outcome and how the class rotates
nodes.text: Teachers need a game that teaches something and works for a whole class. The two most valuable questions are the learning outcome and how many play at once versus how many wait. Default short sessions (2-3 minutes) and a leaderboard or watching role for waiting students. Never ask about individual students.

nodes.title: Event organiser: queue speed, spectators and very few rules
nodes.text: Event and booth organisers care about queue speed, a game that explains itself in seconds, and something the crowd can watch. Default 2-3 minute sessions, 1-2 rules, a leaderboard on a screen, and key moments on the audience side. Ask visitors per hour only if session length is unclear.

nodes.title: Brand creator: ask brand rules once, early, and store them as constraints
nodes.text: A brand or sponsor brings rules: colours, product presence, words to avoid, audience age. Ask once for must-haves and must-nots with choices like 'brand colours', 'product appears in the game', 'no competitor themes', 'nothing scary'. Store them as constraints. Do not invent logos; scenery uses library models and the palette can follow brand colours.

nodes.title: Thai ghosts for kids: friendly versions only, and check first
nodes.text: Thai folk ghosts such as Krasue or Pret can genuinely frighten Thai children who grew up with the stories. For kids, use friendly cartoon versions, warm lighting, and story roles where the ghost is helped or befriended. Ask the creator whether ghosts are fine for these children before using them.

nodes.title: Temples and Buddha images: never hazards, enemies or things to step on
nodes.text: Temple themes are popular, but sacred items must be treated with respect. Never make a Buddha image, a monk or a sacred object a hazard, an enemy, or something on the walking floor that players step over. Use temples as backdrops and destinations, and keep Buddha images out of play unless the creator wants a respectful tour.

nodes.title: 'Make it cooler' or 'เท่กว่านี้': look, action, or scale
nodes.text: 'Cooler' usually means a stronger look (lighting, palette, hero scenery), more action (more hazards, a time limit, a tougher boss), or bigger scale (giant models, the void drop). Offer these three as quick choices, or change the one most likely from the chosen feelings and say which you changed.

nodes.title: 'Not very wow' or 'ไม่ค่อยว้าว': add one stronger reveal moment
nodes.text: This comment means sensation lacks a peak. Pick one moment, usually the climax panel or the finish portal, and make it bigger: a giant hero model revealed around a turn, a lighting change at the boss, or a void drop at the end for experienced players. Keep everything else and point to the changed panel.

nodes.title: 'Boring' or 'น่าเบื่อ': find whether pacing, choice or stakes is missing
nodes.text: Boredom has three common causes: nothing changes over time (pacing), the player has nothing to decide (choice), or nothing is at risk (stakes). Fix with a ramp of hazards across the session, a planning element such as a tactics board, or a time limit and leaderboard. If the comment is general, ask which part felt boring.
nodes.source: Koster, A Theory of Fun; design practice

nodes.title: 'Too hard' or 'ยากไป': lower one difficulty lever, not all
nodes.text: Difficulty has levers: hazard count and spacing, time limit, guard speed on a tactics board (keep 3 s or slower), enemy count per battle chapter. Lower the lever the comment points to, or the one that hurts first-timers most, usually the time limit. Keep the climax so the game still has a peak.

nodes.title: 'Make it more Thai': change scenery, labels and palette, keep mechanics
