nodes.text: This is a theme comment. Add or swap Thai library models (temples, village, festival props), Thai-flavoured checkpoint labels, and a palette with gold, red and deep green, and leave route, genre and rules untouched. Apply the temple respect rules.

nodes.title: Change what the comment names, keep everything it does not
nodes.text: A creator who comments on the boss did not ask to change the route, story or palette. Keep all unmentioned parts exactly, because they are implicitly approved. If a requested change forces another (a bigger boss arena needs more space), say so in one line.

nodes.title: Turn each comment into a concrete engine-level change
nodes.text: Map every comment to something the builder can do: a lighting preset, checkpoint count or labels, hazard count and placement, time limit, scenery models, play mode. 'More spooky' becomes spooky lighting and ghost lantern models; 'longer' becomes 2 more checkpoints and a 5-minute flow. Write the mapping so the creator sees exactly what will change.

nodes.title: If a comment has two very different readings, ask one quick question
nodes.text: Most comments can be applied with a stated interpretation, but some split badly: 'make it bigger' can mean bigger models or a longer route, which affects safety in MR. When readings lead to very different builds, ask one tappable question; when they are close, apply the likely one and say so.

nodes.title: Write test_questions from the biggest remaining uncertainty
nodes.text: The prototype's test_questions should target what is still uncertain, not what is known. If difficulty for 6-year-olds was assumed, ask 'Can a 6-year-old step out of the rings in time?' If daylight readability is a risk, ask 'Are the red hazards visible in afternoon sun?' This carries design as uncertainty reduction into real play.
nodes.source: Fullerton, Game Design Workshop; design practice

nodes.title: Ask feelings with plain, picture-like choices
nodes.text: Instead of MDA names, write choices like 'Wow, beautiful sights' (sensation), 'Be a hero or a monster' (fantasy), 'A story with an ending' (narrative), 'Hard, needs skill' (challenge), 'Play with friends' (fellowship), 'Find secrets' (discovery), 'Show off a high score' (expression), 'Relax, easy fun' (submission). Offer the 6 most relevant to the concept and ask for up to 3.

nodes.title: Ask age as bands that change the design
nodes.text: Use bands where design rules change: 'under 7', '7-12', 'teens', 'adults', 'mixed families', 'seniors'. Each band shifts scariness limits, hazard spacing, label length and session length. Do not ask exact ages or names.

nodes.title: Ask who watches and from where, with 'nobody' as a choice
nodes.text: In MR, spectators shape where key moments go. Ask 'Who watches from the side?' with choices 'parents', 'friends waiting their turn', 'passers-by', 'nobody'. If someone watches, ask or assume the side they stand on so the finish and a key dodge face them. Skip this on PC.

nodes.title: When the creator says 'not sure', default or narrow, never repeat
nodes.text: A 'not sure' or 'up to you' answer is information: the creator does not care strongly or lacks the knowledge. For defaultable fields, apply the default and state it. For required fields like MR floor size, narrow with familiar comparisons ('About a classroom? A living room? A badminton court?'). Never ask the identical question twice.

nodes.title: Read free-typed answers for several fields at once
nodes.text: Creators often type more than was asked: 'my class of 25 kids, in the gym after lunch'. Extract every field it covers (players, group size, venue, indoor, time of day) and skip those questions, then ask about the most valuable remaining gap. Confirm the extracted facts in the next why-line or the summary.

nodes.title: On PC, skip real-space questions and spend the budget on players and feelings
nodes.text: When the platform is PC there is no real room: floor size, indoor, obstacles, venue and spectator side are not asked and not set. Use the saved questions to sharpen the genre: what kind of challenge, how long, solo or with friends watching the screen.

nodes.title: Order questions so early answers prune later ones
nodes.text: Ask platform first because PC removes all space questions. Ask players before feelings because age limits what feelings fit (no real horror for 6-year-olds). Ask the MR floor before session and play mode because size caps players at once. A good order often lets the interview finish in 4-5 questions.

nodes.title: Worked example: 'a fun ghost game for my kid's party' resolved in 5 questions
nodes.text: Start (typed in Thai): 'a fun ghost game for my kid's birthday'. Inferred: kids, families, first-time VR, parents watching. Q1 platform: MR. Q2 age band: 5-7. Q3 how scary: 'spooky but fun' (resolves the conflict). Q4 floor: living room 4 x 5 m, with Q5 obstacles: a sofa on one side, so 4 x 3.5 m usable. Defaults stated: 3 minutes, solo turns with a leaderboard, evening lighting indoors, no sudden scares.

nodes.title: 'Fun for everyone' or 'เล่นได้ทุกวัย': mixed ages playing together, or a wide public audience
nodes.text: 'For everyone' can mean a family where a 6-year-old and a grandparent play the same session, or a public booth where any single visitor of any age walks in. For mixed groups, design the floor for the youngest and add an optional harder layer (time bonus, leaderboard) for older players. For a wide public, pick the safest settings: first-time VR, no void floor, 3 minutes, 1-2 rules. Ask 'Will different ages play at the same time, or one visitor at a time?'

nodes.title: 'มันส์' or 'action-packed': fighting, high pace, or head-to-head
nodes.text: The Thai word in the title means intense, energetic fun. It can mean constant action (battle with many grunts per chapter and falling warning rings), high pace with no pauses (a runner with a tight time limit and checkpoints close together), or the buzz of competing live (race mode with a leaderboard the crowd watches). Ask 'What makes it intense?' with choices 'slashing lots of enemies', 'non-stop rushing', 'beating friends'. In MR, intensity comes from density and timing, never from running.
nodes.source: Swink, Game Feel; Meta MR safety guidelines

nodes.title: 'Relaxing' or 'ชิลๆ': no pressure, beautiful stroll, or light easy goals
nodes.text: 'Chill' points to the submission aesthetic, but it can mean no failure pressure (no hazards, no time limit), a beautiful walk to look at (sensation: a scenic route with evening or morning light), or a small casual goal (touch 5 friendly checkpoints). Ask 'Chill like...?' with choices 'a pretty walk', 'easy goals, no losing', 'calm with a little surprise'. A tour or explore loop on the runner usually fits; battle rarely does.

nodes.title: 'Competitive' or 'แข่งกัน': live race, best time, or best score
nodes.text: Competition can be a live race against people in the room or online (race mode), a personal best against the clock (time limit plus leaderboard), or a score fight where fewer hazard hits wins (score: checkpoint +100, hazard -25). Ask 'Who do they compete against?' with choices 'each other at the same time', 'the clock', 'the high score of the day'. Tactics boards also race on time with a leaderboard.
nodes.source: Caillois 1961, Man, Play and Games (agon); FortalLand engine

nodes.title: 'With a story' or 'มีเรื่องราว': a goal with a reason, a journey of beats, or a twist
nodes.text: 'A story' can be light (a clear reason for the goal on the intro card: 'Return the lost lanterns'), a journey of beats (every checkpoint label is a story step leading to an ending), or a reveal (the finish or boss changes what the player thought). Ask 'How much story?' with choices 'just a reason to play', 'a story step at every stop', 'a surprise ending'. The engine tells stories only through the intro, labels, scenery and the finish.

nodes.title: 'Realistic' or 'สมจริง': the art is always stylized, so find what should feel real
nodes.text: Everything is stylized low-poly, flat shaded, so photoreal looks are not possible. 'Realistic' usually means believable scale (models at true 1:1 size, a house that is house-sized), real physical effort (walking the real floor in MR already gives this), or a real place or process (a local market, a real temple layout, the real order of steps). Say the style limit in one line, then ask which kind of real matters.

nodes.title: 'Like Pokemon', 'like Fortnite', 'like Roblox': borrow the feeling, never the IP
nodes.text: Famous franchise names point to a feeling: Pokemon to cute creatures and discovery, Fortnite to competing and bright action, Roblox to playful blocky worlds. The engine cannot copy their mechanics (no creature catching, no shooting, no building), and their characters, names and logos are owned by others. Ask what part they love, then offer original creatures from the model library, a race or battle for competition, and a bright toy-like theme. Write original names in the brief and prototype.

nodes.title: 'Something new' or 'แปลกใหม่': new place, new twist on the room, or new rule
nodes.text: Novelty can come from an unusual theme (an underwater temple, a candy volcano), from using the real space in a surprising way (the real walls as the edge of a cliff, the void floor under a classroom), or from an unusual combination of engine rules (a tactics board as a heist). Ask 'New in what way?' with choices 'a world nobody has seen', 'surprise the room itself', 'a twist in how you play'. Never solve novelty with mechanics the engine lacks.

nodes.title: 'Looks plain' or 'ดูธรรมดา': add a hero piece and contrast, not clutter
nodes.text: Plainness is usually a missing focal point or flat colour, not too few objects. Add one hero piece seen from the spawn (a giant statue, a dragon, a tower), raise palette contrast between the floor and the route, and group decor into 2-3 vignettes along the route. In MR, keep the 1.2 m route clear while adding. Say which of these you changed.

nodes.title: 'Make it scarier' or 'อยากให้น่ากลัวกว่านี้': darker mood and dread, within age and safety
nodes.text: First check the players: for kids, scarier should mean spookier, not frightening. Levers: lighting preset from evening to spooky or night (only indoors or after dark in MR), scarier Thai ghost or haunted models along the route, a darker palette, and story labels that build dread toward the finish. No sudden scares and nothing that makes players run.
nodes.source: Meta MR safety guidelines; FortalLand engine

nodes.title: 'The colours are not nice' or 'สีไม่สวย': ask which way, then change the palette only
nodes.text: Colour complaints can mean too dull, too loud, wrong mood, or not matching a brand. Offer 3-4 alternative palettes as tappable choices (warm, cool, pastel, high contrast), each with 4-6 named colours, or ask 'More bright, more soft, or more dark?'. Change only the palette and the lighting preset if needed; keep the route, story and scenery. In MR outdoors, keep enough contrast for sunlight.

nodes.title: 'Can kids play this?' or 'เด็กจะเล่นได้ไหม': answer with a checklist, then adjust
nodes.text: Treat this as a concern, not a change request. Check and report: rules fit in 1-2 short lines, checkpoint labels under about 5 words, hazards spaced for small steps, no time limit or a generous one, session 3 minutes or less for under-8s, no scary or void moments, and the route clear by 1.2 m. Fix any item that fails and say which ones, and add a playtest question like 'Can a 6-year-old finish without help?'
nodes.source: Meta VR comfort guidelines; design practice

nodes.title: 'Too long' or 'ยาวไป': cut checkpoints or chapters, keep the climax
nodes.text: Length comes from checkpoint count, route length, the time limit, and battle chapters. Cut from the middle: remove 1-2 middle checkpoints or one chapter, shorten the route, and keep the opening and the climax. Update the flow so the new session length is visible ('ends at 2:30'). If 'too long' meant the intro text, shorten the story to 2 sentences instead.

nodes.title: 'Confusing' or 'งงๆ': find whether the goal, the order, or the danger is unclear
nodes.text: Players get lost in three ways: they do not know the goal (fix the goal line and intro to one sentence), they do not know where to go next (fix checkpoint order with a clearer route shape and visible next stop), or they do not understand what hurts them (make hazards look like hazards and say so in the rules). Ask which part was confusing if unclear, and simplify rules to 1-3 lines.
